blocks.text: The Imperial Eulogy of Emperor Chongzhen on the Portrait of the Venerable Master Hanshan

inline.s: How
(so)

venerable was this old monk, and what a manner of life was his! He propped up the Dharma-gate and became its pillar and beam. He bore the hammer and tongs of the Son of Heaven, and stood as a model for Buddhas and patriarchs.
Inscribed with the imperial brush by Zhu Youjian, the seventeenth generation (with the imperial seal, reverently offered in the Court of the Nine-Lotus Bodhisattva within the palace).

blocks.text: Eulogy on the Portrait of the Venerable Kang Senghui, with a Preface, Sent to Master Hanshan

inline.s: The monk Zhenke (Zibai)
The Three Kingdoms were a gathering of heroes and also a gathering of weapons and armies; compassion and prajna had no way in. Yet our Patriarch Kang
(Kang Senghui)

crossed the river on a single staff, called on the Tathagata three times, and shed blood from both eyes, casting his relics into a vase whose radiance lit the six directions and whose grace has flowed through a thousand ages. At that time not one of the rulers and ministers of Wu but was moved in heart and changed in countenance: from the event they inferred the principle, and knew there was a Buddha and no longer doubted. When the six paramitas had been translated and the gate of anapana was opened, with no choosing between black and white, all gained the pure Dharma-eye. And those who entered the subtleties of Chan contemplation in numbers beyond reckoning were all made possible by our Patriarch as the whistling arrow that leads the way.

Now Master Hanshan Qing, because he spread the Dharma, was exiled to the miasmic seas, yet he skillfully used the samadhi of a compassionate heart to make withered bones put forth spring everywhere. The layman Shenghua, hearing of his manner and moved with admiration, specially painted a portrait of the Patriarch and sent it up to Caoxi, as a shadow and echo of the Master.

Alas! Wherever Caoxi's flesh-body Buddha has appeared, from Tang through Song, there has never been a generation lacking those who drank of Caoxi and gained the Way. Of late Caoxi has run dry, its jeweled grove desolate; and again, through Master Han's exile, it was made into a swelling wave, and Caoxi came back to life. Patriarch Kang's divided body, his skull opening its eye, is beyond the sands of the Ganges to number: how could anyone measure the depth or shallowness of his merit with a mind of discursive thought!
The man of the Way Daguan does not understand holding the helm against the wind, but only understands pushing the boat along with the current. And so he praised him, saying:

Patriarch Kang came to Wu; Lord Qing was banished to Yue. The Great Master of the Skull, the diamond eye bursts forth. The misery of the miasmic seas, bone-piercing, soul-startling: the Master gained his exile, and all the more we feel the imperial clarity.

The sorcery of Caoxi: all who drank of it perished. The Master drank of it, and dissolved every miasma. With his fingers he took up the relics: Patriarch Kang's greed. Yet that greed was not for himself. What shame could this heart feel?

For spreading the Dharma he incurred guilt, his life as slender as a single thread. Over a thousand li of miasmic peaks, his straw sandals trod them all. The road to Lei is high and steep, the hurricane at its height; bowl and vase pass on alone, yet the mark of his tongue is bright and clear.

The specters of southern Yue clap their hands in broad daylight. If I am without mind, I am the bodhisattva's shadow and echo. If with mind I answer them, then Patriarch Kang was a fool, and one who wears a scholar's cap into Yue: who would not doubt him?

At Shitou's parting, liver and diaphragm ran cold as ice. Young Ding blew up the fire and painted Patriarch Kang's portrait. From the painted shadow one gains the mind; mind gone, nature is dark. The great function is impermanent: the bell is heard with the eye.
Root and dust, host and guest, gathering and releasing, dream and waking: in his palm he holds up the jeweled stupa, on the summit of Laoshang.
(Master Da, by means of a eulogy on Patriarch Kang's portrait, praised Patriarch Han, and so the meaning is all the truer. The portrait's inscription is at Fayun Temple on the Five Teats Peak.)

blocks.text: Hanshan's Own Inscription, Written as He Neared Death, for the Portrait in the Shadow Hall at Caoxi

inline.s: Majestic and imposing, clear and profound. No city of walls or moats within, no cliffs or banks at all. His spirit covers heaven and earth, his eyes prop up the Milky Way. Adrift at the gate of present affairs, he never leaves the farther shore of Weiyin.

Whether as layman or as monk, a carrying pole never left his shoulder. If not a slave of the Buddhas and patriarchs, then surely a peddler in the field of enlightenment. Had he not entered the great smelting furnace, who would know he was a man of iron? He waits only for Maitreya to be born below before settling this weighty case.
(The original manuscript is at Hanshan Temple in Caoxi.)

blocks.text: Eulogy on the True Likeness of the Dharma-Patriarch Hanshan

inline.s: The monk Zhixu (Ouyi), dharma-heir by heart

A grand countenance, abundant spirit; firm courage, the great power. In empty samadhi he gathered his spirit; the light of the dawn had just cleared. His care was for the Dharma-gate: how could he reckon fortune or calamity? Lightning-flash and racing thunder: Deshan, Linji.

Working in secret, walking hidden: within the circle, the edge of the sea. Those who know him say he is a man who lifts the sky with one hand; those who know him not say he is a hero who covers the age. Who would think he must dwell neither in the school nor in the teaching, but between the teaching and the school at once, never passing away with the common run of the times?
(Master Xu
Master Ouyi
, whose style was Suhua. When he compiled this chronicle and its annotations, he happened to be hearing the Profound Meaning of the Surangama Sutra explained in the abbot's quarters at Kangju.)

blocks.text: Eulogy on the Portrait of My Root Master Hanshan

inline.s: (Tan Zhenmo (Saohan), a disciple who took refuge)

Our flesh-body patriarch, the root Master Hanshan, was a master of the school at Cishou in Yan and an heir-patriarch of Caoxi in Yue. His flesh body stands like a tripod, and the palm-leaf scriptures' lamp blazes. Among the Chan monks who have come to the fore in recent times, who could bear to be likened to a ten-thousandth part of him? Yet sun and moon both set, and no light is greater; and the single eye amid the dust of the world is hard to open when dimmed and eclipsed. Had his course not been made bright and handed down, who would know how heaven and earth are embraced? The Minister of the Court at Haiyu inscribed the Five Teats, yet could not avoid hearsay and variant reports. The disciples of Zizhu transmitted his restoration, yet still fell short of following him and receiving his teaching in person. His body was wrapped in sandalwood; apart from the stupa, what inscription is there? Now the chronicle is complete as a book, tallying exactly with the biography. Though the roads of the sea courts are perilous and distant, the man of the Way far away flies his letters without feet; and by the spiritual power of Yu Ridge, the disciple Sao bows in incense and has it carved and spread abroad. Humbly reading the Chan Master Yongming Zhijue's Records of the Mirror of the School, I find: "Awakening to the mind makes one a patriarch; thus the former sages handed it down one to another." Hence the First Patriarch Bodhidharma said: "To understand the Buddha's mind-school without the least error, with practice and understanding corresponding, is what is called a patriarch." And his verse says: "He does not look on evil and give rise to aversion, nor look on good and labor to cultivate it; he does not cast off the foolish to draw near the worthy, nor abandon delusion to reach awakening. He penetrates the great Way beyond measure, comprehends the Buddha-mind beyond degree. He does not share the same track as the ordinary and the sage: transcendent, he is named a patriarch." Fuzheng, having obtained these words, finds that they correspond exactly, first and last, with the meaning of our Master's title of patriarch at Baolin; and that they tally besides with Master Da's eulogy of the Caoxi flesh-body patriarch. Therefore he proposes to style him "the Caoxi-restoring flesh-body heir-patriarch, the Venerable Master Hanshan." Reverently composing a eulogy on his dharma-image, he says:
Manifesting as Buddha, manifesting as patriarch, heir of the school, heir of the teaching. He received Caoxi's robe and wrote out the Lankavatara's radiance.
Dragon Gate and Sea Seal, Qingliang's vital wonder. Through kalpas his flesh body endures: one body, two places reached at once.
In the eighth year of Shunzhi, the year xinmao, on the third day of the third month, the annotations to the chronicle were completed. Reverently recorded by Fuzheng.

blocks.text: Inscription on Master Hanshan's Handscroll of Six Poems

inline.s: In the eleventh year of the Republic, the year renxu, Li Guosong requested an inscription on the Master's handscroll of six poems, and so I wrote this, which was then included in the Collected Writings. It is appended here especially, to express my admiration. Reverently recorded by the monk Yinguang.

Master Hanshan was a great sovereign's manifestation. Deep was his merit in spreading the Dharma; the envious framed him with slander. He was exiled to Guangzhou, to guard against disaster and disorder. Happily there were great officials who looked on him with different eyes.

Spreading the Dharma at Caoxi, he continued the broken thread of the wisdom-life. Teaching according to circumstance, he scattered the great abuses. He protected the state and brought peace to the people; his merit towered over that of the great ministers. After his death his flesh body remains, undecayed and unchanged.

When Yue and Gan contended, he returned to the banks of Caoxi. The Sixth Patriarch and the Seventh Patriarch are made known in the proverbs of the time. He added luster to the Buddha-sun and served as the moat of the Dharma-city. His writings are vast and broad, bright as sun and moon.

In the Great Treasury's circulation, alas, only half is missing. Much has been lost, though now and then it reappears. The six wondrous verses, their brushwork vigorous and strong; their meaning transcends the wondrous: the more one reads, the more they shine.

More than three hundred years, and happily nothing is lacking. A son of the Buddha who perceived the truth obtained them in a shop in Shanghai. Wishing to display the great plan, he specially made a handscroll and asked me for an inscription, to make the Dharma-model known.
And so I have briefly set out the general outline, in the hope that later sages may hear and see it.

blocks.text: Preface to the Printed and Circulated Edition of the Annotations to Master Hanshan's Chronicle

inline.s: (In the twenty-third year of the Republic, the year jiaxu, on an auspicious day of the first month, sent to press.)

Mencius said: "In poverty, one cultivates one's own person alone; in success, one benefits all under heaven." This is spoken with regard to worldly dharmas. If we speak with regard to the Buddha-dharma, then in success one can certainly benefit others, and in poverty one can benefit others as well. Strictly upholding the precepts, earnestly fulfilling human relations, leading others by one's own person, and causing all people to look on one another and become good: when their joyful longing heart has arisen, then one shows them the principle and the practice of the three periods of cause and effect and the six paths of rebirth. The mind is originally Buddha; through Buddha-recitation one is reborn in the Pure Land: only thus may one personally realize it. What person with a heart would not gladly follow? Therefore the eminent monks of old, wherever they went, were in most cases taken as refuge. Compared with the teaching of royal government, the benefit is deeper.

In the late Ming, the royal order was not upheld and the great ministers had no authority; those who held real power were all ignorant, uncomprehending eunuchs. The treacherous and wicked relied on their power to work mischief, while the well-meaning had no wisdom with which to devise remedies; and so the people were distressed and the state endangered, past all cure. Hanshan, Zibai, Lianchi, and Miaofeng all came forth into the world at this time, and their hidden support of the way of governance and their secret protection of the people's livelihood were very great.

Hanshan, for spreading the Dharma, met with slander and was exiled to Guangzhou; his saving of the people of Yue and his prolonging of the altars of state were deep and far-reaching. Had Hanshan not been exiled to Guangzhou, the people of Guangzhou would long ago have turned to desperate courses and become a grief to the state. His great deeds, such as abolishing the timber ships, settling the popular uprising, and bringing peace to Qinzhou, were all settled with a single conversation. Had he not been one who appeared in birth by the power of his vow, to save the people from water and fire, who could have done it?

Laymen such as Ye Yufu established a Zhanshan Temple in Qingdao, the very place where Hanshan spread the Dharma and met with slander. Thinking on Hanshan's abundant virtue, they have specially printed and circulated the chronicle and its annotations, so that readers of later times may be stirred to arise.
Respectfully composed by the ever-ashamed monk Shih Yinguang.
Recorded by Fushan, attendant of the Narayana Cave of the Eastern Sea
Annotated and expounded by Fuzheng, a disciple of the Kaiyuan Prefectural Office in Wu-Yue
Annotated by Zhanran
[Fushan]
His style was Zhiwei. He was the recorder of Master Hanshan’s Chronicle and the
Dream Roam Collection

. He did not shrink from danger or hardship, but followed Master Hanshan from first to last, and his cultivation and attainment were exceedingly high. The Master Hanshan’s Own Chronicle of His Life records: “In the fifteenth year of Wanli (
), the year dinghai, I was forty-two.

In the eighth month of autumn, Vice-Censor Hu (Hu Shun’an; vice-censor: provincial governor) asked leave to return to his fields (to retire in old age), and so brought his own son and presented him for ordination as an attendant, naming him Fushan.” The Annotations to Master Hanshan’s Chronicle say: “(I, Fuzheng), when Patriarch Han journeyed east, came to meet the secretary-attendant Shan, whose style was Zhiwei. Then at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci (Jingci Temple), morning and evening we met and conversed (spending whole days together, constantly talking), and together we studied the mysterious ferry (studying the Dharma together with him, Fushan). The Master (Fushan) assisted the abbot with brush and inkstone, and in the end completed the

Dream Roam Collection. Among Patriarch Han’s eminent disciples of the time, none surpassed Master Zhiwei. In hardship, danger, and obstruction, wherever he went he followed; and the full collection’s records all came from his hand. Later he was entrusted with residence in the Five Teats abbot’s quarters, and presided over Fayun Temple on Mount Kuang, passing away seated (passing into quiescence) at the age of seventy.” It also says: “The foremost disciple whom our Master most approved was none other than Master Zhiwei, named Fushan. At first he shared in good and ill fortune alike, appearing six times in our Master’s chronicle of the year before his passing (that is, appearing six times in the Master Hanshan’s Own Chronicle of His Life, written in the year before Hanshan’s parinirvana); and at the last he ran about supporting the coffin, and wrote in detail the causes and conditions of our Master’s final affairs. He was truly a worthy son of the Five Teats.”
[Fuzheng]
Tan Zhenmo (

), whose courtesy name was Liangsheng, also styled Fuzheng, whose sobriquet was Sao and also Saohan, and who signed himself the Bearded Man of the Way, was a man of Jiaxing and the annotator of the Master Hanshan’s Own Chronicle of His Life. At the age of twenty-seven (the forty-fourth year of Wanli,
), he took refuge with Master Hanshan; and at sixty-one (the seventh year of Shunzhi,
), he obtained Master Hanshan’s own chronicle and wrote his annotations to it. He was a scholar of the Ming, and a presented scholar of the first year of Chongzhen (

He successively held the offices of secretary of the Ministry of Works in the Department of Crafts and Supplies, vice-official of the Court of Judicial Review, vice-minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud, and director of the Directorate of Education concurrently serving as libationer. In the early Qing he was recommended to serve as acting director, but declined and returned home, ending his days in his native place. The gentleman read widely in all books, and was known as one who “read everything”; he had deep associations with Qian Qianyi, Chen Zilong, and others. He wrote a great many books, but because the literary inquisition was severe in the Qianlong era, only the Tanzi Diaochong, the Saohan Collection, and the Sanjing Jiansheng Bian have come down to us. Among these, the Tanzi Diaochong is our country’s first monograph on insects, describing nearly a hundred kinds. His mother, Lady Yan, was a devout Buddhist. According to the Record of Good Women·Tan Zhenmo’s Mother Lady Yan, it is recorded: “Lady Yan was the mother of Tan Zhenmo, a secretary of the Ministry of Works. Her family was generations noble and prosperous, yet she wore cloth and ate simple food, taking the Diamond and Lotus sutras as her constant daily lesson, and in her later years also upholding the Avatamsaka, a full scroll each day, from time to time explaining the general meaning to her son and daughter-in-law. In the fifth year of Chongzhen she fell ill and knew she would soon die. It being the hot season, she rose at dawn, changed her clothes and bathed, and prayed before the Buddha: ‘If in my whole life of serving the Buddha there is truly a Buddha-connection, let my body after death not be touched by foul odors.’ Then she sat cross-legged upright and passed away; and seven days after death her countenance was as in life, a rare fragrance wafted about her, and flies kept far away. Of the crowds who came to mourn and make offerings, not one but sighed in admiration.”
Jiajing
(Emperor Shizong of Ming)
the twenty-fifth year, bingwu
(AD

I am a man of Quanjiao County in Jinling, of the Cai clan. My father was named Yancheng, my mother of the Hong clan, and all her life she loved to honor Guanyin Bodhisattva. At first she dreamed that the Bodhisattva came in through the gate leading a child; my mother received him and embraced him, and so conceived. At the birth, the white-clothed afterbirth was doubled. In that year, the tenth month, on the jihai day, the twelfth day, the bingshen day, at the chou hour
(one to three o’clock at night)
I was born.
(My father saw it once, my mother once.)
[Birth horoscope]
The heavenly stems and earthly branches governing the year, month, day, and hour of birth, each written with two characters, eight in all.
His disciple Zhuan
zhuān

Yu Guanheng, in his biography The Restoration of Caoxi by the Great Master Han, says: The Master was named Deqing, his courtesy name Chengyin, his sobriquet Hanshan. When his mother gave birth, he came forth wrapped double in a white-clothed caul. When the clothes were taken off and washed, the bathwater had a rare fragrance. After he left home and entered Bao'en Temple, one day before the relic stupa he met a brahmin monk, who said: ‘This young master will one day turn the great Dharma-wheel; his mouth is like a lifted moon, which is the Buddha's mouth.’ Again, in the cloister of the same temple he met a man who said: ‘The Emperor Yao had eyebrows of eight colors; you have eyebrows of five colors, and you bear the charge of the three teachings
(Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism)
. Later, at Mount Wutai, passing the Great Stupa Temple, when he was a dhutanga mendicant
(a wandering monk)
, he met a monk of great stature
(of tall and mighty build)
, who took the Master by the hand and said: ‘You are a great man come again; all your hair is dark violet, and hereafter you will surely accomplish great Buddha-work.’

[Courtesy name] A style-name, a person's alternative name. In speaking of oneself one uses the name, to express modesty; in speaking of others one uses the style, to express respect. [Sobriquet] A by-name: an appellation besides name and style.
Fuzheng notes:

In the chronicle, under the forty-second year of Wanli, the year jiayin, the eleventh month, it is recorded that a disciple, Wuxin Zhuanyu, came to visit. In the Hanshan Dream Roam Collection there is a dharma-word addressed to the Chan man Zhuanyu Heng. It says in brief: 'Zhuanyu first relied on Great Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai and learned the sutras and treatises by hearing them. After a long time he swept them all away, and single-mindedly took up one thought, earnestly investigating the matter of his own portion. Wandering south a thousand miles, he crossed Caoxi and paid his respects to the Old Man, seeking instruction. The Old Man showed him the one road of turning about, and he bowed and took his leave with assent, then went to dwell on Mount Nan. Before long the Old Man also arrived. The Chan man, being ill, went to Baoqing for medical treatment, and the Old Man sighed that in the Chan gate a true student of birth and death is the hardest to find. On the first day of the third month of the year bingchen, in the middle of a windy, rainy night, the Chan man suddenly came pushing through the mud in the rain. The Old Man saw that his illness had healed and was overjoyed. Then, again offering incense, he sought instruction, and the Old Man specially told him: since the Chan man's bodily illness is already cured, he must by no means be invaded by the Chan illness. The ancients said: To renounce feeling is easy; to renounce dharma is hard. The Chan man renounces the body, which is to renounce feeling; he renounces views, which is to renounce dharma. With feeling and dharma both forgotten, is he not a person of great unimpeded liberation?'

This instruction runs to several thousand words. In the collection, those whom he approved are not many, and it is fitting that there should be a work, the Restoration Biography. What is to be regretted is that the biography is full of errors, easily misleading later students. For the visits and requests for instruction happened twice but within a single time, and the days of following him were few. Later he never saw the chronicle written by the Master himself, and so what he heard was a different account; the matter is by no means small. Here I take the chronicle as the principal text, and consult and supplement it with one or two other reports, pressing tales and sayings from the biography, such as the whole story of the hermit of Panshan, which is of deep benefit. Other rambling and unfounded matters I have all deleted. In general the fault of Chan is to run after the school and shun the teaching; people do not understand that Patriarch Han and the Sixth Patriarch were both masters of school and teaching together, both manifested flesh bodies at Caoxi, and both were without a single-transmission robe and bowl. The dharma-heir and grandson Suhua Zhixu
(Master Ouyi)

, who had the cause of first resolve and the karma of being received in a dream, was a man who united school and teaching in one in his age. He composed the Records and Eulogies of the Eighteen Patriarchs, ending with Patriarch Han. The eighteen patriarchs are precisely those who did not transmit robe and bowl. His one biography of Patriarch Han, an abridgment of Zhuan's biography, accords exactly with the chronicle, and should be reckoned a meritorious servant of one who admires privately
(one who admires and imitates in private without directly taking a master and receiving transmission)
[The cause of being received in a dream]
In his own autobiography Master Ouyi wrote: “At twenty-three,
I resolved to leave home and investigate the great matter. At twenty-four, I dreamed of bowing to Master Hanshan, weeping with regret at the poorness of the connection, that we had met so late.

Within one month I dreamed of Master Han three times. The Master was going to Caoxi, and I could not follow him afar. So I received ordination from Master Xueling and was named Zhixu. Master Xue was a disciple of old Master Han.”
In
the Verses and Preface to the Annotations on the Chronicle he wrote: “Thinking then of the year renxu (
, when Master Ouyi was twenty-four), when Zhixu first left home, he dreamed of old Master Han three times. In the winter of the year guihai (

), when he was about to enter quiescence (when Master Hanshan was about to enter quiescence), he again showed himself in a dream (again showed himself in a dream to me); all this was the compassionate, true empowerment of grace — how could it be by chance!”
(From the Lingfeng Zonglun.)
A flesh-body Buddha and patriarch, his model for appearing in the world was already present in his mother's womb through kalpas. The supreme cause through kalpas is no small matter.
Jiajing, the twenty-sixth year
year)
dingwei●

I was one year old. A wind-illness came on, and I nearly died. My mother prayed to the Bodhisattva, and so vowed to give me up to leave home, enrolling me by name in the Long Life Temple of the county; and for this reason my milk-name was changed to Heshang.
(My mother saw it a second time.)

Fuzheng: The Master's milk-name was Damei, and in the end it was fully realized. One should know that his dharma-name Deqing came from old Master Xilin, and was given at the time of leaving home; the chronicle does not record it. Nor does it record the name his father gave him before it was changed.
Jiajing, the twenty-seventh year
year)
wushen●
I was three years old. I often sat alone, and did not like to play with other children. My grandfather often said of me: This child is like a wooden post.
(My grandfather saw it once.)
Fuzheng: Looking at how he in the end became a post indeed, his grandfather may be said to have had the eye.
Jiajing, the twenty-eighth year
year)
jiyou● Jiajing, the twenty-ninth year gengxu● Jiajing, the thirtieth year xinhai● Jiajing, the thirty-first year renzi●
I was seven years old. My uncle doted on me. My mother then sent me to the village school. One day my uncle died and was laid out on the bed. When I came home, my mother deceived
dài
, tricked)

me, saying: ‘Your uncle is asleep; call him to get up.’ I called several times, and my aunt, pierced with grief, wept and cried: ‘O Heaven, where has he gone?’ I was astonished and doubted it, and asked my mother: ‘Uncle's body is here; where else could he go?’ My mother said: ‘Your uncle is dead.’ I said: ‘Where does the dead go?’ And at once I doubted it deeply. Before long my aunt bore a son; my mother went to see, and I went with her. Seeing the infant, so large, I asked my mother: ‘Where did this child enter my aunt's belly from?’ My mother gave me a slap and said, ‘Silly child! Where did you enter your mother's belly from?’ And again I doubted it deeply. From this the doubt of where the dead go and where the living come from could not be resolved in my heart.
(My mother saw it a third time; my uncle, my aunt, and my young cousin, once each.)

Fuzheng notes: How did this seven-year-old boy come by this bone-piercing, marrow-piercing crux of birth and death? Mother and child, facing each other and questioning, such a great mass of doubt — a most extraordinary case. The present manifestation of Maya
(Lady Maya, the birth-mother of Shakyamuni Buddha)
, a brand-new hammer and tongs, the foremost great case for smelting Buddhas and refining patriarchs.
Jiajing, the thirty-second year
year)
guichou●

I was eight years old. I studied and took my meals at a relative's house across the river. My mother warned me that I was not allowed to come home, but only once a month. One day when I came home, I clung to my mother and refused to go; my mother was angry and whipped me, and drove me to the riverbank, but I would not get into the boat. In her anger my mother seized me by the topknot and threw me into the river, and without a look back went home. Then my grandmother saw it, urgently called for help and had me pulled out, and sent me home. My mother said: ‘If this good-for-nothing child is not drowned, what is the use of keeping him?’ And she beat me and drove me out again, with not the least reluctance to let me stay. At that time I privately thought my mother's heart hard, and from then on I did not think of home. My mother often wept across the river, and my grandmother scolded her. My mother said: ‘One must cut off his affection, and only then can he study.’
(My grandmother saw it once; my mother, a fourth time.)

Fuzheng: Reading to this point, every word and every sentence, my tears fall like rain. One who reads it without weeping is not of human kind. Joining my palms, I praise him, saying: How compassionate, how sorrowful! How good, how faithful! Being so, how could she not cast away her child, how could he not scrape off his flesh and return it to his mother!
Jiajing, the thirty-third year
year)
jiayin●
At nine I studied in the temple, and heard a monk recite the Guanyin Sutra
(that is, the Universal Gateway Chapter of the Guanyin Bodhisattva)

, which can save the world from suffering, and my heart rejoiced greatly. So I asked the monk for its text, and secretly read it, and could at once recite it. My mother honored Guanyin Bodhisattva, and whenever she burned incense and bowed, I always followed her. One day I said to my mother: ‘Guanyin Bodhisattva has a sutra in one scroll.’ My mother said: ‘I do not know it.’ And I at once recited it once through for my mother. My mother was overjoyed and said: ‘Where did you get this? The sound of your reciting is like an old monk's.’
(My mother saw it a fifth time.)

Qian Muzhai Qianyi, in his Stupa Inscription for the Great Ming Master Hanshan on the Five Teats Peak of Mount Lu, says: ‘At nine the Master could recite the Universal Gateway Chapter.’ This is what the chronicle calls the Guanyin Sutra. In the dingmao year of Tianqi, Chen Dixiang of Nanhai, together with Fushan, a disciple of the Five Teats, entrusted the account of his deeds to Muzhai for a stupa inscription. The matter of his restoring Caoxi he seems to have heard in outline from Xiao Xuanpu Yuju of Xuanhua. But the journey east is not set out in full, and differs greatly from the chronicle. Now his flesh body is at Caoxi, and the Five Teats stupa inscription has been lost — truly so. What I have gathered from it can be no more than a tenth.

Fuzheng: Reading this, one understands that to win a degree and become a magistrate, one need not bother with true study. But to have right knowledge and views and become a Buddha or patriarch, there has never been anyone who did not begin from true study. This one scroll of the Guanyin Sutra, which he could recite in his early years, came about entirely through study. And by reciting it once through for his mother, he was able to repay his mother's kindness in beating and driving him out.
Jiajing, the thirty-fourth year
year)
yimao●

I was ten years old. My mother supervised my lessons very strictly, and I suffered under it. So I asked my mother: ‘What is study for?’ My mother said: ‘To become an official.’ I said: ‘What sort of official?’ My mother said: ‘Beginning from the bottom, if one has ability, one may reach prime minister.’ I said: ‘And when one has been prime minister, what then?’ My mother said: ‘Then one is dismissed.’ I said: ‘A pity — a whole life of hardship, and in the end dismissal. What use is it to do it? I think one should do something that is never dismissed.’ My mother said: ‘A good-for-nothing like you could only be a monk who hangs up his bundle.’ I said: ‘What is a monk who hangs up his bundle, and what good is there in it?’ My mother said: ‘A monk is a disciple of the Buddha, who walks the whole world, free and at ease, with offerings wherever he goes.’ I said: ‘That is exactly the thing to do.’ My mother said: ‘I fear only that you have not the blessing for it.’ I said: ‘Why is blessing needed?’ My mother said: ‘In the world, men who become first scholars are common; but one who leaves home and becomes a Buddha or patriarch — how could that be common?’ I said: ‘I have that blessing; I fear only that my mother could not give me up.’ My mother said: ‘If you have that blessing, then I can give you up.’ Privately I marked it in my mind
(and so I secretly kept these words in my heart; shi: to remember)
(My mother saw it a sixth time.)
Fuzheng: A deep sigh — tsk, tsk! Mother and son, gathered in a circle
(reunited)
, speaking the words of the unborn. The instruction was so clear (
nèn

), the guidance so broad, the sharp point of the exchange so tight, the response so swift! At ten, in Jinling, his mother gave up her son's flesh body. At seventy-eight, at Caoxi, the son's flesh body repaid his mother. A truly great cause and condition, a great wonder indeed!
Jiajing, the thirty-fifth year
year)
bingchen●

I was eleven years old. By chance I saw several wandering monks, carrying their gourds and bamboo hats on their shoulders as they came. I asked my mother: ‘What sort of people are these?’ My mother said: ‘They are monks who hang up their bundles.’ I was secretly delighted and watched them. When the monks arrived, they set down their loads and leaned against a tree, then exchanged greetings and asked for a vegetarian meal. My mother said: ‘Please sit.’ She quickly boiled tea and set out the vegetarian food, with great reverence. When they had finished eating, the monks rose, shouldered their loads, and lifted a hand. My mother quickly avoided it, saying: ‘Do not thank me.’ The monks went straight off. I said: ‘How ill-mannered the monks are, not to thank us for the meal!’ My mother said: ‘To thank would be to lose the blessing.’ I said privately: ‘This is what makes a monk exalted.’ I thought on it deeply, and so brought forth the resolve to leave home, only lacking a convenient road.
(My mother saw it a seventh time.)

Fuzheng: See how suddenly they fed the monks, leaving no trace at all — a case as great as this! Zhaozhou's testing of the old woman of Mount Tai is no more than this. People know that the merit of feeding monks is worldly blessing; but this mother and son proved the blessing of the Two-Footed Honored One.
The above settles the case of his life at home.
Jiajing, the thirty-sixth year
year)
dingsi●

I was twelve years old. In my daily life I was never happy with worldly things, and when my father arranged a marriage for me, I at once stopped it. One day I heard a monk from the capital say: ‘Great Master Xilin of Bao'en Temple has great virtue.’ My heart at once wished to go and follow him. I told my father, and my father would not listen. I told my mother, and my mother said: ‘To raise a son is to follow his aspiration; let him simply be allowed to accomplish it.’ And so she sent me. In the tenth month of that year I reached the temple, and the old Master's Master was overjoyed at first sight, saying: ‘This child's bone and spirit are uncommon; if he were to be merely an ordinary monk, that would be a pity.’ At that time Great Master Wuji had just begun lecturing in the Three Treasuries Hall of the temple. The old Master took me to visit him. It happened that Zhao Dazhou was there, and at first sight he was delighted, saying: ‘This child will be a teacher of gods and men.’ Then, stroking me, he asked: ‘Would you rather become an official, or become a Buddha?’ I answered at once: ‘Become a Buddha.’ Master Zhao said: ‘This child must not be slighted; he should be well taught.’ And when I heard the lecture, though I did not know what was being said, my heart churned as if there were something I knew but could not yet express.

(My father saw it a second time, my mother an eighth; the monk Xilin, Great Master Wuji, and Zhao Dazhou, once each. Dazhou was named Zhenji, styled Mengjing, a man of Neijiang. He served successively as Minister of Rites and Grand Secretary of Wuying Hall, and was given the posthumous name Wensu.)

Fuzheng: Consider that had Patriarch Han in those days not had this mother, he could not have left home, and could not in the end have become a Buddha and patriarch with his virgin body — truly a Buddha-mother! Again, according to the Record of the Buddhist Temples of Jinling: ‘In the Jiajing era the abbot of Bao'en Temple was the monk Yongning, styled Xilin. He kept a horse, and whenever he went from the temple to the Ministry of Rites he would ride it. Mounting, he would always silently recite the Diamond and Lotus sutras. On reaching the gate of the Ministry he would dismount, and the sutras would be finished. Later a woman who lived next to the temple was in childbirth, and the horse died that night. The woman dreamed the horse entered her room, and so bore a son. He was extremely dull, able only to recite the two sutras aloud, and so entered Xilin and became a monk. Other sutras he could not get into his mouth, nor did he know a single character.’ Hence the chronicle says: ‘The Master's Master recited the Diamond Sutra all his life, and did not cease at the end.’
Jiajing, the thirty-seventh year, wuwu● Jiajing, the thirty-eighth year
year)
jiwei●

I was fourteen years old. At first the old Master's Master chose from among his grandsons one of learning and practice, Master Jun, to be my teacher. He first taught me the Lotus Sutra, and in three months I could recite it from memory. The circulating sutras I had all memorized as well. The old Master's Master said: ‘This child can be taught and must not be misled; let us engage a bright teacher to instruct him.’
(The old Master's Master and the old Master, both being the monk Xilin; a second time.)
Jiajing, the thirty-ninth year, gengshen● the fortieth year, xinyou● the forty-first year
year)
renxu●

I was seventeen years old. The old Master's Master again engaged a teacher, first to instruct me in the scholar's calling. At the outset I read the Four Books all at once; next I studied the Five Classics, the philosophers
(the works of the hundred schools of the pre-Qin)
, the histories
(historical books)

, ancient prose, lyrics, and rhymeprose. I could at once compose poetry, and wrote of a gathering of the literary society; my rhymeprose ‘On the River’ was admired and respected by all the company at the time. In those days, being often ill, I wished to abandon the studies I had been pursuing.
(The old Master's Master seen a third time.)

[The Four Books and Five Classics] The Four Books: the Great Learning, the Doctrine of the Mean, the Analects, and Mencius; the Five Classics: the Book of Songs, the Book of Documents, the Book of Rites, the Book of Changes, and the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Jiajing, the forty-second year, guihai● Jiajing, the forty-third year
year)
jiazi●

I was nineteen years old. Because all my friends in the society passed the examinations, some urged me to go and sit for them. At that time Great Master Yungu, a true Dharma-eye, was dwelling in Qixia Mountain. The old Master's Master had long made offerings to him, and whenever he came or went he would always lodge him for ten days or a month. I waited on him very diligently, and from time to time heard his teaching. It happened that when Great Master Yun came out from the mountain, he heard that some had urged me, and feared I might be inclined to go. The Master with all his strength instructed me in the wonder of leaving the world, investigating Chan, and awakening to the mind-ground; and he recounted one by one the patriarchs of the Transmission of the Lamp and the Biographies of Eminent Monks, and told me to fetch and read them. I searched my book-chest
sì
, book case)

, and found the Extensive Records of Zhongfeng. Reading it, before I had finished the scroll I was greatly delighted, and sighed: ‘This is what my heart delights in!’ Then I resolved to do the work of one who has left the world. I at once asked the old Master to shave my head and give me the robe, and I burned and cast away all that I had studied, and set my mind solely on investigating the one matter.
[Shaving the head and donning the robe]
Putting on the monk's robe and shaving the head: this refers to first leaving home to become a monk or nun.

Not having grasped the essential, I then devoted myself to Buddha-recitation, day and night without interruption. Thus before long, one evening in a dream I saw Amitabha Buddha appear, standing in the air where the sun had set. I saw his face and the marks of his radiance, perfectly clear. I bowed at his feet in profound reverence. I also wished to see the two great ones Guanyin and Dashizhi, and they at once appeared half-length. From then on the three holy ones were always brilliantly before my eyes, and I was confident that the work of cultivation could be accomplished.

In the winter of that year the Chan hall of our temple established a practice assembly and invited Great Master Wuji to lecture on the Profound Meaning of the Avatamsaka, and I received the full precepts. Following the lecture, when he reached the ten mysterious gates and the abiding place of the ocean-seal's vast array, I suddenly understood the meaning of the Dharma-realm's perfect interfusion and inexhaustible extent. I deeply admired the character of Qingliang
(National Master Qingliang)
, and so I named my own courtesy name Chengyin. I asked the Master to confirm it, and he said: ‘Is your aspiration to enter this Dharma-gate?’ Then he showed me the words about Mount Qingliang
(that is, Mount Wutai)
, where in winter thick ice accumulates and in summer snow still flies, and there is never any summer heat, and so it is called Qingliang
(that is, Mount Wutai, where Master Chengguan dwelt in this cool place and annotated the Avatamsaka Sutra, and so called himself Qingliang)

. From then on, walking or resting, that realm of ice and snow was ever present before my eyes, and I vowed to dwell within it. Nothing in all affairs could please my mind, and the thought of leaving the world never left me for a moment.
(Great Master Yungu seen once, Great Master Wuji a second time, the old Master's Master a fourth time.)
[The complete precepts] The fully complete and perfect precepts, such as the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikshu and the three hundred and forty-eight of a bhikshuni.
[National Master Qingliang] That is, Master Chengguan,

the fourth patriarch of the Avatamsaka school. He dwelt on Mount Wutai and annotated the Avatamsaka Sutra. Later he resided in the capital, and Emperor Dezong of Tang welcomed him into the palace and bestowed on him the title National Master Qingliang. He lived through nine reigns and was the teacher of the gate for seven emperors.

Fuzheng notes: Patriarch Han's learning and letters were already fully formed, and again he saw the Dharma in decline and wished to accomplish for the public good the work of Chu's talent, bearing both the Dharma and the world on one shoulder. Therefore, moved by his friends' urgings to sit for the examinations, he too conceived the thought of seizing fame, hoping thereby to fulfill his vow of widely spreading the great Dharma. But the road of office is dangerous, and a single careless step brings downfall. Happily he received Great Master Yungu's warning and admonition, and so set his mind wholly on the affairs of leaving the world, burned and cast away his manuscript drafts
(in old usage, the poems and essays written as exercises by students in a private school)
, and at once asked the old Master to shave his head and give him the robe. His wholehearted practice and the opening of his resolve were entirely from Yungu.

And yet, there are those who devote themselves to Buddha-recitation, and even after long years still find it hard to see the Buddha: how could one, in so short a time, have Amitabha, Guanyin, and Dashizhi, the three holy ones, all appear, suddenly as he wished, and again have the three holy ones always brilliantly before his eyes? There are those who attend lectures in the practice hall and receive the precepts and investigate, yet all rely on words and language: who confirms body, mind, nature, and life? How could one, while hearing the lecture, wholly take up body, mind, nature, and life and see no words or language! At a single hearing of the ten mysteries of the Avatamsaka, he could suddenly understand the meaning of the Dharma-realm's perfect interfusion and inexhaustible extent, and could realize and enter the gate of Qingliang, and with ice and snow before his eyes take the name Chengyin. At that moment the spiritual power of Wuji and the spiritual power of Patriarch Han were long since within the inconceivable. Who would say that with words or without words, a great Dharma-master and a great school-master, are two truths? One must know that a man like Patriarch Han is truly one who came from the West through kalpas.
Jiajing, the forty-fourth year
year)
yichou●
I was twenty years old. On the sixteenth day of the first month, the old Master's Master entered quiescence. On the last day of the preceding year
(on the day of the previous year's New Year's Eve)

, the Master gathered all his family and disciples and said: ‘I am eighty-three, and my going is a matter of morning or evening. I have ordained more than eighty disciples, and not one upholds my work.’ Then he stroked my back and said: ‘This child I had hoped would grow to manhood, and now I cannot. Though he is young, he has the views of an elder. After I die, in all matters of the house, great and small, let all be decided by him, and do not treat him lightly because he is young.’ The assembly wept and received his command. On the seventh day of the new year, the Master put on his robes and went around the cloisters to take leave of each, and all were astonished. Three days later he entrusted his final affairs, showed a slight illness, and when medicine was offered would not take it. He said: ‘I am going; what use is medicine?’ Then he assembled the assembly to recite the Buddha's name for five days and nights, holding his rosary in his hand, while I cradled him in my arms, and he passed away sitting upright. Because the Master had recited the Diamond Sutra all his life, he did not cease even at the end. The old Master's Master was the officially appointed abbot of Bao'en for thirty years, dwelling in the abbot's quarters until his extinction. On the eighteenth day of the third month the abbot's quarters caught fire, and all sighed at the wonder of it.
In the tenth month of that year, Great Master Yungu established a Chan retreat at Tianjie
(Tianjie Temple)
, gathering the famous and virtuous of the realm,
fifty-three in number
(he assembled fifty-three men of fame and virtue from within the country)

, and opened the gate of seated Chan. The Master with all his strength urged me to go and join, and at that time the younger Master's Master consented, and so I was able to take part in the assembly. At first I did not know the secret of applying the mind, and suffered greatly. So I offered incense and asked for instruction
(and so I burned incense, bowed, and asked for teaching)
, and the Master instructed me in the public case of verifying Buddha-recitation
(inquiring into Buddha-recitation)

. From then on I inquired, with one thought unmoving. Within three months I was as if in a dream, and saw no great assembly at all, nor did I know there were daily affairs; and the whole assembly took me for one of resolve.

[The public case of verifying Buddha-recitation] That is, inquiring into Buddha-recitation: taking the single phrase of the Buddha's name (Amitabha Buddha) as a huatou, and inquiring into who it is that recites the Buddha's name. (See
Inquiring into Buddha-Recitation

Before many days had passed, because I applied the mind too urgently, I developed a carbuncle on the back, red, swollen, and enormous, and the Master found it very difficult. I put on my robe and prayed earnestly and mournfully before Weituo, saying: ‘This must be a debt of resentment demanding my life. I vow to recite the Avatamsaka Sutra ten times and ask leave of absence for three months, to complete the Chan retreat, and afterward I shall repay it.’ Thus it was that, in the latter part of the night, utterly exhausted, I climbed onto the Chan bed and fell fast asleep, and did not even know when the board was struck to rise
(in the Chan grove the board is struck at dawn to rouse the assembly from sleep)
nor when I got up, for I had forgotten it
(the carbuncle on the back had completely disappeared; ‘forget’ in ancient Chinese is interchangeable with ‘perish’)
. At daybreak the Master asked how my illness
yàng
, ailment)

was. I said: ‘It is nothing.’ And when he looked, it had already healed over, and the whole assembly sighed in amazement. For this reason I was able to complete the retreat. And when I came out, I was still as though I had never left the Chan seat; even walking in the marketplace, I saw no one, and at the time all thought it strange.

The Chan way was first opened in Jiangnan and flourished from Great Master Yungu onward; yet among the resident monks who practiced Chan, I alone. At that time the monks of the temple all dressed according to worldly custom, many in bright colors. At this time I cast away all the clothes I had been used to, and sought out only a single patched robe to wear, and those who saw me thought it strange.
(The old Master's Master seen a fifth time, the younger Master's Master once, Great Master Yungu a second time.)
Fuzheng: Observe old Master Xilin of the Western Forest: greatly was he no ordinary monk. He lived out his years
(a long life)

and ended well, knowing beforehand the time of his coming. He gained a grandson with the eye, entrusted him with his final affairs, and in the end was able to repay the command given with a stroke on the back; in worldly dharma and Buddha-dharma both were fulfilled — how rare!

Nowadays Chan retreats are everywhere, and those who sit in them take only the ease of a settled place as their joy; who understands that the applying of the mind is suffering? When Patriarch Han first brought forth the resolve to recite the Buddha's name, he had already again and again seen Buddhas and bodhisattvas appear in radiance. People today, gaining a little, take it for enough: who is willing to ask for instruction and inquire into the public case of verifying Buddha-recitation? Patriarch Han once said to me, Fuzheng: ‘In reciting the Buddha's name, if one is unwilling to set one's heart to death, but recites only on the surface of floating thoughts, then in truth the habitual tendencies in the storehouse consciousness flow on unseen, and one never sees a single thought of recitation settle. If Buddha-recitation gains power, it is far better even than inquiring into the cypress tree or the dry shit-stick.’ The public case of verifying Buddha-recitation has its own source and lineage. It is for this reason that afterward, journeying east, he passed through Jiahe, came to Qizhen, and bowed to the stupa of the late Great Master Yungu, to make clear the milk of Dharma. And when he dwelt at the Five Teats, he established a Buddha-recitation practice hall for the six periods, to take the place of the Chan retreat.
Praying to Weituo and having the carbuncle removed — how came such a spiritual response? Had it not been
(if it were not that)

that ‘the three-month Chan retreat was like a dream, so that he saw neither the assembly nor daily affairs, and leaving the Chan seat to walk in the marketplace he was still as though seated in Chan and seeing no one,’ then with such earnest application of mind, do not expect that praying to Weituo would come so easily as this.

blocks.text: 4. The Great Fire at the Monastery

inline.s: Jiajing, the forty-fifth year
year)
bingyin●
I was twenty-one years old. I had come out from the Chan retreat. On the twenty-eighth day of the second month of that year, at the hour of noon
(from eleven in the morning to one in the afternoon)

, the rain fell as if pouring from a basin, when suddenly a great thunderbolt came down from the stupa, and fire broke out in the stupa hall; before an hour had passed, the great hall was burned. By the hours of shen and you
(from five to seven in the afternoon)

, all the halls and cloisters, more than a hundred and forty bays, were reduced to embers. At that time my young master's master was abbot, and when the matter was reported to the throne, an edict came down to the judicial authorities, and eighteen of those involved were arrested. As the monks of the whole temple feared being drawn in, each fled. And among the monks who held office in the temple there was no one with whom to take counsel. I stepped forward and with all my strength sought to save them, carrying salt and vegetables on my own back to the prison to supply them. From the temple to the Ministry of Justice was twenty li, and for three months I went and came without weariness. Moreover, I protected and adjusted matters in many ways, and all those implicated in the end escaped death.
At that time Xuelang En
(Master Xuelang, whose dharma name was Hongen)

was one year older than I. We took refuge together under the Great Master Wuji and were so close that people at the time took us for brothers of one womb. Together with him I resolved to restore the temple, and I said: “This is a great causal occasion; it is not easily met save by one of great merit and wisdom. You and I must throw our lives into practice and nourish our strength to await the time.” At that time I formed the resolve to travel far.

Before long, the junior grandfather entered stillness, and there was none to support the affairs of the household of the great grandfather. Earlier, when the Grandmaster entered stillness, he had left no savings; the funeral expenses were all met by borrowing and came short, so there were many debts. When the household came to be divided, I knew that it could not be kept together. Mindful of the Grandmaster’s dying charge, I contrived to repay in full all that had been borrowed; what remained I divided among the disciples, each to take up his own work, and so the household was preserved.

That winter I followed the Great Master Wuji and heard the Lotus Sutra at the Tianjie Temple. Because my heart was set on traveling far, I kept looking among the monks of the region for one who might be my companion; for a long time I found none. One day, seeing that the rear shelf
(the latrine)
was spotless, I thought that its latrine-keeper
(the monk whose duty was to sweep the latrines)

must be no ordinary man, and I went to visit him. When I saw him, he was merely a sallow, swollen, sick monk, which made me wonder at him the more. Every morning when I rose, the work was always already done
(that is, the latrine was sure to have been swept clean)

, and I never knew when he had swept and sprinkled it. So I kept myself from sleep and secretly paced beneath the eaves to spy on him. When the assembly was dismissed from sitting, he had already finished putting all in order.

Some days later I saw that it was unclean again and that the man was nowhere to be seen. I asked the officers, who said: “The latrine-keeper is sick in the guest room.” I went to look at him; his condition was past bearing. I asked: “Is the Master at ease?” He said: “This body of karmic hindrance is already hard to sustain, and the sickness of craving is harder still to bear.” I asked why. He said: “Whenever I see the food handed out at the meal, I only hate that I cannot put everything down at once.” I laughed and said: “That is only a long illness craving food.” Thereby I knew the man to be genuine. So I prepared cakes and fruit and, carrying them in my sleeve, went to see him, and asked his name. He said: “Miaofeng, a man of Puzhou.” I at once arranged to join him as companion on the road. Some days later, when I looked for him again, he was gone. I knew in my heart that the man, fearing he would be a burden to me, had slipped away.
(The junior grandfather, that is, the junior master; seen a second time. Xuelang En seen once, the Great Master Wuji a third time, and the latrine-keeper Miaofeng once.)

Fuzheng’s note: Master Xuelang was named Hongen. At thirteen he went with his father to hear the Great Master Wuji expound the Lotus rules at the Bao’en Temple. Wuji was a man of Huaiyin who had fully mastered the cardinal tenets of both nature and characteristics of the Xianshou and Cien schools, so that the lecture halls of the time flourished under him. Gong was then a boy with his hair still hanging
(in childhood)

: for ten days he listened with all his ears and would not leave, and at last cut off his own topknot, begging his father to give him up as the Great Master Wuji’s little novice. The Patriarch Hanshan was just twelve and had lately left home at Xilin; in those young years they were close in spirit, as the chronicle’s earlier words about “going to the Tripitaka Hall to hear the teaching” record. From this point on, though they were close as brothers, the Patriarch had a mind that stood apart and above. At twenty, when he sat in meditation with the Great Master Yungu at Tianjie, Gong saw how withered and still he was and scolded him for not going to hear Wuji’s lectures, saying: “What use is a village-shrine earth-god?” The Patriarch said: “The ancients have a saying: when one has penetrated the nature through the ancestral school, looking back on words is like opening a door and the pestle dropping into its socket.” Xuelang said: “If that is so, then you are my elder brother.” At that time Bao’en was destroyed by fire from heaven, and the two wept for three days, vowing to restore it. Later the Patriarch went from Mount Tai to the capital; the palace’s plan to raise the temple came near to fruition but never quite aligned, and though he passed through the Eastern and Southern Seas, he never for a moment forgot the affair of Bao’en. Gong, seeing the pagoda’s finial leaning awry, went from door to door with his bowl, begging at the great houses of the city, and in three years brought the work to completion. Ah, both of them may be called men who did not fail their word. Zibai
(the Great Master Daguan)
in his heart made light of Gong, and from time to time spoke slightingly
(criticized him)
, but when the Patriarch told him the circumstances of Gong’s leaving home, he was startled and said that he must be Kuiji

(the chief disciple of the Great Master Xuanzang, who studied the languages of India and transmitted the doctrines of Consciousness-Only and Buddhist logic, composed a hundred commentaries, and was known as the Master of a Hundred Commentaries, the founding patriarch of the Faxiang school)
reborn. Most of the above I heard from Master Yiyu.

Master Miaofeng of Puzhou, named Fudeng, went to the Southern Sea on behalf of the Prince of Shanyin to offer incense. Returning by way of Jianye, the northerner, newly come to the south, took a damp chill and broke out in sores, and so he asked at the Tianjie monastery for the work-post of latrine-keeper, meaning only to rest. The Patriarch found him out by the spotless latrine floor and the bright, clean latrine lamp, pledged with him a friendship of life and death, and wished to dwell on the mountains and go on pilgrimage with him. Master Miao said: “If you have this resolve, on pilgrimage I will carry your straw sandals, and if we dwell on a mountain I will supply the water and firewood.” Soon
(before long)

his sores healed and he left. Six years later, when they sought each other out in the capital, it was clear that at that time his public business was unfinished and the karmic occasion still waited, and so he had shaken out his robe and gone. The chronicle passes over it lightly, saying: “for fear of burdening him, he slipped away.” In it, the one word “genuine” spoken of Master Miao suffices to sum up
(in ancient usage interchangeable with “kǎi”, to sigh with feeling)
a hundred thousand buddhas and patriarchs.
In Pinggu county of Shuntian prefecture there is a mountain called Miaofeng, and he took his name from the mountain.
Longqing
(on the accession of Muzong of the Ming the era name was Longqing, in the year
CE),
the era was changed; dīngmǎo ●
I was twenty-two. I especially proposed the Venerable Yungu of Zhonggong as abbot of the temple, to save it from ruin. This was the affair of Hui Lu
(the fire-god, that is, a fire)

: the community’s debts came to nearly a thousand in gold, and all of them passed through my hands. The assembly could think of no way to settle them; I devised a plan and fixed a term of three years, and repaid them all. That year, by a ministry dispatch, this temple established a charity school to teach the monks, and I was asked to be the teacher. The novices who received instruction numbered nearly two hundred, and so I again took up my old studies of the Zuo Commentary and the other masters.
(First meeting with the Venerable Yungu of Zhonggong.)
[Reign change]
— the changing of the era name by a sovereign or a dynasty; the first year of each era name is called the “first year” (yuánnián).

Fuzheng’s note: this act not only settled the entanglements of one household of the family, it settled the entanglements of the abbot of the whole temple — worldly dharma and Buddha-dharma together, one great stroke of strategy. He is called Zhong Gong to distinguish him from the Great Master Yungu.
Longqing, second year
CE),
wùchén ●
I was twenty-three. That year I gave up the temple school and taught again at Gaozuo Temple, such was the burden of my household.
Longqing, third year, jǐsì ● Longqing, fourth year
CE),
gēngwǔ ●
I was twenty-five. In both years I answered the invitation to teach at Jinshan.
Longqing, fifth year
CE),
xīnwèi ●

I was twenty-six. With my elder brother in the Dharma, Xuelang En, I traveled to Mount Lu. Reaching Nankang, we heard that the mountains were much troubled by tigers and dared not climb. So we took boat by wind to Ji’an and visited Qingyuan; seeing the temple in ruins and the monks all wearing their hair long, I was moved to the resolve to restore it. I therefore spoke to the authorities
(those who held power)
, selected those under forty years of age, had them all shaved, and gained more than forty men.

In summer I returned from Qingyuan and set my own master’s affairs in order, settling them well. In the eleventh month of winter I set out with a single bowl on a long journey. As I was about to go north, Xuelang stopped me, fearing that I could not endure the bitter cold, and urged me to go rather to Wu and Yue, where there are many fine mountains and waters to delight the eye. I said: “Our habitual tendencies cling to softness and warmth; only where they cannot be indulged are they easily mastered. As for Wu and Yue, they are but a couch and a mat.” So with a single bowl I went far away.
(Xuelang En, my elder brother in the Dharma, seen a second time)

Fuzheng’s note: I am moved that the Patriarch, having formerly made the contemplation of cool ice and snow, suddenly went north, roused great courage, and gave himself up to the trial — already had he made both the person and its realm drop away, and empty space itself melt into nothing.
With the above, the affair of the household of the temple is concluded.
Longqing, sixth year
CE),
rénshēn ●

I was twenty-seven. I had just reached Yangzhou when a great snow blocked me and sickness came on. After a long while, begging food in the market, I could not get in at a single door. I asked myself why, and quickly examined myself, saying: “It is only that I have a few coppers, some two mace of silver at my waist, to rely on.” Thereupon, seeing monks and Daoists in the snow who begged and got nothing, I invited them all into an eating-house, threw down the silver, and finished it in a single meal. The next day, going out into the street, I entered one or two doors and could call out, and so got food. Then I said to myself with joy: “My strength is enough to make light of ten thousand measures of grain
(that is, my strength is enough to make light of ministers whose stipend is ten thousand measures of grain)

.” I inscribed my bowl: “A vessel that makes light of ten thousand measures.” I named my robe: “A thing that makes light of the whole world.” And I made an inscription for it, saying: “You entrust me with form, I entrust you with mind. Yet this one body is made sufficient by it, and all things are in truth made light by it. Soon I shall trail sleeves of long wind and wear a collar of white clouds. In its rising it is like the wings of a swan; in its ease it is like the scales of a hidden dragon. I roam free in the universe, going and staying among mountains and forests. Why then display the splendor of crimson and purple? I prize only what frost and snow cannot invade.”
In the seventh month of autumn that year I reached the capital
(Yanjing, that is, present-day Beijing)

, with nowhere to set my foot. Begging, I went a whole day without food; toward evening I came to the tea-shed at the Western Peace Granary and got a single meal, and lodged at the Hecao Yijiao Temple. The next day the Left Minister of War, Lord Wang Boyu, learning that I had come, invited me, because I had been a fellow member of a literary society with his younger brother, Wang Cigong Zhongyan. So I was able to lodge there for ten days, and at once called on the Dharma Master Mohe Zhong, and went with him to the Western Hills to hear the Miaozong Chao
(by the Venerable Siming of the Song dynasty, his commentary on Tiantai’s Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, entitled the Miaozong Chao)
, and there composed the poem “Longing for My Elder Brother in the Dharma in the Western Hills
(Master Xuelang)

.” When the session ended, Mohe kept me for the winter, and I heard the Lotus Sutra and the Consciousness-Only teachings, and asked the Dharma Master An to explain the three-part syllogism of Buddhist logic
(one of the five sciences, that is, logic)
In the eleventh month Master Miaofeng came to visit me. The Master had grown a long beard and hair and wore coarse cloth
(rough hempen cloth, such as the poor and lowly wore in ancient times)

. He first had it announced: “A salt-merchant has come to call.” When he entered the door, the Master asked at once: “Do you still recognize me?” I looked at him closely, saw his two eyes, and suddenly remembered that he was the sick latrine-keeper of Tianjie in former days
(I suddenly recalled that he was the latrine-keeper who had been sick at the Tianjie Temple in former days)

, and said: “I recognize you.” The Master said: “I have changed my head and swapped my face.” I said: “The original face is at ease.” We smiled together, with no leisure to speak of other things. I only asked where he was lodged, and he said: “Longhua
(the Longhua Temple)

The next day I went to inquire after him, and as we sat at night I asked him why he looked as he did. The Master said: “Because I have long dwelt in the mountains, my hair has grown long uncut. Just now, because the donor, His Highness the Prince of Shanyin, is building a monastery
(it happened that the patron, His Highness the Prince of Shanyin, wished to build a temple)
, he charged me to come to the capital to request the inner canon
(he ordered me to come to the capital to request the Great Canon)
, and so I came.” He asked about me, and I said: “I came specially to seek you, Master, and also to view the capital
(the capital city)
, to call upon men of knowledge
(and to visit good and wise teachers)
, and so to cut off the vain thoughts of other days
(to cut off the vain regret of not having met them in days to come)

.” The Master said: “Since we parted I have thought of you without cease, and had begun to think there was no karmic link. Now that you have happily come, I wish to accompany you in begging, and to go ahead of you to drive off the dogs.” We talked the whole night through, and at first light
(when dawn was about to break)
, smiling, we parted.

I then went to call upon the Great Master Bianrong. I bowed and begged the Master for instruction; he said nothing, only gazing straight at me. I called upon Master Xiaoyan. The Master asked: “Where have you come from?” I said: “From the south.” The Master said: “Do you remember the road by which you came?” I said: “Once past, it is done with
(once I have walked past, I pay it no further heed)
.” The Master said: “Yet your place of coming is clear.” I bowed, stood in attendance, and begged for further teaching, and the Master opened to me a few words on the upward way.

(The Left Minister of War, Lord Wang Boyu, his younger brother Cigong Zhongyan, the Dharma Master Mohe Zhong, and the Dharma Master An: each seen once. Xuelang En, my elder brother in the Dharma, seen a third time; Master Miaofeng a second time; His Highness the Prince of Shanyin once; the Great Master Bianrong and Master Xiaoyan each once. Boyu was named Daokun, styled Nanming, a man of Xin’an; he wrote the Taihan Collection. His younger brother Zhongyan was named Daoguan, a noted scholar.)
[The upward way] means the one road upward. The uttermost point of the ancestral school is called the “one road upward.”

Fuzheng’s note: when I think on the scene of “opening his hands to beg and entering men’s doors,” it is truly beyond speech, beyond conception. The Dharma Master Yiyu said: “The Patriarch was resolved on going north; Gong tried hard to keep him back, and the Patriarch tricked him into going into the city, and then went off through the great snow. When Gong returned to the temple he wept bitterly for a long time.” Hence there should be the poem “Longing for My Elder Brother in the Dharma in the Western Hills.” The two Masters Bianrong and Xiaoyan both spoke with him in accord
(of one mind or one view)

. Xiaoyan was a man of Yan; he built himself a hut in Willow Lane in the western city of Yanjing. He was born in the renshen year of the Zhengde reign, and when he met the Patriarch at the latter’s age of twenty-seven, Master Xiao was already sixty-two. He left the Record of the Moon Heart, in two southern and two northern volumes, a rarity among Chan records. Every phrase of this meeting foretells
(predicts in advance)
matters of the upward way.
In this year began the karmic occasion of Mount Wutai.

blocks.text: 6. First Realization of the Emptiness of Form

inline.s: Wanli
(on the accession of Shenzong of the Ming, aged ten, the era name was Wanli, in the year
CE),
the era was changed; guǐyǒu ●
I was twenty-eight. In the first month of spring I set out to visit Mount Wutai, first seeking the Record of Qingliang
(one of the nine gazetteers of Mount Wutai)

, and traveled following its traces. Reaching the North Peak, I saw that the affairs of Hanshan were very good, and asked where that mountain was. A monk pointed it out; delighted by its rare beauty, I silently took it as my style-name. I made a poem to record it, with the lines “Do not
(the word zhemo means ‘do not’)
follow others away; here let me rest the workings of the mind.”
Because I could not bear the bitter cold of ice and snow, I could not stay. I returned to the capital and wandered east, begging my food. Reaching Mount Pan
northwest of Ji county in Tianjin municipality, a spur of the Yan Mountains and a famous mountain east of Beijing, hailed as “the first mountain east of the capital”)

— at the Thousand-Images Peak, I saw a monk who did not speak. I asked nothing either, but at once joined him, gathering firewood and drawing water. I begged my way through the summer, and the Minister of War Wang sent a letter inquiring after me, saying: “I fear you have become a starving man of the eastern suburbs.” In autumn, again, because Ou Zhenbo of Lingnan, who had sent me a letter some years before without our ever meeting, was now an erudite of the National Academy and eager to see me, I returned.
(The silent monk seen once, the Minister of War Wang Boyu a second time, and the court erudite Ou Zhenbo of Lingnan once.)

Fuzheng’s note: reading the Record of Famous Mountains, I find it said: “At the Dragon Gate of Wutai there is a mountain. When the First Emperor of Qin whipped the stones into a bridge and crossed the sea in search of immortals, he whipped this mountain and it did not move, and so it was called Hanshan.”

could not bear the bitter cold of ice and snow” — this exactly echoes the earlier manifestation of the cool ice-and-snow realm, and the words with Xuelang about not bearing the bitter cold, with a hidden meaning leaping out.

The affair of the silent monk is recorded with particular fullness in the biography written by Master Zhuan Gong. He says: “The Master and Miaofeng met again at the Yan capital and agreed to go up Mount Wutai together to dwell in stillness. At that time Master Miao had not yet set out to request the canon for the Prince of Shanyin, and the Master was lodging in the private residence of the Minister of War Wang Nanming. After a time, he made a pilgrimage to Mount Pan. Climbing to the summit of Mount Pan, he came to a stone crag, and within it was a recluse, gray-headed and ashen-faced. The Master bowed; the man gave no response at all, and to questions he said nothing. The Master knew him to be no ordinary man and sat silently with him. After a little, the recluse boiled tea, took a single cup and drank it himself; the Master likewise took a cup and drank. When the tea was done, the recluse put the tea things back in their place and sat upright as before; the Master did the same. After a short while the recluse cooked rice; when it was done he set it before his seat, took a single bowl and a single pair of chopsticks and ate; the Master likewise took a bowl and chopsticks and ate with him. When the meal was over, again he sat upright as before, and the Master did the same. In the night the recluse went outside the crag to walk in meditation; the Master followed him, each pacing his own east-west line. The next day the Master, knowing the hour for tea, brewed tea, and at the hour for food cooked rice; the recluse drank and ate with the Master, and at nightfall walked in meditation as before. Thus it went for a full week
(seven days passed in this way)

, and only then did the recluse ask the Master: ‘Where has the Good Man come from?’ The Master said: ‘From the south.’ The recluse said: ‘What have you come here for?’ The Master said: ‘I came specially to visit a recluse.’ The recluse said: ‘A recluse’s countenance is just this; there is nothing else remarkable.’ The Master said: ‘Crossing the threshold, I had already seen through it.’ The recluse laughed and said: ‘I have dwelt in this crag for over thirty years, and today for the first time I meet one of the same wind
(a man of the same style)

.’ He asked the Master to stay, and the Master too forgot to return. One night, as the Master walked in meditation, suddenly there came a crack at the crown of his head, crashing like thunder; the mountains, rivers, and great earth, body, mind, and world, all at once became utterly empty, a state not to be likened to the ordinary emptiness before the eyes. In this emptiness-samādhi he remained for about the time of five inches of incense; then gradually he felt body and mind again, gradually felt his feet on solid ground, and opening his eyes gradually saw the mountains, rivers, and great earth, and all conditions returned as before. Body and mind were light and quick, and the bliss was beyond all description. Lifting his feet as lightly as the wind, he returned to the crag. The recluse said: ‘Tonight you walked in meditation a very long while.’ The Master told him fully the state he had attained. The recluse said: ‘That is but a state of the form aggregate; it is not the original own-nature. I have dwelt in this crag for more than thirty years, and save for cloudy rain, wind, and snow, every night I walk in meditation in that state. Only if one does not cling to it is one not kept in the dark by it as to the original own-nature.’ The Master deeply assented to his words, bowed, and thanked him for the teaching. The Master stayed long at Mount Pan. When Master Miao set out with the canon, he asked Lord Wang where the Master had gone. The Lord at once sent a messenger up to the summit of Mount Pan to find him, and asked whether he was in the crag. Seeing the Master, he told him how earnestly his host and Master Miao awaited him. The Master then bowed and took leave of the recluse, reluctant to part, but there was no help for the old agreement. The recluse escorted him, his tears falling like scattered pearls, and turned back only halfway down the mountain. The Master returned to the capital, and Master Miao and Lord Wang welcomed him, laughing: ‘Why have you come back so late?’ The Master told them fully the karmic circumstances on the crag. The Lord said: ‘If it is so, then our Master’s dwelling on the mountain is complete.’ The Master said: ‘It is still only a state on the roadside.’ The Lord and Master Miao looked at each other and laughed aloud.”
Ah, such wondrous manifestations as these — how many the Patriarch met with in his life
(gòu,

, to encounter), I do not know how many, and they are hard to exhaust with pen or tongue. Even what Master Zhuan Gong records, the true record of Mount Pan, runs to six hundred words, and may be called an immense karmic occasion. In the chronicle, only the few words ‘at the Thousand-Images Peak of Mount Pan a monk did not speak, and I joined him gathering firewood and drawing water, begging through the summer’ are given, so that it seems no more than an ordinary meal of tea and rice. A wondrous realm may be loved, yet he let it go and went on his way; though this was because of his old agreement with Master Miao, he was also unwilling to become a follower of the Two Vehicles, a man who saves only himself. The merit of Master Zhuan Gong’s biography is greatest in this one case.
In Shuntian prefecture, in Ji prefecture, several peaks rise sheer and lone; it is called Mount Pan, also named Mount Panlong. On the summit is a great rock which moves when it is shaken.
Wanli, second year
CE),
jiǎxū ●

I was twenty-nine. In spring I traveled in the Western Hills of the capital. At that time the famous men of the day — the Wang brothers Fengzhou and Linzhou, the Wang brothers Boyu and Zhongyan, and Ou Zhenbo of Nanhai — were all gathered at once in the capital, all of them men I had long admired.

One day I visited the elder Wang, Fengzhou. When we met, because I was young, he took me lightly, and I bore myself proudly as host and guest alike. He at once earnestly instructed me in the method of composing poetry; I stared at him wide-eyed and in the end took my leave without a single word. He was displeased, and spoke of it to his younger brother Linzhou. The next day the younger brother came to visit; at the first sight of me he said: ‘Last night my elder brother lost one eye.’ I said: ‘Has the Lord the one eye?’ He clasped his hands and said: ‘The young man has seen it.’ We laughed together.
