Returning, he said to his brother: ‘Elder brother, you have lost to Vimalakīrti.’ So he gave me a poem, with the lines ‘
One may know that Wang Yishao
(Wang Xizhi, styled Yishao)
, in pure conversation yields to Master Zhi
(the eminent Jin-dynasty monk Zhi Dun)

.’ One day Wang the younger was lodging with me, reading the Zuo Commentary. He said to me: ‘Your natural gift is especially bright; you have the air of a great writer. My elder brother is the literary leader of the age — why do you not take up his teaching and make a name for one school?’ I laughed and spat, saying: ‘Keep your elder brother’s knee; one day he will bow to this old monk and receive the meaning of the coming from the West
(the purport transmitted by Bodhidharma when he came from the West)
.’ The younger Wang was much displeased, and on returning told the Minister of War. The Lord said: ‘Truly! I observe that Lord Chengyin’s
(Lord Chengyin, that is, the Patriarch)
frame is of the Way; in days to come he will enter the chamber of Dahui and Zhongfeng
(in the future he will enter the inner chambers of Chan Master Dahui and Chan Master Zhongfeng)
— would he be willing to be content with mere letters! I fear only
(I only fear)
that idle drifting may be his undoing.’ One day, seeing on the fan of mine and the younger Wang’s a poem with the lines ‘This body and world are the two wings of a cicada
tiáo
, the cicada in ancient books)

, and heaven and earth a single hair of a horse,’ he showed it to the younger Wang and said: ‘Is this a monk of mere letters?’ Another day he made a special vegetarian feast and invited me and Master Miao to come together. In the midst of the gathering the Lord said to me: ‘The Chan gate is desolate and greatly to be feared; I earnestly ponder it. I observe that your bearing is broad, and your future attainment will not be small; why do you wander so idly?’ I said: ‘This poor monk has come on foot solely for the great causal occasion, to call upon good and wise teachers. It is only that now I let my eyes roam over the men of the age, to be done with future vain longing. It is no idle wandering, and I am about to set out.’ The Lord said: ‘Truly so. I observe that in these days there is none who can be your teacher; and without Miaofeng you would have no friend.’ I said: ‘Formerly I had already sought him out among the crowd and made a pact with him as a fellow student; and so of late I have been seeking him, and unexpectedly met him here.’ The Lord said: ‘How strange! If you two really go, I wish to help with the expenses
(I am willing to provide the funds)
.’ At that time Master Miao had returned with the canon, and the Minister of War accordingly gave me two travel warrants, and also wrote a piece to see me off.

One day the Lord summoned me in haste and asked: ‘Miaofeng has gone; why did you not take leave of him?’ I said: ‘I am going slowly.’ The Lord said: ‘I know you do not wish to turn on another man’s heels, yet you are quite mistaken. The ancients were not ashamed of small matters but ashamed that their merit and fame should not be known to the world. I only hope that one day you will accomplish a work of light for the Dharma-gate; why then weigh comings and goings so narrowly!’ I was moved and thanked him, and thereupon resolved to go. I went at once to see Master Miao, who had already loaded his carriage. Seeing me arrive, he asked: ‘Are you going too
(elder brother in the Dharma, are you going too)
?’ I said: ‘I am going
(I am going too)
.’ I at once mounted the carriage and departed without taking leave of anyone
(I at once climbed into Miaofeng’s carriage and left without bidding farewell to anyone)

In the eighth month of autumn I crossed at Mengjin and saw the place where King Wu reviewed his troops; I made a poem to mourn there: ‘A lonely stone and ruined stele lean where the river flows; / Here once the King assembled all the lords, as story goes. / Had but the royal
(the sovereign’s rule and discipline)

order lasted long as heaven and earth, / It should have flowed with Yellow River, endless from its birth.’ Passing the place where Boyi and Shuqi reined in the horses, I mourned: ‘They put away their kingdom, honor left behind; / An ancient shrine alone remains, with cypresses entwined. / Shouyang’s hills keep the selfsame clear and quiet hue, / Still the heart that once those royal horses drew.’ Then I entered Shaolin and paid my respects at the First Patriarch
(bowing to Patriarch Bodhidharma)

. At that time the Chan Master Daqian Run had just entered the monastery, and I visited him but did not meet him. Leaving the mountain, I viewed the ancient city of Luoyang, the Sutra-Burning Terrace, and the White Horse Temple.
[Boyi and Shuqi reining in the horses]

In the last years of the Shang dynasty, Boyi and Shuqi were sons of the lord of the state of Guzhu. After the lord of Guzhu died, the two yielded to each other, unwilling to be king, and went to King Wen of Zhou. After King Wen died, King Wu sent out troops to punish the tyrant King Zhou of Shang, carrying King Wen’s tablet in the chariot as he marched. Boyi and Shuqi reined in his horses and remonstrated: “Your father is dead and unburied, yet you take up shield and spear — can this be called filial? As a subject you would slay your lord — can this be called loyal?” The guards wished to kill them, but the Grand Duke Jiang said: “These are righteous men.” So the guards did them no harm but drove them away. King Wu gathered eight hundred lords at Mengjin, and after crossing the river joined battle with King Zhou’s army at Muye. King Zhou was defeated because his troops turned their weapons about in the front ranks, and he burned himself on the Deer Terrace, and the Shang dynasty perished. Boyi and Shuqi, ashamed to eat the grain of Zhou, withdrew to Mount Shouyang and gathered wild ferns for food. A woman said to them: “You are righteous in not eating the grain of Zhou, but these plants too are Zhou’s.” The two, ashamed and indignant, refused food and died, and were buried on Mount Shouyang.

I then followed Master Miao, and in the ninth month reached Hedong, where I met the Prince of Shanyin, and so stayed to pass the winter. At that time the prefect Lord Chen, Master Miao, and I were all most attentive, and had the Zhongwu Collected Explanations of the Zhaolun printed, which I collated and read. Hitherto the purport of ‘the whirlwind fells the mountains’ in the Essay on Non-Shifting had not been clear to me, and I had long held the doubt keenly. Now when I came to it, I was still bewildered. But at the words ‘The brahmacārin left home and returned white-haired; a neighbor saw him and said: “Is the man of former days still here?” The brahmacārin said: “I resemble the man of former days, but am not the man of former days”’ — I suddenly awakened and understood, saying: Truly all dharmas neither come nor go. I at once stepped down from the meditation bed to bow to the Buddha, and there was no sign of rising or moving; I lifted the blind and stood before the steps, and suddenly the wind blew on the courtyard trees and flying leaves filled the sky, and there was utterly no sign of motion. I said: ‘This is the whirlwind felling the mountains, yet ever still.’ Afterward, when I went out to pass water
(urinate)

, there was utterly no sign of flowing, and I said: ‘This is the rivers racing on, yet not flowing.’ Thereupon the doubt of birth and death melted away like ice. And I had a verse: ‘Birth and death are as day and night; / Water flows and flowers fall in flight. / Today at last the truth I know: / The nostrils downward ever go
(it has always been so, never changed. Chan Master Fanyuan Cong said: “The nostrils have always hung downward.” From the Complete Lamp of the Five Lamps.)
[The Zhaolun]

The Zhaolun was written by the monk Sengzhao of the Later Qin, a collection of essays that fully and systematically develops the thought of prajñā. Sengzhao was one of the most outstanding and influential disciples of Kumārajīva, and the youngest and most richly gifted of them all. [The whirlwind fells the mountains] This passage of the essay reads: “The whirlwind fells the mountains, yet it is ever still; the rivers race onward, yet they do not flow; the wild horses toss and drum, yet they do not move; the sun and moon traverse the sky, yet they do not go round.” (Translation: a fierce wind fells the mountains, yet it is ever still; rivers race and pour, yet they do not flow; dust tosses and drums, yet it does not move; the sun and moon patrol the sky without rising or setting.) In these phrases — ‘the whirlwind fells the mountains,’ ‘the rivers race onward,’ ‘the wild horses toss and drum,’ ‘the sun and moon traverse the sky’ — these are the marks of appearance, the marks of the world. Yet seen from the true nature of all dharmas, whirlwind, rivers, wild horses, sun, and moon do not exist at all (originally there is not a single thing), so how could there be any felling of mountains, racing onward, tossing and drumming, or traversing the sky? Hence it is said: ever still, not flowing, not moving, not going round. (See the article
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”

) [Whirlwind] It is also called vairambha, translated as ‘great fierce wind.’ This is the great fierce wind of the kalpa-disasters. [Kalpa-disasters] The three disasters of fire, water, and wind that arise at the end of the kalpa of destruction; these three disasters sweep away the whole world. [The whirlwind fells the mountains] The great fierce wind of the kalpa-disasters blows down Mount Sumeru. [Wild horses] A figure for dust. It means that in the season of youth, when the yang force stirs, one gazes far off at the dust above lakes, marshes, and grassy plains, and it seems like galloping horses; hence it is called ‘wild horses.’
The next day Master Miao met me and said with delight: ‘What have you attained?’ I said: ‘In the night I saw two iron oxen by the river
(existence and nonexistence, coming and going, motion and stillness, birth and death)
fight and go into the water
(the two opposites are both extinguished)
, and to this day there is no more news of them
(entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality)

.’ The Master laughed and said: ‘I am glad you have the capital to dwell on a mountain.’ Before long, Shanyin invited the Chan Master Faguang of Mount Funiu to come. I had long admired him; when we met, I was delighted to be able to sit in inquiry with him. In conversation our minds accorded. I begged for further teaching, and he opened to me ‘to inquire with mind, intellect, and consciousness left behind, and to learn by stepping out of the road of sage and commoner’ — I deeply grasped its purport
(I deeply grasped the essential purport of the one road upward)

. Whenever I saw the Master in discussion, his voice came forth like the sound of a heavenly drum. At that time I knew that one who has awakened and made clear the mind-ground does indeed speak and breathe differently, and I deeply yielded to
(was deeply and sincerely convinced by)
that man.

One day he found my poems in his bag and read them, and sighed: ‘Such fine lines — where did you come by them?’ Then he laughed and said: ‘Fine they are, but there is one aperture still unopened.’ I said: ‘Has the Master that aperture opened?’ The Master said: ‘For thirty years I have seized dragons and caught tigers, and today a rabbit has run out of the grass and given me a fright.’ I said: ‘The Master is no dragon-seizer or tiger-catcher.’ The Master picked up his staff to strike; I at once held it fast, and stroking his beard with my hand, said: ‘You say a rabbit, but it is just a toad
(the Patriarch laughed, likening himself to one whose tone was too big)
.’ The Master laughed and left it at that.

One day the Master said: ‘You need not go elsewhere; I wish you would stay with old Funiu — that is my hope.’ I said: ‘I observe that the Master’s Dharma eloquence is not less than Dahui’s, yet in daily life you seem to have a mad manner, humming and muttering without ever stopping hand or mouth — why is that?’ The Master said: ‘That is my Chan sickness. When I first awakened, verse poured from me like a stream, day and night without cease, and I could not stop it myself, and so it became a sickness.’ I said: ‘When this sickness first came on, how should it have been treated?’ The Master said: ‘When this sickness breaks out, if one cannot see through it oneself, one must get a man of great eye and great skill to give one a sound beating and make one sleep deeply; on waking it naturally vanishes. I only regret that he had no venomous hand.’
The Master knew that I was going to Wutai at the New Year
(the first month of the lunar new year)

, and so sent me off with a poem, with the lines ‘Ride the lion in the clouds and come to see; / Let the hidden dragon in the cave go free.’ He asked: ‘Do you understand?’ I said: ‘No.’ The Master said: ‘I would have you not grasp a dead snake.’ I nodded
(I nodded and agreed)
. For a long time the Chan way had been without masters; only when I met Master Guang did I know that the ancestral school still had its strategy.

The Prince of Shanyin, asking whether my two parents were living, gave me two hundred in gold as provision for their support to the end. I declined, saying: ‘This poor monk has but begun his pilgrimage and cannot yet save himself — how should I dare to burden my two parents?’ I firmly yielded it and sent it to Master Guang.

(Ou Zhenbo of Nanhai seen a second time; the elder Wang Fengzhou and his younger brother Linzhou, each once. The Minister of War Wang Boyu a third time, and his younger brother Zhongyan a second time; Master Miaofeng a third time; the Chan Master Daqian Run once; the Prince of Shanyin a second time; the prefect Lord Chen once; the Chan Master Faguang once. Fengzhou was named Shizhen, a man of Taicang, an official to the rank of Junior Minister of War; his brother Linzhou was named Shimao, an official to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.)

Fuzheng’s note: it may be said that the Patriarch in those days, through Zhongyan, came to see Boyu, and of those two brothers Wang the elder was the finer; and through Fengzhou he came to see Linzhou, and of those two brothers Wang the younger was the finer. How rarely in this world are brothers so evenly matched!
staring wide-eyed without a word’ — what place does that leave Fengzhou? ‘His knee will bow to the old monk’ — that shows how far Nanming
(Wang Boyu)

saw. How great was Lord Wang’s eye, how great his vow-power, that he should have brought to fulfillment the great karmic occasion of Mount Wutai and its great merit — a great man indeed! He set out a vegetarian feast and invited the two Masters; the talk of that one gathering was all true speech, no lying speech, the most cutting and thorough speech, speech of the world and beyond the world. He set his heart on urging the carriage on, adding ever more, giving himself to mud and water for others, with no thought of his own person — among the buddhas and patriarchs of a thousand years, is there one who would not be moved and give thanks!

The two Masters set out for Wutai; their sharp exchanges matched point for point, their footing was tested and fitted — how then the begging and the slow going? The gratitude and the mounting of the carriage were all because Nanming
(Wang Boyu)
had awakened first.

The two men went one road: together yet each going his own way, parting and joining as they pleased, neither before nor behind the other. Everywhere they visited the ancient sites; at the river bank they caught up with each other and shared a boat, wearing through their straw sandals, swifter than the post. Their verses shone with light, quicker than the Book of Songs. King Wu might view his troops, and what harm if Boyi and Shuqi reined in the horses? If he did not meet the Master Daqian Run, he had long since met the First Patriarch of Shaolin.
How excellent and how fair!
(how wonderful)

The whirlwind felling the mountains seals afar the non-shifting of Caoxi; day and night, death and birth, he awakened to the non-duality of Buddha and Confucius. Only a Buddha knows a Buddha; only a patriarch knows a patriarch. Was it Master Miao who sang it out? Was it Nanming
(Wang Boyu)
who drummed it abroad? Wuji, Yungu, Mohe, Bianrong, and the Silent One
(the silent monk, the recluse of Mount Pan)

— these five teachers, were they not the first voices that roused his spirit and shook him awake? Xiaoyan and Faguang — were they not the stones from other hills that polished his jade? His entering Shaolin and paying respects at the First Patriarch — was that not the first cause of the robe and bowl that came from the West? His exile to Caoxi and revival of the Sixth Patriarch — was that not the fruit of sitting in the succession of the flesh-body? The Prince of Shanyin gave two hundred in gold, and he firmly yielded it and sent it to Master Guang of Funiu: was that to detain him? was it to seal his understanding? He sent the gold and departed at once: was that because of his old promise to Master Miao of Wutai? Was it because, a lion and a hidden dragon, he would not suffer any halter, and so showed forth the strategy of the ancestral school? The disciple Fuzheng, reading to this point, joins his palms in praise and says: ‘Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Bodhisattva Inexhaustible Intention unloosed the strings of pearls and jewels from his neck and gave them to Avalokiteśvara, yielding them to Master Golden Light. Prince Nata tore out his bones to repay his father and scraped off his flesh to repay his mother, taking leave of the means to support them to the end. A mother may cast her son into the river — may a son then neglect his parents’ support? Men of clear eye call this the utmost kindness and utmost filial piety of a hundred thousand million kalpas.’

Fuzheng’s note: again, according to the biography by Master Zhuan Gong: “Master Miao set out with the Master to fetch the canon, going through Henan and on into Shanxi, until they reached Puzhou. When the Prince of Shanyin heard that the canon was about to arrive, he led all the princes of the clan, with banners, canopies, music, incense, and flowers, to welcome the canon into his palace. Master Miao told the Prince: ‘The Master Chengyin of whom I spoke
(Chengyin, the Patriarch’s style-name)

, has come with me as well.’ The Prince, hearing it, was greatly delighted, and first asked to see the Master, only afterward having the canon put in place. He invited the Master to lodge in the palace, and sat facing him at every hour, probing the essential purport of the Surangama. The Prince asked Master Miao to request the Master to expound the Surangama Sutra, and the Master, with tears like rain, declined bitterly, saying: ‘I came to dwell on a mountain, not to expound sutras; I mean to flee at once.’ The Prince, knowing his resolve could not be turned, bowed to him and earnestly kept him for two or three months, and then asked Master Miao to accompany the Master to dwell on the mountain.” Alas! The Patriarch had early known Master Miao at Tianjie, and Master Miao had early recommended the Patriarch to Shanyin; and so when they met so suddenly, it was as with old friends at first sight. The fine affair of discoursing on the sutra came to an end when it could not be. As it is said: in knowing a man, what is prized is knowing his heart.

blocks.text: 8. Realizing the Way on Mount Wutai

inline.s: Wanli, third year
CE),
yǐhài ●

I was thirty. In the first month I went up Mount Wutai from Hedong together with Master Miao, passing through Pingyang, which was the Master’s native place. The Master, poor from youth, had met a year of famine; his father and mother died, and there was nothing in which to lay them out for burial. Now Shanyin and one or two of the authorities helped him. I chose for him a high, open site and had them buried together, and composed the tomb inscription. The Master’s family name was Xu; he lived in the eastern quarter of Pingyang, and was a descendant of Xu Juju of the Spring and Autumn period.

At that time the prefect Lord Hu, styled Shun’an, a man of Donglai, heard that I had come and lodged outside the city, wishing to see me once but unable to. When I set out, the Lord gave me post warrants. I said: ‘A man of the Way on pilgrimage has his straw sandals; what use has he for these?’ After I had gone, the Lord followed after me and only caught up with me at Lingshi; we went together to the provincial capital, where he kept me in talk for several days, and sent attendants to escort me to Mount Wutai.
[Post warrant]
A credential issued to travelers permitting them to eat and lodge at the post stations and to use their carts and horses.
On the full moon day of the second month I lodged at the Tayuan Temple; Dafang
(the Dharma Master Dafang)

was the host, and he divined for me a dwelling at the Dragon Gate of the North Peak, the most secluded and steep of places. On the third day of the third month, in the midst of snowdrifts, I cleared out several rafters of an old house and dwelt there.
[Tayuan Temple]
The great white stupa at Taihuai town on Mount Wutai in Shanxi; the temple takes its name from the stupa.

At that time, seeing the ice and snow over ten thousand mountains, a realm I had long admired, my body and mind were washed clean, as though I had entered the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Before long Master Miao went off to visit Yetai, and I dwelt there alone, raising a single thought; when people came I did not speak, only looked at them. After a long time I saw people as stumps
wù
, a tree stump)
, until I reached the place where I did not know a single word.

At first the great wind often rose and ten thousand apertures roared with rage; when the ice melted, the mountain torrents rushed and surged like thunder. In the stillness I heard sounds like a thousand armies and ten thousand horses marching out, and I found it very disturbing, so I asked Master Miao. The Master said: ‘The realm arises from the mind; it does not come from outside. I have heard the ancients say: if for thirty years one hears the sound of water without turning the root of the mind, one will realize Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration.’ So, because there was a single-plank bridge over the stream, I sat and stood on it every day. At first the sound of the water was clearly there; after a long time, when a thought stirred I heard it, and when no thought stirred I did not. One day, sitting on the bridge, I suddenly forgot my body, and the sound ceased utterly. From then on all sounds were still and did not disturb me.

Each day I ate only bran mixed with wild greens, washed down with a broth of coarse rice. At first people sent me three pecks of rice, and after half a year there was still some left. One day, after my gruel, as I walked in meditation, I suddenly stood still: body and mind were gone, and there was only one great treasury of light, perfect, still, and clear, like a great round mirror, in which the mountains, rivers, and great earth appeared as reflections. When I came to, all was lucid; I sought my body and mind and could not find them at all. Then I spoke a verse: ‘In a single flash the mad mind’s one thought rests; / Within and without, sense-roots and dust are wholly clear. / I turn and shatter the great empty space; / The myriad forms in array arise and cease.’ From then on, within and without were still and clear, and sounds, voices, forms, and marks were no longer obstructions; the doubts of former days vanished at once. When I looked at the cauldron, dust had gathered on it; because I was alone with no companion, I did not know how long it had been.
(Returning to the hut, I saw that the cauldron was covered with dust; because I dwelt alone without a companion, I did not know how much time had passed.)
That summer Xuelang came north and made a special visit to me, reaching Mount Wutai. He sat in my room and could not hold back his grief; he stayed two nights
(lodging two nights together)
and then took his leave. In winter I built a plank hut to dwell in.

(Master Miaofeng seen a fourth time; the Prince of Shanyin a third time; the prefect of Pingyang, Hu Shun’an, and the host Dafang, each once. Xuelang seen a fourth time. Shun’an is the later Censor-in-Chief Hu.)

Fuzheng’s note: at the Zongjing Hall of the Jingci Temple I heard it from three of the Patriarch’s eminent disciples — Zhiwei, Xuzhong, and Xiuliu — who said: ‘The Master and Master Miao were at the Dragon Gate of Mount Wutai, on Dragon-Turning Rock, sitting to listen to the boiling spring. After a whole year, when the sound of the spring never ceased and yet he did not hear it, he was able to enter samādhi. Master Miao, knowing that the Master was about to enter samādhi, made a separate hut at Muwa Liang. The Master entered samādhi, and no one knew how many days passed before he came out.’ From this we know that the dust gathering on the cauldron is precisely the affair of his dwelling alone in samādhi. Hence we know that one who has not awakened cannot enter samādhi, and one who has not practiced austerities cannot awaken. The ancient venerable ones speak of eighteen great awakenings and countless small ones. To say that after one awakening there is no further awakening is a great mistake. In those years his vow-power took ice, snow, and coolness as its contemplation, and when the karmic time came ripe he gained his strength from ice, snow, and coolness. This is what is meant by the fuel being spent while the fire is passed on; this is what is meant by the transmission of the lamp. The monks of today who transmit the lamp are simply transmitting fuel.

The few words written plainly of Gong still carry the meaning of that year’s pleading against the bitter cold, and to the end he did not forget the bond of shared birth and death. The Life of Gong says: at that time he sought in his own person for where the Master Hanshan was, passing Songshan and Shaoshi and Funiu, and going up to the Dragon Gate of Mount Wutai, where he found him amid the heaps of snow, with warm rice in the wallet at his waist
yǎn

, pledged to share life and death. The Master said to him: ‘Each man has his own resolve and his own karmic affinity. Your affinity lies in practicing the Dharma to continue the life of wisdom; you should not grow old in bare silence. This way has long been buried in the south of the Yangtze; you should succeed to the Dharma seat of our teacher Wuji, shoulder the charge laid upon you, and become the eye for gods and men, so as not to fail the karmic occasion of your leaving the world.’ Gong agreed, and so they parted with solemn feeling. Afterward he carried his staff through the various prefectures of the three Wu and taught the Dharma for thirty years, with great assemblies around him, and the lecture seats of the southeast flourished greatly.

In Wutai county of Taiyuan prefecture in Shanxi there is Mount Wutai; its five peaks rise above the clouds, and since their tops and backs can all be climbed, it is called the Five Terraces. It is the dwelling of Mañjuśrī and is called Mount Qingliang. This was the karmic thread of coolness, ice, and snow that ran through the Patriarch’s whole life. That the Tathāgata practiced the Way in the Snow Mountains, and that the Patriarch stood in the snow to receive the transmission — now I believe it.
Wanli, fourth year
CE),
bǐngzǐ ●

I was thirty-one. After my awakening, having no one from whom to seek further teaching, I opened the Surangama Sutra to verify it. I had never heard this sutra expounded and did not understand its meaning at all, and so now I simply illumined it with direct perception. As soon as a thought of mind-consciousness stirred, I would not allow it to deliberate. Thus for eight months
(eight months passed in this way; yueyue means the passing of a month)
, and the whole purport of the sutra was clear without doubt.

In the third month of spring the Master Lianchi visited Mount Wutai and called on me, staying ten days; at night we talked heart to heart with deep accord. In the seventh month of summer the prefect of Pingyang, Lord Hu, having been transferred to the post of military defense commissioner at Yanping, came into the mountains to visit me. In the quiet room there was nothing but oat
jīn
qū
noodles and minced wild greens
jī
, minced wild greens)
. At that time the heat was at its height, and the carriage driver
cān
and his attendants
(the men who drove the carriage)
went into the mountain ravine and broke ice to chew it. The Lord saw it and said: ‘This is another world. When I come here, worldly thoughts are like this ice.’
In the tenth month of winter that year the host of the Tayuan Temple, Dafang, was falsely accused and brought to trial before the circuit authorities, who proposed to sentence him
(in ancient times a criminal sentenced to exile was escorted station by station along the road, which was called peidi)

to return to lay life, and the monastery was near to ruin. At that time the Master Chekong of Mount Lu came and dwelt with me; he happened to see the affair and was greatly distressed by it. I said: ‘It is no matter.’ So I went in person to Lord Hu, traveling through the great snow. When we met, Lord Hu said with delight: ‘I was just thinking how the great snow in the mountains must be past bearing, and had written a letter and was about to send someone to welcome you. Your coming now is truly a response to my feeling.’ In the end he released the host
(and so the Dharma Master Dafang was released)
, and the practice-place was preserved whole. He firmly kept me for the winter, questioning me of the Way morning and evening, and I expounded for him the Prologue
(the Prologue of Hanshan)

At that time the Grand Coordinator Lord Gao was transferred to command at Daijun, and hearing that I was in the prefect’s residence, he said to Lord Hu: ‘I have a garden pavilion with many inscriptions; I would like to ask a man of high attainments for a poem.’ Lord Hu agreed and told me. I said: ‘There is not a single word in my breast; how can I make a poem?’ I refused firmly. Lord Gao asked again and again, and Lord Hu, at a loss, begged me earnestly. So he took collections of ancient and modern poetry and set them on the desk to stir my thoughts. I happened to open one, and as I was pondering, suddenly the mechanism stirred, and phrases came rushing so fast that they could not be held back. When Lord Hu came back from the hall, I had already written twenty or thirty poems. I suddenly became aware and said: ‘This is the demon of literary habit.’ I stopped at once and took only one piece to make up the number, not daring to bring out the rest. Yet the mechanism could not be stopped; before I knew it, all the poetry, books, and rhapsodies I had studied before, everything that had ever entered my eyes, appeared at once, crowding and filling the void, so that even if my whole body were mouth I could not utter it, and I no longer knew what my own body and mind were. Silently I looked at myself, on the verge of flying up, and there was no help for it.

The next day, after Lord Hu had seen Lord Gao off, I thought to myself alone: ‘This is what the Chan Master Faguang called the Chan sickness. Now that I am in its midst, who is there who can cure me?’ There was no way out
(no alternative)

but sleep, which alone might dispel it; if I could sleep soundly, that would be my good fortune. So I shut the door and forced myself to lie down. At first I could not at all, but after a long time I suddenly sat forgetting myself, as though asleep. The boy knocked at the door and I did not open; he pounded and I did not answer. When Lord Hu returned he urgently
jí
, urgently)
asked after me. Learning of this, he had them break a window and enter. They saw me sitting upright wrapped in my robe; they called and I did not answer, they shook me and I did not move.

Earlier, a Buddha had been set up in the study, and on the offering table there was a small striker. Lord Hu picked it up and asked: ‘What is this used for?’ I said: ‘When a monk of the Western Regions enters samādhi and cannot be wakened, this is sounded and he wakes.’ There had been such a saying, and the Lord suddenly remembered it and said: ‘Has the Master entered samādhi?’ He hastily took the striker and sounded it several dozen times at my ear, and I slowly came to; opening my eyes and looking about, I did not know where my body was. The Lord said: ‘I left, and you shut the door and sat; it is now five days — how do you find it?’ I said: ‘I do not know; it was but
(only)

a single breath.’ When I had spoken, I sat silently and examined closely, and in the end did not know what place this was, nor how I had come in. Then I looked back on the mountains and on all my former pilgrimage, and each thing was a matter of dream, sought for and not found. And all that had filled the void with turmoil
(the poetry, books, and rhapsodies that had so unbearably disturbed the whole void before he entered samādhi)

scattered like rain and cleared like clouds, and the vast sky was as if washed, all still and without a trace of image. Mind empty and realm still, its joy beyond compare. Then I said: ‘When stillness is utter, light penetrates; / In silent illumination the void is contained. / Turning back to look upon the world, / It is as a thing seen in a dream’
(a saying from the Surangama Sutra)
, and the Buddha’s words truly do not deceive me.

As I planned to return to the mountains at the New Year, I said to Lord Hu: ‘The forests of Mount Wutai are being grievously felled by wicked merchants; the Bodhisattva’s sanctuary will soon be bare and without a blade of grass.’ The Lord drew up a memorial requesting a strict prohibition. After that, when the state built various temples, they all relied on the timber protected by this prohibition; otherwise there would have been no wood to be had.
(The Master Lianchi seen once; Lord Hu Shun’an and Dafang each a second time; the Master Chekong and the Grand Coordinator Lord Gao each once.)
Fuzheng’s note: I have heard that the First Patriarch
(Patriarch Bodhidharma)
sealed his mind with the four fascicles of the Lankavatara, and now the Patriarch Hanshan sealed his mind with the whole of the Surangama. The sages before and the sages after — their measure
kuí
is one

(sages before and sages after: the standard by which they sealed the mind was always the same — using the teachings to seal the school. The Great Master Ouyi says in his Explanation of the Essentials of the Teaching and Contemplation Schools: “If one does one’s work without the seal of the teachings — without confirming it by the sutras — then one practices blindly and recklessly, and cannot avoid walking a perilous bypath.”)
The Master Lianchi was a man of Renhe in Hangzhou, of the Shen family, a family of note
(a distinguished clan)
, a notable scholar of the county school
(the county academy)
. At the age of thirty-two he went to the monk Xingtian Li and had his head shaved
(shaved his hair and left home as a monk)
, receiving the dharma name Zhuhong and the style Fohui. He then received full ordination from the Vinaya Master Wuchen Yu
(received the complete precepts)
. Because the mourning period for his mother was not yet complete
què
, as the three years of mourning for his mother were not yet finished)
, he carried his mother’s wooden tablet
(memorial tablet)

with him on his travels, and wherever he stayed he honored it, and at every meal he made offering. He called upon teachers everywhere; he traveled north to Mount Wutai, where he was moved by Mañjuśrī’s emission of light. He came to Funiu and joined the assembly in refining away demons. He entered the capital and called upon the two great elders Bianrong and Xiaoyan, from both of whom he received opening. Passing through Dongchang, he suddenly had an awakening, and made a verse: ‘The matter of twenty years ago was doubtful; / Three thousand li away, what strange encounter. / Burning incense and casting away the halberd, all as a dream; / Demon and Buddha vainly contend who is right and who wrong.’ Returning south, he joined five Chan sessions, and to the end he did not know the name of the monk on the next mat.
In the xinwei year of Longqing

, he begged his food at Fancun, and gradually entered the excellent karmic conditions of Yunqi, where he threw open the one gate of the Pure Land, gathering all three capacities universally to the end. Of his works, the Commentary and Notes on the Amitabha Sutra and The Chan Gate’s Spur to Advance were both praised by the Patriarch, for they reveal the dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land as not going beyond the one mind. His use of the power to transform was most subtle and discreet (his exercise of the power to teach and transform beings was exceedingly fine and cautious), and from the beginning to the end of his leaving the world there was nothing to be criticized; he may be called one who obtained the Buddha’s whole body and great function for the Dharma-gate.
[Gradually entering the excellent karmic conditions of Yunqi]
In the fifth year of Longqing (

), the Great Master Lianchi entered Mount Yunqi in Hangzhou, and seeing the seclusion and beauty of its mountains and waters, built a thatched hut and chose to dwell there, cultivating the samādhi of Buddha-recitation. His teaching reached far and near, monks gathered like clouds, and the Yunqi Temple became a great monastery.
In the dingsi year
(the forty-fifth year of Wanli,
, on his eastern journey he carried a text from Mount Heng and went to make offering
(on the Patriarch’s eastern journey he carried a text from Mount Heng and went to make offering to the Great Master Lianchi)
; yielding to the request of the monks and lay disciples, he composed a stupa inscription for him
(yielding to the request of the Great Master Lianchi’s monastic and lay disciples, he composed a stupa inscription for him)

, and also wrote seven praises for his portraits. The disciples of Yunqi painted a portrait of the Patriarch and kept it hanging in the mountains, and he wrote a praise for it himself. This was the great conclusion of the karmic occasion of the Master Lianchi’s visit to Mount Wutai in the bingzi year and their night of heart-to-heart talk

(this was the great conclusion of the Master Lianchi’s visit in the bingzi year and the karmic occasion of a night of heart-to-heart talk. The Chronicle of Master Hanshan records: ‘Master Lianchi traveled to Mount Wutai, called on him, stayed ten days, and by night faced him in talk with deep accord.’)

The Master Chekong first dwelt at the Yellow Dragon Pool of Mount Kuang, and on this occasion came to dwell with me at the Dragon Gate. From the tenth month of winter to the fourth month of spring he returned to Mount Kuang, having lodged at Mount Wutai more than half a year. This was because the Patriarch was kept there by Lord Hu of Yanping, and Master Che took his place overseeing the cooking pots. I had heard that Dafang’s false accusation was brought about by the wicked merchants who cut timber in the mountains, and the other mountain temples begged the Patriarch to go and seek a settlement from Lord Hu. Thus, having begun by resolving Dafang’s trouble, he ended by securing the prohibition on felling timber at Mount Wutai, and for a time all the mountain temples were moved by it. Truly
xún
, which truly shows that the Patriarch regarded
the dharma of the world and the Buddha-Dharma as not two.

The Prologue, spoken in Lord Hu’s residence, was set down from mouth and hand as it came, and finished within a month. Lord Hu had it transcribed into a volume and at once sent to the block-cutters, asking that it be entitled the Prologue and circulated; it was in truth his first work
(in truth the very first of his writings)

. In its ordering of chapters and sentences it seems to imitate Laozi, but the purport of its teaching lies in the three teachings being one Way. Fourteen years later, at Mount Lao, he wrote the Essay on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, which in truth illumines the earlier work and is illumined by it. I respectfully record three passages of the Prologue
(see
the Prologue of Hanshan
in the Dream-Roaming Collection
) to show the pattern of the rest:

It says: He who is meticulous in affairs is slack in mind; he who is meticulous in mind succeeds in affairs. Hence the more meticulous the affairs, the slacker the mind; the more meticulous the mind, the more successful the affairs. One whose mind is unwashed has no way to be meticulous; therefore the sage prizes washing the mind and withdrawing to hide in secrecy.

Again it says: The eye can contain heaven and earth, yet a mote of dust can spoil its clarity. The mind embraces the vast void, yet a single thought can block its breadth. Hence we know that a single thought is the root of birth and death and the source of calamity. Therefore, to know the incipient and perceive the subtle, the sage keeps his guard.

Again it says: When thought exists, things exist; when the mind is empty, dharmas are empty. Therefore if thought is melted into emptiness, one is free wherever conditions arise; if the mind is like a round mirror, coming and going are ever at leisure. One skilled in this does not go beyond the ordinary, yet sits upright in the wondrous realm. For the way of letters and the way of Chan are always one way; the demon of letters and the demon of Chan are always one demon. When the Way is a thousand feet high, the demon is a thousand feet high. Therefore it is said: demons come, Buddhas come; so long as the Chan sickness has not gone, how can one who flies up or sits forgetting himself ever enter samādhi?

Do those of this age who claim to be men of Chan concentration understand this case of the striker? Hu Shun’an’s karmic bond was deep and his feeling sincere; he asked about the striker to no purpose, and in the turning of an eye the omen was fulfilled — how could this be within human power! When I, Fuzheng, attended at the Zongjing Hall, what I saw morning and evening was this: he
(the Patriarch)

would sit cross-legged, and closing his eyes would enter samādhi, and opening his eyes would leave it; his two pupils would open like lightning, and he would answer a thousand words like an echo. Compared with that five-day samādhi then, this was mere beginners’ business.
The biography by Master Zhuan Gong
(the Life of the Great Master Hanshan, Restorer of Caoxi, written by his disciple Zhuanyu)

says: “That year the great snow lasted ten days on end, and the snow of all the peaks was blown and gathered at the Dragon Gate, burying the quiet hut more than ten fathoms deep. The Master and Master Che sat shut in, day by day kindling a fire to warm tea and food. The assemblies of the North Peak, the White Horse Temple, and the Central Peak, two or three hundred in all, made the resolve to take hoes, mattocks, baskets, and brooms, and with probing poles came down from the peak to find the road to the Dragon Gate. Probing as they dug, coming and going, the great assembly pressed on with courage, and only after two full days of probing with poles did they reach the quiet hut, shouting for joy as they came in. They all said: ‘After such a time in the mountains, it is very hard to have fire; this is the protection of Buddha and heaven.’ The Master and Master Che gave thanks, and then said: ‘One must pass through it, that is all.’ Then they melted snow for soup and gladly drank with the assembly. The next day the other mountain temples, hearing that the two Masters were unharmed, came bringing rice, flour, fruit, and cakes, until there was scarce room to set foot.” Later I also heard that when he dwelt with Master Miao, they too met this great snow and together dissolved it by entering samādhi. The ice and snow of the Dragon Gate were looked on as ordinary, and the chronicle for the most part does not record them.
Wanli, fifth year
CE),
dīngchǒu ●

I was thirty-two. In spring I returned from Yanmen, and thinking that the boundless kindness of my father and mother could never be repaid, and that in the Dharma I had many hindrances, and having seen the vow-text of the Great Master Si of Mount Heng, I made the resolve to prick my blood and mix it with gold to write out one copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra — above, to form a supreme karmic bond with prajñā; below, to requite the boundless
(unending)

kindness of my parents. It was in this year that the idea was formed. Earlier, the Holy Mother, the Empress Dowager Cisheng, to protect the realm, had chosen monks to recite sutras, and I presumptuously
jiàn
, expressing self-deprecation)
had my name entered. When she heard
(when the Holy Mother heard)
of the sutra-writing, she at once bestowed gold and paper in aid. In the fourth month of the following year the writing of the sutra began
(began to write the sutra)
. At that time Master Chekong returned to Mount Kuang, and I made ten poems to see him off.
(The Holy Mother Cisheng, that is, the Empress Dowager Li, seen once. Master Chekong, a second time.)

[Pricking the blood and mixing it with gold to write out one copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra] To prick out the fresh blood of the tongue, blend it with gold powder, and write out one copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra. The Great Master Yinguang says: “When the Great Master Hanshan wrote sutras, it was the Empress Dowager who supplied the paper and the gold. The paper for writing in gold must be blue for the writing to show; on white paper it does not show.
Thus Hanshan, at the Miaode Hermitage on Mount Wutai, pricked the blood of his tongue and ground it with gold to write the Avatamsaka Sutra.” (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
First Letter in Reply to Master Hongyi.)

Fuzheng’s note: the blood-written Avatamsaka is the very thing spoken of later as ‘sharing a vow with Master Miao to establish the Unhindered Assembly and place it in the pagoda treasury.’ The vow was made before the writing, and there was a spiritual response first. As for ‘the emperor heard and bestowed gold and paper,’ it means that because his name had been entered for the sutra-recitation, the Holy Mother heard of it and made the gift — not that it was the Emperor Shenzong. The bestowal of gold and paper for the sutra-writing, for the protection of the realm, was the beginning of the Holy Mother’s karmic occasion of leaving the world.

The Holy Mother, the Empress Dowager Li, was the principal mother of Shenzong; her faith in the Buddha was most fervent and her giving most ample, and the people of the capital called her the Buddha Old Lady.
Wanli, sixth year
CE),
wùyín ●

I was thirty-three. I applied myself to writing the sutra: no matter whether the stroke was large or small, with every falling of the brush I recited the Buddha’s name once. Whenever monks or laymen came from roaming the mountains, I always had an attendant announce them. Though my hand never ceased
chuò
, to stop)

from writing, I yet did not fail to respond, and to everyone who came to pay respects I would speak a few words. To men of high attainment and old friends I would always extend a seat on the meditation bed, and talk with them without failing, nor did it hinder my writing. Copying against the original, I made no error or omission. Each day was as usual, with not the slightest sign of disturbance. The neighboring
(neighboring counties)
elders
(senior and experienced men of letters)
secretly thought it strange. One day they brought several people to test me and deliberately made a disturbance; when the writing was done and they read it, they believed it thoroughly
(very much)
. So they asked Master Miao: how could Master Yin
(Chengyin, the Patriarch’s style-name)
do such a thing? Master Miao said: My friend has simply become thoroughly familiar with this samādhi.
In the Dream-Roaming Collection

‘Instructions to the Chan-man Xingchu Yuan on Sutra-Writing,’ it says: “When this old man (the Patriarch’s own name for himself) formerly dwelt at Mount Wutai, he pricked his blood and mixed it with gold to write out the great Avatamsaka Sutra. In the writing, without regard to the dots and strokes of the characters, their size or length, with each stroke laid down he recited the Buddha’s name once. Thus, dot by dot and stroke by stroke, the light of the mind streamed forth, thought after thought unbroken and unforgotten, without error or omission. After a long time it was no longer a matter of writing or not writing, and even in sleep and dreams it all became one piece. Thereupon, in all conditions, however moving, turbulent, or clamorous, his mind was still and clear, and he attained the gate of liberation, free and unobstructed in all conditions; and even all that he saw and heard was nothing but the true sutra appearing before him.”
From the time I began dwelling on the mountain
(from the time I came to dwell on Mount Wutai)
, and on through the writing of the sutra, I had many auspicious dreams.
At first, one night I dreamed I entered the Vajra Grotto; the stone gate was beside
bàng
the Great Prajñā Temple
(the stone gate is beside the Great Prajñā Temple)

. Entering, I saw it vast as space, with halls and pavilions and towers of incomparable adornment. In the main hall there was only a great couch and seat, and I saw the Great Master Qingliang reclining on the couch, with Master Miao standing in attendance on his left. I hastened in and bowed, and stood on the right, and heard the Great Master open to me the contemplation of the realm of the dharma-realm’s perfect interpenetration as first entered — the mutual entering of Buddha-lands, the intermingling of host and retinue, the mark of coming and going without motion. As he spoke of that realm, it appeared at once before my eyes, and I knew that my body and mind were in mutual accord and interpenetration. When he had finished, Master Miao asked: ‘What realm is this?’ The Great Master laughed and said: ‘The realm of no-realm.’ When I awoke, I saw of myself that mind and realm were fused and penetrating, and there was no further doubt or obstruction.
Another night

I dreamed that I trod on space and rose up, higher and higher without limit. Coming down, I saw the ten directions utterly void of anything, only a ground level as a mirror, of clear and lucid crystal. Far off I saw a single vast tower; its size was as space. In the tower was contained everything in the world — all persons, things, and undertakings, down to the smallest vulgar business of the marketplace — all embraced within, with nothing coming or going outside. In the tower was set a high seat of purple-gold flame color, which in my mind was the Vajra jewel seat. The tower was adorned with a wonder and beauty beyond conception. I was delighted and wished to draw near, and thought in my mind: how is it that in the realm of Qingliang there is such impurity? No sooner had the thought arisen than the tower receded. Then I thought again to myself: purity and impurity arise from my own mind — and the tower came near again.

Before long I saw ranged in attendance before the seat a great assembly of monks, of the tallest stature and incomparable dignity. Suddenly a bhikṣu came out from behind the seat, bearing a scroll of sutra, and coming down, gave it to me, saying: ‘The Master is about to expound this sutra and has specially commanded that it be given to you.’ I received it and unrolled it: it was written in gold in Sanskrit letters, which I could not read. So I put it in my bosom, and asked: ‘Who is the Master?’ He said: ‘Maitreya.’ I was glad, and followed the bhikṣu up, and at the steps of the pavilion I closed my eyes and gathered my thoughts and stood. Suddenly I heard the sound of a gong; opening my eyes, I saw that Maitreya had already ascended the seat. I at once looked up and bowed, and gazing up at his face, saw it shining with a purple-gold light than which nothing in the world can compare. When I had bowed, I thought to myself: now he speaks specially for me, so I am the one who fits the occasion — and so I knelt long, took up the scroll, and unrolled it. I heard him say: ‘Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Depending on consciousness, one is defiled; depending on wisdom, one is pure. Defilement has birth and death; purity has no Buddhas.’ At this, body and mind suddenly became empty, and I heard only the sound in the air, clear and distinct. When I awoke, it was as in a daze, the words still in my ears. From then on the distinction between consciousness and wisdom was clear to my mind and eye. And I knew that the place I had reached was the Tuṣita heaven, the pavilion of Maitreya Buddha.

Another night I dreamed that a monk came to announce: ‘On the summit of the North Peak Mañjuśrī has prepared a bath; you are invited to come.’ I went with him and entered a vast, pure hall filled with fragrance, whose attendants were all Indian monks. I was led at once to the bathhouse, undressed, and entered the bath, where I saw someone already in the pool. Looking, I saw it was a woman, and my mind was disgusted and I did not wish to enter. The person in the pool then deliberately floated her form, and I knew it was a man, and so entered and bathed together. The man, with his hand
bailed
hù
water

and washed me, from the head downward, pouring into my five viscera like washing a tub of meat, so that each of the five organs was scoured clean and nothing remained; there was left only a skin, like a cage of crystal, utterly transparent.

Then the man in the pool called for tea, and I saw an Indian monk holding half a skull, as if a melon had been cut open. Looking at it, with the brains dripping, I felt great loathing. The monk then scooped some out with his finger and showed it to me, saying: ‘Is this impure?’ and at once put it in his mouth and ate it. Thus he took and ate, and it was sweet as syrup. When the brains were all eaten, only bloody water remained. The man in the pool said: ‘You may give it to him.’ The monk then handed it to me, and I took it and drank; its taste was like sweet dew. Drinking it down, it penetrated the pores of my body, flowing out in every direction. When I had drunk, the Indian monk rubbed my back and gave a great slap with his palm, and I awoke. Then my whole body streamed with sweat like water, and my five viscera were clear. From then on body and mind were as if washed, light and quick beyond compare. Dreams such as these were mostly auspicious omens. In short, they were all exchanges
zuò
. I have once heard the Buddha’s words, ‘one often has such good dreams’ — truly so.
(Master Miaofeng seen a fifth time)
[One often has such good dreams] The Buddha said: “
The Buddhas’ bodies are golden-hued, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits. Hearing the Dharma and expounding it for others, one often has such good dreams.” (Lotus Sutra)
Fuzheng’s note: in my attendance I often saw the Patriarch’s calligraphy; both his regular and his running script were excellent, all founded on the standards of the two Wangs
(Wang Xizhi and Wang Xianzhi)
, entering and departing with flexibility and change. When he pricked his blood to write the Avatamsaka, he did not stop his brush nor refuse his guests
(did not turn away visitors)

, and with every stroke he wrote he recited the Buddha’s name once; even when talking with men of high attainment he still did not cease writing. Copying against the original and checking it, there was not a single error or omission. Without great Chan concentration and great spiritual power, how could one be utterly free of error or omission?

To speak truly of this one great dream-samādhi: in the first dream he saw the Great Master Qingliang in person, in the Vajra Grotto, leaning on the couch and giving him a prediction, and at once the realm appeared before him and body and mind were without obstruction. This accords with the earlier record of his never forgetting Qingliang and never forgetting the karmic bond with Master Miao.

In the second dream he came to the Tuṣita heaven and the pavilion of Maitreya; he saw with his own eyes the adorned jewel seat, and Maitreya Buddha commanded a monk to give him the sutra. He ascended the seat and, face to face, heard the teaching of defilement and purity, clear in his ears, and at once the distinction between consciousness and wisdom was clear to his mind and eye.

In the third dream he went in person to the bath prepared by Mañjuśrī on the summit of the North Peak. His disgust at the woman and her floating forth as a man was simply the Patriarch’s own manifestation of a boy’s untouched body. Single-minded and undistracted, originally pure, without the least entanglement or defilement, he was able to enter the ocean of fragrant water and shed his skin and change his bones. Yet again the dream showed forth fair and foul, pure and impure; fright and loathing, love and attachment, and all manner of marks, transformed and made strange to the uttermost, so that the five colors had no master.

In the end it is like Fotudeng, who at the water’s edge broke open his chest and washed his stomach and intestines clean, so that his body was transparent as crystal. In the end it is like Huangbo and Linji, each blow leaving its mark, each slap its blood. In the end it is like Xuanni
(Confucius)

seeing King Wen and the Duke of Zhou in person. Long and short, black and white, eyes open and eyes shut — none of it is other than true dream. With clarity within him and his will and spirit like a god’s, the real is the dream real, and the dream is the real dream; therefore it is said that the utmost man has no dreams.
[Fotudeng]

The Lives of Eminent Monks records: “When Dao’an first came to Ye, he entered the Zhong Temple and met Fotudeng; at the first sight of An, Cheng recognized his worth, and they talked together all day.”

Nevertheless, had he not cast aside body and life and dwelt deep in the heaps of ice and snow, buried alive for six years and all but dead many times over, how could he have come to life out of death, lifted his head out of the great dream, wrapped heaven and enclosed earth, illumined the past and shone upon the present, and become a man beyond measure? Had he not, at the place on the ridge of Dayu where the robe and bowl were seized
(Huiming seizing the Sixth Patriarch’s robe and bowl; see
“A Detailed Explanation of the Sixth Patriarch’s Platform Sutra”

, died and been born again, passing through three turns and nine revolutions and renewing two temples, how could he today sit upright in his flesh body, manifest at Caoxi, seal in the north at Qingliang, and in the south keep company with Patriarch Lu
(the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, called Patriarch Lu because his family name was Lu)
Hanshan’s Dharma-word says: ‘From the tip of a single hair, a Buddha-realm of jewels wells forth.’
(the Patriarch said: “Suddenly I saw at the tip of a single hair the appearance of the jewel king’s realm.” (From the Dream-Roaming Collection
‘Memorial on Rebuilding the Halls of the Patriarch’s Court at Caoxi’))
On the day when he took up his brush and spread out his paper
chǔ
, a term for paper)

to set down his own chronicle, he was no more than one austere old man within the four seas, one who had taken refuge in the venerable elders. Monks of Chan in every quarter, seeing the chronicle of the three dreams in his lifetime, would surely laugh and call it raving. Hearing the account of the three dreams after his passing, they would go so far as to denounce it as a demon-realm. Only the Patriarch himself could believe it; in all the world and in after ages there was certainly not one man who could believe it. But now
(the Patriarch has already attained the indestructible vajra body)

we know that Maitreya’s giving of the sutra fully confirms that the future kalpa is as the kalpa without beginning, and that Mañjuśrī’s preparing of the bath was to bathe this skin-and-flesh body into a solid body. When Fuzheng’s commentary reaches this point, he is dazed as in a dream, entering Caoxi. In the inexpressible, inexpressible, inconceivable, he joins his palms once more and says: ‘Rare indeed, World-Honored One.’
Wanli, seventh year
CE),
jǐmǎo ●
I was thirty-four. In the autumn of that year the Great Cishou Temple in the capital was completed. At first the Holy Mother, to make offering for the late Emperor and to protect the imperial person
(to sacrifice to the late Emperor and to bless the present sovereign)
, wished to build the Tayuan Temple and the precious relic stupa at Mount Wutai. She instructed the ministers,
who considered
Mount Wutai too far from the capital
(distant)

, and so a lucky site near the capital was divined, and the Great Cishou Temple was built. When the work was done, it was reported back. The Holy Mother, thinking the vow to Mount Wutai unfulfilled, instructed the Emperor, who again sent eunuch officials with three thousand workmen and craftsmen to the mountain to build. At that time the court had but lately begun to do Buddhist works, and eunuch officials had but lately been sent outside; it was feared they could not finish the task, and that it would injure the Dharma-gate. At that time I did all I could to mediate and protect, and to the end nothing went amiss.
(The Holy Mother seen a second time. The late Emperor is Longqing
(Muzong of the Ming)
, seen once. The Emperor is Wanli
(Shenzong of the Ming)
, seen once.)

Zheng: I once rejoiced in the Great Temple of Compassionate Longevity built by the Sage Mother, the Empress Dowager Li. Going by the Grand Canal from Tongzhou, one reaches Zhangjiawan and enters the temple. It lies fifteen li south of Tongzhou city and twenty-five li north of the capital's Haidai Gate. The local people
(those whose families have lived here for generations)

say: 'This place was long a ruined shrine, commonly called Horse-Shed Temple.' The Buddha's Old Lady, on its former site, made all things new and grand, and the imperial title was fixed as Great Compassionate Longevity. First the Hanshan Patriarch, and afterwards Master Daguan, were invited, and both dwelt in this temple. That the chronicle writes in large letters, 'In the autumn of that year the capital completed the building of the Great Temple of Compassionate Longevity,' is to show that the karmic cause of his entering the capital, spreading the Dharma for the state, and meeting with disaster began here. Truly, for one who has attained the Dharma, life hangs by a thread. The meaning is set forth at the outset, in the manner of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
[The brush of the Spring and Autumn Annals]

Confucius revised the Spring and Autumn Annals upon the facts of history: what deserved to be written he wrote, and what deserved to be cut he cut. Praises and censures were lodged in the very words; he flattered none and fawned on none, so that rebellious ministers and villainous sons were afraid. Thereafter 'the brush of the Spring and Autumn' came to mean the historian's brush that records events as they are.
The eighth year of Wanli
), the gengchen year

I was thirty-five. In that year a special edict ordered the measuring of fields and grain throughout the empire, not an inch of soil to be left out. Mount Tai had never entered the tax registers; the knavish men of that county, in their deception, wished to shift five hundred shi of grain quota onto Mount Tai, and repeatedly sent out documents to have the land there surveyed and reported. In all the monasteries and quiet retreats of the mountain there was not one man who could be at peace, and from this Mount Tai became a den of foxes. The elders of the various mountains
(the aged and the greatly respected)

said to me, 'Be at ease, masters; have no anxiety — we shall take thought for it in good time.' Thereupon I strove with all my strength, turning this way and that to devise a means, and laid the whole matter plainly before the authorities, and in the end the survey was remitted and not a single pint or peck was added. Thus the sanctuaries of Mount Tai were preserved whole.
Zheng: know that conditioned merit, regarded simply as unconditioned merit, is naturally accomplished.
The ninth year of Wanli
), the xinsi year

I was thirty-six. I established the Unhindered Assembly. At first Master Miao had also pierced his blood and written out the Avatamsaka Sutra, and, sharing my vow, wished to build a perfect sanctuary to be called the Unhindered Assembly. Master Miao went about collecting alms, and money and grain were gathered in full. From the capital five hundred greatly virtuous and famous monks were invited, and every arrangement for the sanctuary was complete.
[The Unhindered Assembly]

The assembly without restriction. Such an assembly offers alms to all alike, like the thousand-monk feasts of people today, binding ten thousand into one karmic bond: anyone at all may take part, with no barrier and no restriction.
It happened that the emperor had issued an edict praying for an heir
(praying for the birth of an imperial son)
, and sent officials to Wudang
(Emperor Shenzong believed in Daoism)
. The Sage Mother sent officials to Wutai
(the Empress Dowager believed in Buddhism)
, to this very temple. I held that every Buddhist rite performed by monks is nothing but a prayer for the state's blessing and a secret aid
(to aid and assist)
to the imperial virtue
(the emperor's character and measure)

. Now the prayer for an heir is the very root of the state, and nothing is greater than this. I wished to merge the entire work prepared for the sanctuary, all of it, into the single matter of praying for the heir
(praying for the birth of a crown prince)
and not to do it for the sake of my own petty name.
It is the chronicle's
grand
as the karmic cause of his entering the capital, spreading the Dharma for the state, and meeting with disaster, began here.
Truly, for one who has attained the Dharma, life hangs by a thread.
Master Miao did not understand the meaning; nor did the eunuch envoy sent from above understand the matter, but set his heart only on currying favor
(flattering and going along with others).

I thought it wholly wrong, and so contended with all my strength, offending them; yet in the end my proposal was carried out. Still, the name of having offended the eunuch envoy also got abroad. Presently the sorcerers of Jiangnan stirred up trouble, and those who envied me straightway wished to seize on this to wound me and break up the sanctuary. Yet because the matter was titled a prayer for the heir and for the state, it was preserved whole to the end without mishap.

In that year the pagoda was completed, and I straightway deposited the gold-written Avatamsaka Sutra in the pagoda's treasury, together with a single scroll of vow-text. For the sanctuary I had had built, at my own begging, a revolving-treasure-reel of the Huazang World; for its use within, the offerings, utensils, vessels, and provisions — everything needed. Master Miao, in the capital, seemed not to know of it; all was managed by me alone, for ninety days and nights without closing my eyes. When the tenth month came round, Master Miao brought the more than five hundred monks he had invited, and in a single day they were all assembled: a thousand men within and without, and the seating, offerings, tea, rice, and food provided for the retreat were orderly and without loss or confusion, and no one knew whence it all came. Onlookers were all astonished. At the outset, the land-and-water rite was opened for seven days and nights. For those seven days I ate not a grain of rice, only drinking water. Yet nothing was lacking in the handling of affairs; the offerings made to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, five hundred tables changed daily, came in due order without fail, and no one knew whence they came. Onlookers took it for the work of spirits; I myself knew it to be the added power of the Buddha.
(The Sage Mother saw him three times, the emperor twice, and the crown prince — that is, Taichang
(the Guangzong emperor after Emperor Shenzong) —
once; Master Miaofeng six times.)

Zheng: born in the Shenzong reign, he knew that the matter contended over, the imperial succession, was the greatest. What the Hanshan Patriarch's coming into the world chiefly concerned was the succession above all else. For his merit lay in being the first to advocate it, and in the lords who settled the succession, who took thought for the numinous crux of the altars of state; it did not lie in attaching himself to the last-ditch arguments over establishing an heir, which opened the calamitous arena of factions. The blood-written sutra and the Unhindered Assembly were the first cause of the prayer for an heir. The emperor sent eunuchs to Wudang, secretly to pray for an heir for Consort Zheng — a prayer made to Daoists. The Sage Mother sent eunuchs to Wutai, secretly to pray for an heir for Consort Wang — a prayer made to monks. Each had her own faith, each her own petition. The eunuch, spying out the emperor's mind and fearing the unpredictable, therefore set his heart on currying favor, and so was of two minds toward the Sage Mother's command: he did not wish to merge the blood-sutra-completed Unhindered sanctuary that had been made with Master Miao into the single matter of praying for an heir, so as to proclaim a splendid deed.

The Unhindered Assembly was gathered by alms and had nothing to do with the prayer for an heir; the prayer for an heir was sent from within the palace and did not establish the Unhindered Assembly. That is why Master Miao did not understand: his view rested on the Buddhist affair. The Hanshan Patriarch contended with all his strength: his sworn heart rested on the foundation of the state. The excellent cause happened to gather, and his single-hearted sincerity touched Heaven. Managing it alone, he went ninety days and nights without closing his eyes. When the whole company of monks was assembled, he drank water for seven days and ate not a grain of rice. The smallest tasks were borne as if by ghosts, and the great offerings moved as if by spirits. Had it not been the radiance of samādhi, how could he have drawn such added power from the Buddha? Thereafter
(afterwards)
came the disaster at Mount Lao, and the emperor
(Emperor Shenzong)
said: 'The whole court is for the monks; I alone am for the Daoists.' This binds together from afar the one case of Wudang and Wutai.

[Born in the Shenzong reign, he knew that the matter contended over, the imperial succession, was the greatest.] Those who lived in the reign of Emperor Shenzong knew that the dispute over the imperial succession was the greatest of matters, and in it both the Hanshan Patriarch and Master Daguan were implicated. Let the dispute over the imperial succession be briefly set out here: the birth mother of Zhu Changluo, Emperor Shenzong's eldest son, was Consort Wang Gongfei, originally an ordinary palace maid who served the Sage and Compassionate Empress Dowager (Emperor Shenzong's own mother) in the Palace of Compassionate Tranquility. One day Emperor Shenzong came to that palace to pay his respects to his mother; it happened that the Empress Dowager was not there, and the emperor noticed the fresh and comely woman of the Wang clan, and thereupon privately favored her, and she conceived. The Sage and Compassionate Empress Dowager herself had been a palace maid, and when she learned of it she not only did not make trouble for the woman but was greatly delighted, and summoned Emperor Shenzong to ask him the truth of it. Yet Emperor Shenzong flatly denied that he had ever favored her. Only, since the emperor's daily life and conduct were recorded by appointed officials, the matter had long since been entered in the Inner Diary of Activity and Repose. In the end Emperor Shenzong, unable to deny it further, blushed and silently admitted it. In the eighth month of the tenth year of Wanli, Consort Wang gave birth to Emperor Shenzong's first son, Zhu Changluo. Though the palace woman Wang was made Consort Gong, the eldest imperial son Zhu Changluo was never established as crown prince. Four years later, in the first month of the fourteenth year of Wanli, Consort Zheng, whose favor overshadowed the whole inner palace, gave birth to a son, named Zhu Changxun. Consort Zheng was clever and quick, and Emperor Shenzong loved her deeply and kept her to the end of his life. Because the emperor followed her every word, for a long stretch she was the figure on whom court and realm fixed their eyes, and she drew the curses of nearly everyone. Since Emperor Shenzong's empress had no son and Consort Zheng was the emperor's favorite, upon the birth of her son the emperor at once raised her to Noble Consort. The Grand Secretary Shen Shixing and others held that the eldest imperial son, Zhu Changluo, was already five years old, that his birth mother Consort Wang Gongfei had never been heard of as receiving any promotion, while Consort Zheng, having just borne an imperial son, was at once enfeoffed — plainly showing that Consort Zheng monopolized the emperor's favor. The ministers feared that in time the elder might be set aside and the younger raised up, and so submitted memorials asking that the Eastern Palace be established. But Emperor Shenzong, urged on by Noble Consort Zheng, wished always to seize the chance to make Zhu Changxun crown prince, and so devised every kind of delay, meeting the strongest opposition from the ministers. At that time the crown prince was also called the foundation of the state, and therefore this struggle between emperor and ministers was also called 'the dispute over the foundation of the state.' The ministers strove to have Zhu Changluo established as crown prince, while Emperor Shenzong put it off again and again; so the ministers contended again and again, and this went on for fifteen years, raising a great hue and cry throughout the city and making the palace struggle tangled and complex. In the eleventh month of the thirty-first year of Wanli (

), someone wrote A Continued Discussion of Hidden Dangers and Great Designs, which was spread widely through the capital as a handbill; overnight it was found everywhere, from the palace gates above to the streets and lanes below. The text said that Shenzong had been forced to establish Changluo as crown prince and that the crown prince's position was precarious, and roundly criticized the chief minister Shen Yiguan and the Grand Secretary Zhu Geng. When Emperor Shenzong learned of it he was greatly enraged, and ordered the Eastern Depot, the Embroidered-Uniform Guard, and the patrol offices of the five wards to search and seize at once — 'the author's name must be found' — and thus arose the 'Sedition Case.' Thereupon Shen Yiguan of the Zhejiang faction seized the chance to frame the Donglin Party men Guo Zhengyu, Shen Li, and others. Master Daguan too was falsely accused of connection with the seditious book, arrested and thrown into prison, and after cruel interrogation sentenced to death.
The tenth year of Wanli
), the renwu year
I was thirty-seven. In the spring of that year I lectured on the Profound Discourse on the Avatamsaka. Within a hundred days the resident monks
(that is, the monastery, since a monastery is the dwelling-place where monks permanently abide)
and the assembled monks and laity who gathered from all ten directions —
jì
, to arrive)
monks in black and laity in white
(zi is purple-black and su is white; monks wear purple-black robes and laypeople mostly wear white, hence monks and laity are called zi and su)

were never fewer than ten thousand a day. They ate at one meal as though seated in a single hall, without mixture or confusion, and no sound of summons or knocking was heard. All was directed by me alone, and no one else had a hand in it; even the wise could not tell how it was done. So the strength of my whole life was spent to the utmost here. When the assembly ended, I examined what remained in the storehouse: all the money and grain, some ten thousand in all, I sealed and handed over to the temple's keeper, to be the permanent holding. Then Master Miao and I, with a single bowl, drifted off light and free.

Master Miao went to Luya; I, being ill, went to the Zhangshi Cliff at Zhending to recover. I wrote a poem, with the lines 'Sheer cliffs propped against the sky must bar the sun; on the broken cliff there is no road, only a flying ladder.'
In the eighth month of that year the crown prince was born
(Consort Wang gave birth to the eldest imperial son).
I returned to the Zhongfeng Temple west of the capital and wrote the 'Preface to the Re-engraved Zhongfeng Collected Records,' and passed the winter in a water-fast in a stone chamber.
(Master Miaofeng saw him a seventh time; the crown prince, that is Taichang, a second time.)

Zheng: reckoning it, in the tenth month of the xinsi year, because of the prayer for an imperial heir, the great Unhindered sanctuary was established at the Great Pagoda Temple on Mount Tai, completing the merit of seven days and nights. And it happened that in the eighth month of the following year, the renwu year, Consort Wang of the inner palace gave birth to the imperial heir Taichang. The chronicle writes in large letters: 'In the eighth month of that year the crown prince was born.' Before the heir was born it first wrote of an imperial heir; when he had not yet been established as crown prince it wrote plainly 'crown prince' — great indeed is this brush of the Spring and Autumn! Reckoning the ten months of human gestation, it tallies exactly and without error; plainly this was the Buddha and the patriarchs responding in incarnation and bringing about a noble birth. Therefore in the end he mounted the great treasure, and benevolence was suddenly spread abroad; though the state's fortune was on the verge of change, the reign was altered and it did not perish — truly there was reason for it. Consort Wang, after the succession was settled, was enfeoffed as Consort Gong, and in the thirty-seventh year she died
hōng
, in antiquity the term for the death of a feudal lord or a high official holding rank).

When Emperor Guangzong ascended the throne he added the posthumous title Empress Xiaojing. At her death it was kept secret and not made known abroad. Four days later, at the request of the cabinet ministers, it was proclaimed. At that time Shen Youze, a herald
(Shen Youze, under observation in the Ministry of War and appointed a herald of the Herald's Office),
submitted a memorial asking that the rites be increased
(memorializing for increased rites for the deceased Consort Gong),
but no reply was given
(no answer was made).
The affairs of the palace women's quarters
(the palace)
are hard indeed to speak of.

From this Master Miao parted from the Hanshan Patriarch; two years later he went with Dafang to the capital to receive the imperial bounty, and it seems the two never met again. The Hanshan Patriarch from this point completed eight years of coming and going on Mount Tai: one great period of cultivation, great realization, great sanctuary, great functioning of his powers, great spiritual response. He sealed up the temple treasury with its ten thousand measures of money and grain, and with a single bowl drifted off light and free. Before this
(prior to this)

came the Wutai Dragon Gate — a grand finale, a grand clearing of the stage: 'Sheer cliffs propped against the sky must bar the sun; on the broken cliff there is no road, only a flying ladder.' After this
(following this)
came Mount Lao and Caoxi — a grand prophecy
chèn
, a prophecy)
word
(a grand prediction)
