, a grand turning of the outward face of things. The clear-eyed can gather its meaning for themselves.
Here ends the case of ascetic practice and attainment on Mount Tai.
The eleventh year of Wanli
), the guiwei year

I was thirty-eight. In the first month of spring, when the water-fast was finished, I thought that under a great name it is hard to dwell long, and so, on account of my hollow reputation at Mount Tai, I went away to the shores of the Eastern Sea. Here I first changed my name to Hanshan, and from that time I no longer knew myself as Chengyin.

At first, when this temple of mine was destroyed by fire, my resolve was set on restoring it, and so I practiced while waiting for the conditions. But having dwelt at Mount Tai for eight years, and having gathered a fair opportunity, I feared that going far away would lose the time; and so I hid at the Eastern Sea
(had I gone far to another region, I would have feared losing the chance to rebuild this temple; therefore I hid at the Eastern Sea).
This was my true intent. On the eighth day of the fourth month of summer I arrived at Mount Lao.

At first, when Master Miao took his leave, thinking I could not travel alone, he appointed his Dharma-companion Dezong to be my attendant, and he followed me. I had earlier read the Avatamsaka Commentary

the Chapter on the Abodes of the Bodhisattvas, which says: 'In the Eastern Sea there is a place named the Nārayaṇa Grotto, where from of old the hosts of Bodhisattvas have dwelt and abided.' The Qingliang Commentary says: 'In Sanskrit, nārayaṇa means firm and enduring — this is Mount Lao of the Eastern Sea. The Tribute of Yu
(an ancient Chinese classic of geography, one chapter of the Book of Documents)
In the region of Qingzhou, Dengzhou, and Laizhou
of the Documents of Xia: the grotto exists there to this day.' Because I admired it, I made a special visit. Reaching Mount Lao, I did indeed find the place, but it was uninhabitable.

So I explored the deepest recess on the mountain's south side, backed by a host of peaks and facing the devouring sea, utterly strange and exquisite — truly no place of the human world. The place was named Guanyin Hermitage; it was an old shrine, but only ruined foundations remained. On investigation, it was where, at the beginning of the Yuan, the Seven Perfected
(the seven perfected ones revered by Daoism)
came forth in the East and, borrowing the awe and favor of Shizu
(the founding sovereign, here meaning Emperor Taizu of Ming, Zhu Yuanzhang),

seized many Buddhist temples and turned them into Daoist cloisters. When Shizu returned from his western campaign and the monks memorialized him, he ordered many of them restored. Only Mount Lao, lying remote by the sea, was not reached, and so all were left in ruin.

I rejoiced in the place's solitude and remoteness, a true refuge for one fleeing the world and cutting off men, and I vowed to dwell there. At first I spread a single mat beneath a tree; seven months later I found the local layman Zhang Daxin, who cut the thatch and built me a hut to live in. A full year
(one year)

after entering the mountain, no one came or went, and my heart was full of joy. At that time at the Lingshan Temple in Jimo there was Master Guifeng, an eye to that whole region; I was glad to have his company.
(Master Miao's Dharma-companion Dezong, the layman Zhang Daxin, and Master Guifeng — one appearance each.)

Zheng: understand that the reason for the great name at Mount Tai was that the Unhindered sanctuary of those days was too magnificent, and the name of gaining an heir by praying for one on behalf of the palace was too conspicuous; and the tale of offending the eunuch envoy was heard within the palace, which made the matter greater still and the name even less habitable. Therefore Mount Tai was hard to return to, another mountain hard to settle on, and he went far off to the Eastern Sea and hid at Mount Lao.

At first he went from Bao'en Temple to the capital with a mind set on restoration. This time he went from Mount Tai to the capital likewise to look for the conditions of restoration. From the capital he hid at Mount Lao; from Mount Lao he obtained the canon and returned to his temple; again he asked for accumulated reserves, and the matter was about to come to fulfillment. All of it was nothing but the vow to repair the temple at Mount Tai, and so he says, 'this was my true intent.'

Mount Lao stands by the sea in Jimo county of Laizhou prefecture, and is also called Mount Lao. It is where the King of Wu climbed the mountain and obtained the Scripture of the Lingbao Deliverance of Men, and where Feng Meng of the Han also hid himself from the world; the place is the most desolate and remote. Yet he did not shrink from a thousand li: he left the old for the new, the familiar for the strange, the north for the east, the mountain for the sea, the ice for the sun, the civilized for the barbarous, as though there were no choice but this. It was chiefly because his name for contending against the eunuch envoy had got abroad, and so he knew the difficulty and withdrew. In the end, from this the great catastrophe arose, and from this the great catastrophe was also dissolved: season and karmic condition — not even the Buddhas and patriarchs can dodge them.
The twelfth year of Wanli
), the jiashen year
I was thirty-nine. In the ninth month of autumn the Sage Mother, for the merit
(the merit and toil)

of the Wutai prayer for an heir, sought out the three who had charge of the work, namely Dafang, Miaofeng, and myself. The two masters had already arrived and received the bounty; only I could not be found, and so she sought me urgently. She commanded my former host, the abbot Duan'an of Longhua Temple, to seek me in person. He knew I was by the sea, and so came staff in hand and made known her gracious command. I earnestly declined, saying: 'If I am granted the imperial grace to grow old on this mountain, I have received bounty enough; what else should I seek?'

The abbot reported back, but the holy will was not to be stayed; soon a site was chosen west of the capital for a temple, and a eunuch envoy was sent with a set time for me to come. I declined and would not go. When the eunuch returned and reported my firm resolve to lie fast on the mountain, the holy will took pity on me. Asking whether I had a dwelling, and learning I had none, she at once sent three thousand in gold, and again dispatched the same envoy to bring it, that I might build a hermitage. When it arrived I urgently stopped it, saying: 'A few rafters of thatch give me joy enough; what use is more?' and would not accept it. The envoy pressed me, not daring to return without completing his mission. I said: 'The ancients had the case of forging an edict to relieve famine. Now Shandong has had a bad year; why not spread the holy compassion wide over the starving people?' Thereupon I had a monk lead the envoy and scatter the gifts among the monks and Daoists, the orphaned and aged, and the prisoners in every prefecture, each taking a sealed register from the office concerned and reporting the receipts. The holy heart was greatly delighted and sighed in admiration without end.
Later, when I met with disaster and was brought down to the Zhenfu prison, and was interrogated
jú
, to interrogate a criminal)
as to my having several times used the inner treasury's gold
(the money and goods of the state treasury),
I answered: 'Pray examine the issue registers of the inner treasury.' When the emperor
(Emperor Shenzong)
checked them, there was only this one matter of famine relief, and not a thread besides; and the imperial mind was at once appeased.
(The Sage Mother saw him a fourth time, the emperor a third time, and the abbot Duan'an of Longhua once.)

Zheng: concerning this 'inner treasury' — it was not the emperor's purse for expenses, but only the Empress Dowager's own kitchen allowance. To economize and give in charity is the excellent cause of filial compassion; why should there suddenly be a matter of investigation? Was it not that, through the establishing of the heir, a rift in the palace bred trouble that spread to this? Had he not thrice declined the alms of the faithful, one would fear that the Sea-Seal Temple could be raised and could be demolished, while the Western Mountain temple could not be demolished and could not be raised. As for the matter of the gift relieving the famine, great compassion was before his eyes, and great spiritual power was in the turning of an eye. Excellent, excellent!
Wherever 'the holy' is used, it means the Sage Mother, not His Majesty. This particular 'His Majesty' means the emperor himself.
The thirteenth year of Wanli
), the yiyou year

I was forty. The people of the East had never known a monk. When I dwelt in the mountain, the Huang clan was the greatest there, and its sons gradually drew near. The man now called the heretic Luo Qing was a native of Chengyang at the foot of the mountain, the very soil where the heresy grew; and so his teaching spread throughout the East, and men knew nothing at all of the Three Jewels. Dwelling there and gathering and transforming them, in time every one of their teachers came with their followers to take refuge, and from this they first came to know the Buddhadharma — this was the beginning of my work of founding.
[Luo Qing (

His courtesy name was Menghong, his sobriquets Sifu and Wuwei; a native of Jimo in Shandong, and a leader of Ming-dynasty secret sects. Later disciples called him Patriarch Luo, and also 'the Old Patriarch of Non-Action.' The religion he founded was commonly called the Luo Teaching, also the Luo Dao Teaching, the Patriarch Luo Teaching, or the Non-Action Teaching. Once the Luo Teaching arose, nearly all popular religions were influenced by it, including the well-known Vegetarian Teaching and White Lotus Teaching; and later sworn societies such as the Green Gang also honored him as their founding patriarch.
Zheng: from this we know that with affinity one can gather and transform heretics, and without affinity one cannot transform even a Daoist
(a man of the Way).

The heretics submitted because they saw the eunuch envoy coming and going. The Daoists stirred up trouble because they suspected a rift within the palace. Therefore it is said: 'The Buddhadharma is entrusted to kings and great ministers
(the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hengchuan Xinggong says: 'The Buddhadharma is entrusted to kings and great ministers, and to powerful donors
(almsgivers)
, so that lamp may light lamp and the succession continue unbroken.'),
The fourteenth year of Wanli
), the bingxu year

I was forty-one. In that year the canon was bestowed. Earlier, when the canon was first printed at the beginning of the dynasty, there were scriptures composed in this land that had not entered it; now the Sage Mother commanded that they be printed and included. When this was done, the emperor issued an edict bestowing fifteen sets of the canon to be scattered among the famous mountains of the empire. First, four sets were placed at the four frontiers: Mount Lao of the Eastern Sea, Putuo of the Southern Sea, Emei of Western Shu, and Luya in the north
(Mount Luya, in the heart of the Guancen range some

kilometers southwest of Ningwu county town in Shanxi: forests of peaks in close array, range upon range of ridges, sheer cliffs and precipices, green waves and soughing pines, and its main summit most singularly beautiful, with grotesque rocks in jagged ranks, towering and upright, dominating the north).

At that time the Sage Mother, because of the Mount Tai connection — and because she had repeatedly summoned me without my coming, and I would not accept her gifts — sent one set of the canon first to the Eastern Sea. I did not know of it at first. When it arrived, there was nothing in the empty mountain to house it, and by grace of the provincial governor's office the local authorities were ordered to enshrine and supply it.

When I saw that there was an imperial command, I went to the capital to give thanks for the grace shown me. There I received her compassionate command that all the palace ladies each contribute alms, and that a temple be built to enshrine and supply it, and she asked that its name be Sea-Seal Temple. While I was in the capital I happened to hear that Chan Master Daguan had come to visit me by the sea, and I straightway hurried back, traveling stages without rest to overtake him. When I reached the foot of the mountain, it chanced that the Master was coming out of the mountain, and soon we returned together and lingered twenty days. He gave me a poem, with the lines 'Idly I came to dwell beside the sea; through the error of fame I fell to Shandong
(by the error of a great name, I drifted to Shandong)

In the eleventh month of that winter, because from the xinsi year onward I had been mostly toiling, never at rest, I was much fatigued. Now that the meditation room was at last built, I could settle in peace, put body and mind down, and my joy was beyond words. One night, rising from still sitting, I saw the sea calm and the sky clear, a vast single storehouse of brightness, utterly without a thing. Straightway I spoke a verse: 'Sea calm, sky clear, snow and moonlight; here the sage and the common cut off both walk and hiding. The diamond eye bursts forth, and the sky-flower falls; the whole great earth returns to the ground of quiescence.' Returning to my room, I saw the Surangama Sutra on the desk, and opening it at random I came at once upon: 'Your mind and your body, and the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth beyond, are all things within the wondrous luminous true mind.' Then the whole sutra's field of contemplation was clear before my mind and eye. At once I took up the brush and wrote out The Mirror Suspended in the Surangama, one scroll, finished before half a candle had burned. At that moment the meditation hall was just opening for the quiet period, so I called the duty monk into my room and had him read it to me; and I myself heard it as though it were the talk of a dream.
(The emperor saw him a fourth time, the Sage Mother a fifth time, and Chan Master Daguan once.)

Zheng: one may observe that famous mountains are many, yet only fifteen sets of the canon were bestowed. The first four sets were bestowed on the four frontiers, and among the frontiers the first to receive was Mount Lao of the Eastern Sea, because the Hanshan Patriarch had made his dwelling there. Master Miaofeng first went to burn incense at Putuo, then went to Wutai and dwelt at Luya; and so the bestowals at Putuo and Luya were both on Master Miao's account. That Mount Lao and Luya, not being great famous mountains, were first to receive the new canon: though it was by the emperor's edict, it was in truth the Sage Mother's intent, her deep and constant remembrance of the merit of the prayer for an heir at Mount Tai.

From the time the Hanshan Patriarch parted from Miaofeng, the one he called his profoundest Dharma-comrade was none but Daguan. After years of longing for each other, he ordered his carriage a thousand li, to meet face to face like needle against needle, and so they faced each other on that day. Had he not hurried by forced stages to overtake him, he could hardly have escaped returning empty when the mood was spent. That one meeting at Mount Lao is a friendship enough for a thousand ages.

[The Outer Records of the Hanshan Patriarch] says: “All is illusion; everyone knows that. But one must have the capacity to master illusion, and only then is one not turned about by illusion. While I was at Sea-Seal, I once thought of the case of Patriarch Lu and the man who came at midnight to cut off his head, and wished to learn his power of samādhi. Every night I opened the door and practiced contemplation: if someone should come to borrow my head, I would gladly give it up. Tonight so, tomorrow night so, and after a long while I felt a settled power of concentration within me. Then one night word came that a robber had entered the temple. I said, 'Just call him in.' I lit the candles and sat upright, with no thought of fear. When the man reached the door, he crawled on hands and knees and dared not come in, a great tall fellow. I called out to him, 'There is nothing here,' and ordered two hundred coppers taken from the store and given him. Had I not mastered it beforehand, I know not what panic would have come over me. On another evening as I sat, body and world both became empty, Sea-Seal emitted light, and I entered the state where mountains and rivers shake, and gained the corresponding wisdom. Presently I awakened to the crucial passage of the Surangama, and it was suddenly clear before my eyes. I hurried to light a candle and write it down, my wrist unable to keep pace, until the fifth watch was spent, and The Mirror Suspended in the Surangama was finished. My attendant came out to look, and seeing the burnt-out candle on the desk, was astonished. Ah — all these are matters within the storehouse of brightness, not to be sought out by deliberate reckoning.” The latter passage agrees with the matter and meaning of the record, and both the phrasing and the brushwork are excellent. Read them together and one may awaken to the Way and also to letters. One must understand that the two things recorded there are Patriarch Lu making me, not I making Patriarch Lu; the Surangama sealing me, not I sealing the Surangama. Such is the meaning of recording them with care.
The fifteenth year of Wanli
), the dinghai year

I was forty-two. In that year I repaired and built the halls, and first opened the hall to preach the precepts to the assembly. From then on monks from the four quarters came in increasing numbers, and for the laypeople I expounded the Direct Explanation of the Heart Sutra. In the eighth month of autumn, Censor-in-Chief Hu
(Hu Shun'an; censor-in-chief: a provincial governor)
asked leave to return to his fields, and brought his own son to be sent forth from home as an attendant, naming him Fushan.
(Censor-in-Chief Hu, a third appearance; Fushan, a first. The censor-in-chief is none other than Shun'an, formerly prefect of Pingyang.)
[Nazi]
Also called the patch-robe monk; another name for a Chan monk, because Chan monks mostly wear a single patched robe and wander from place to place.

Zheng: when the Hanshan Patriarch journeyed east, he met the scribe-attendant Master Shan Zhiwei. Later, at the Mirror-of-Essence Hall of Jingci, they met face to face morning and evening and shared the same profound ford. The Master assisted in the brush-and-ink affairs of the abbot's quarters, and in the end completed the Dream-Wanderings Collection. Among the Hanshan Patriarch's outstanding disciples of that time, none surpassed Master Zhiwei. In hardship and peril there was no place he did not follow; the records of the complete collection all came from his hand. His kinsman Lord Hu Shun'an, a man of Donglai, on account of an old bond with his native place, sent him forth from home at the Sea-Seal Temple on Mount Lao. Afterwards he was entrusted with the abbot's quarters at Wuru, presided over the Cloud of Dharma Temple on Mount Kuang, and at seventy passed away seated.
The sixteenth year of Wanli
), the wuzi year

I was forty-three. At that time a student read my Mirror Suspended and asked: 'This sutra's contemplation of mind is fully clear, but the words have not been wholly dissolved; I fear later students will find it hard to enter. I beg you to dissolve every word back into the contemplation of mind; that would be the greatest gift of Dharma.' I then first conceived the idea of composing the Comprehensive Commentary
(the Comprehensive Commentary on the Surangama Sutra)
, and had already established its great purport, but had not yet set brush to paper
(but had not yet written it down on paper).
The seventeenth year of Wanli
), the jichou year

I was forty-four. In that year I read the canon and expounded the Lotus Sutra and the Awakening of Faith for the assembly. Since parting from Wutai I had had the thought of visiting my parents, but feared to fall into worldly truth, and so only kept it in mind. One evening, sitting in stillness, a verse came to me unbidden: 'Day after day the misty waves soak the cold sky; fish and birds roam together in a single mirror. Last night the moon beyond heaven suddenly sank; its lone brightness must have mingled with the black dragon.' Then I cried out to my attendant: 'Now I can return to my old home and see my two old parents!'

Earlier, I had begged for one set of the Great Store of Sutras for Bao'en Temple. In the tenth month of winter I went to the capital to ask for the canon, and the emperor at once ordered it sent. Carrying it
jī
, to carry with one)

along, in the eleventh month I reached Longjiang, and the temple's precious pagoda gave forth light for several days together. On the day the sutras were welcomed, the pagoda's light was like a bridge turned northward to welcome them, and the monks walked within the light. When the sutras were enshrined and the sanctuary established, the light remained without break day after day. Those who came to gaze numbered more than ten thousand a day, and took it for a rare auspicious sign.

At that time my old mother, hearing that I had come, first sent someone to ask on what day I would reach home. I said: 'I have come on business of the court, not for my family's sake. If my old mother can receive me joyfully as though we had never parted, I can stay but a single night; otherwise I shall not go home at all.' When my old mother heard this she said: 'To meet again alive, there is joy enough and to spare — how could there be any sorrow? One meeting would do; how much more two nights!' When I reached home, my old mother received me and laughed aloud for joy
(laughed so heartily she could not stop), and I thought it very strange.

That night as we sat, an elder of the clan asked me, 'Did you come by boat or by land?' My old mother answered at once: 'Why ask whether by boat or by land?' The questioner said, 'From where, then, have you come?' My old mother said, 'From the sky.' I was startled and said, 'No wonder the old woman could let me go as she did!' Then I asked my mother, 'Since we parted, have you thought of me?' She said, 'How could I not think of you!' I asked, 'How did you console yourself, Mother?' She said, 'At first I did not know. When I learned you were at Wutai, I asked the monks where Wutai was.' They said: “Beneath the North Star — that is where your son is.” From then on I worshipped the North Star each night and called on the Bodhisattva's name, and thought of you no more. Had they told me you were dead, I would not have worshipped, and would have cut off the thought as well. Now that I see you, you have come as a transformation body
(From 'come from the sky' and 'come as a transformation body' one may know that the old mother was a woman who had seen her own nature; therefore at their meeting there was no trace of grief)

.' The next day I sacrificed at the ancestral graves and chose burial sites for my two parents. When a site was found, my old father was already eighty, and I joked: 'Today we bury the old man alive, and save him the trouble of coming again later.' I took up a mattock to cut the ground. My old mother snatched it from me, saying, 'The old woman will bury herself — why trouble anyone else?' and struck several dozen blows herself. After three days we took leave. My old mother was joyful as ever and never once knitted her brows, and I first knew that my old mother was no ordinary woman.

In Jimo there was a student named Huang Nashan, styled Ziguang, younger brother of the present Grand Marshal Lord Huang. When I first came to the sea, he was nineteen, and at once took refuge and asked for instruction. I gave him the Surangama, and in two months he could recite it. From then on he kept a vegetarian diet, and though his parents reproved him, his mind never altered. He set his will on inquiry and did not let his side touch the mat. When I was returning south, Ziguang thought to himself: 'I was born in a border land, and for long kalpas have not heard the names of the Three Jewels. Now by good fortune I have met a great good friend, a friend who came unasked. If he does not return, we shall lose our refuge.' So before the Great Being Guanyin he tore the skin of his arm and made a lamp offering, praying the Great Being to keep me from staying away long. From this the burn spread and pained him; day and night he sat upright in pain, holding the Great Being Guanyin's name, and only after three months was he healed. When he was healed, he saw that the scar had formed the image of the Great Being, brows, eyes, body, and robes, as clear as if painted — and even his mother and wife did not know of it. He constantly asked to leave home, and I utterly refused. Then he said, 'Your disciple will turn a somersault and come back; why does the Master stop me?' From this we know that in the land of the mlecchas
(the border lands)
the Buddha-seed is never cut off.

At first, because I was determined to rebuild this temple of mine, I dwelt at Mount Tai, and the matter had already found its opportunity; but since the expense would run to several hundred thousand, it was not easy to speak of, and so I waited for the time by the sea. By now the opportunity was nearly ripe, and so, using the sending of the Great Store of Sutras as my occasion, I returned to the Southern Capital
(the people of the Ming called Nanjing the Southern Capital)

, and laying out the whole story of this temple, reported back and memorialized the Sage Mother in full, saying: 'The work is great and the cost immense, and it cannot lightly be undertaken. I beg that the Sage Mother daily reduce her table by a hundred taels, and let it accumulate for three years: then the matter may be begun; in ten years the work can be completed.' The holy heart was greatly delighted, and at once ordered the accumulation to begin in the twelfth month of that year.
(The Sage Mother saw him a sixth time, his father a third time, his mother a ninth time; the younger brother of Grand Marshal Lord Huang of Jimo, Huang Ziguang Nashan, once.)
Zheng notes: by the chronicle, the Hanshan Patriarch went north at twenty-six and returned south at forty-four to see his two parents; he had passed eighteen years.

Enlightenment at Mount Tai, success in the prayer for the heir, teaching at Mount Lao, the sanctuary appearing at Sea-Seal. The imperial edict and the carrying of the canon, the pagoda giving forth light, the whole city gazing in homage, the temple courts stirred with awe. And beyond that, his two parents well, his clan not left orphaned, the ancestral graves still standing, the burial sites chosen and the ground cut with his own hand. In the world and beyond the world, how many are there who return home having passed the examination of an empty mind? The man who goes home in brocade — though he be emperor, king, or general — what is there to envy in him? How much more when Old Lady Pang shows her form and the Old Woman of Tai reveals her wonder, and the whole family gathers round to speak the words of the unborn
(the truth of no birth and no death)
. Question and answer, coming and going, are nothing but states of tears or laughter; and who can tell whether they are kindness or grudge? Ah, this is one great making of monsters.

Huang Ziguang — who was he? He burned his arm in longing for his teacher, and his scar became a Buddha's image; the Yellow Plum oath of old, the somersault and return — and after years had passed he passed away seated. Ah, this is no small making of monsters either.

Where this chronicle says 'the emperor at once ordered it sent, and he reported back and memorialized in full, calling her the Sage Mother,' it does not concern the emperor himself. The later order to accumulate funds was set aside when he met with disaster, through his request that the emperor examine the inner issue registers. The Caoxi condition was fulfilled; the Bao'en condition was not. How could one have been exchanged for the other? In sending the sutras amid the light, he had long since fulfilled the vow of a lifetime for the temple where he left home.
The eighteenth year of Wanli
), the gengyin year

I was forty-five. In the spring of that year I wrote out the Lotus Sutra to repay the Sage Mother. At that time some who wished to seize the sanctuary for themselves stirred up a Daoist priest from beyond the pale
(so they bribed the Daoists)

, claiming falsely that we had occupied their Daoist cloister, and gathered a great crowd to lodge a suit at the governor's yamen. The governor, Lord Li, had already learned the whole matter and deeply detested it, and so sent it to Laizhou prefecture to be thoroughly investigated. I attended the hearing in person and did all I could to save them. Those several hundred rascals raised an uproar in the prefectural city, an encirclement like that of Kuang. At the time I had two attendants with me; I sent them elsewhere, and went on slowly alone. The ringleader among them, flourishing a blade, capered before me and sought to kill me. I looked at him smiling and said: 'If you kill a man, how will you answer for yourself?' His spirit failed him and he at once put up the knife, and they escorted me for some two li outside the city. When the time came to part, the mad crowd suspected their leader of favoring me and wanted to beat him. I calculated silently that if the crowd charged, the man was in danger. What was to be done? So I hesitated. At the point of parting I dragged the mad fellow with me to my lodging, shut the door, took off my outer robe, and sat legs spread
(that is, sitting like a winnowing basket, with both legs stretched out)

, talking and laughing as ever, and took fruit and melon for us to eat together. At that time the whole market was abuzz: 'The Daoists have killed a monk!' When the prefect heard it he at once sent many runners to arrest them. The crowd was terrified and all knocked their heads on the ground begging pardon. I said: 'Do not be afraid; only hear what I have to say.' When we came before him the prefect asked: 'Have the mad ruffians killed the monk?' I said: 'Not at all. When they came to arrest them, the monk was sharing fruit and melon with their leader.' The prefect said: 'Then why the uproar?' I said: 'Only market noise.' The prefect wanted to put them in the cangue. I said: 'You wish to disperse them; the cangue would only hold them fast.' The prefect understood, and ordered the local officers to drive them all out; within three days the whole mad crowd had dispersed, and the affair came to peace. In that year I wrote the Essay on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
(The Sage Mother saw him a seventh time; Lord Li the governor and the prefect of Laizhou once each.)
[The encirclement of Kuang]

When Confucius traveled through the states, he passed through the region of Kuang. Because the men of Kuang had once suffered slaughter and plunder at the hands of Yang Huo of Lu, and Confucius resembled Yang Huo in appearance, they surrounded and attacked him.
Zheng: observe the struggle in this place — every step is the art of war, every step a Chan device. If one is thus, there is no difficult affair under heaven and no man hard to manage.

In the eight essays on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, only the essay On the Dharma of Mind is short in lines and ink, yet comprehensive in the three teachings; it is appended here to preserve its general purport.

The essay On the Dharma of Mind says: 'In youth I took Confucius as my teacher, yet did not know Confucius; I took Laozi as my teacher, yet did not know Laozi. Then I withdrew into the deep mountains and great marshes, and practiced stillness to contemplate the mind. From this I came to know that the three realms are mind only and the ten thousand dharmas consciousness only. Once there is the contemplation of mind-only and consciousness-only, then all forms are shadows of the mind, and all sounds are echoes of the mind. Thus all sages are the tip of the shadow, and all teachings are the smooth echo. Because the ten thousand dharmas are manifested by mind alone, the language of governing the world and the means of livelihood all accord with the true Dharma. Because outside the mind there is no dharma, every dharma is true. The deluded cling to them and so they are not wondrous; if one awakens to one's own mind, then no dharma is not wondrous. Mind and dharma both wondrous — only a sage can do this.' When the Hanshan Patriarch composed these eight essays he happened to be settling his dispute with the Daoists; was this too an allegory of harmonizing the three teachings
(Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism)
? It is fitting that the Daoists bore him no grudge.
The nineteenth year of Wanli
), the xinmao year
I was forty-six. In that year the Sage Mother had a sandalwood Vairocana Buddha image made, and the Great Hall was completed. In autumn my disciple Huang Ziguang passed away seated
(died seated in meditation: one of long practice sits upright and passes away in peace).
(The Sage Mother saw him an eighth time; Huang Ziguang, a second.)
Zheng says: his deep approval of Ziguang, and this special entry answering the matter of the jichou year, are likewise the brushwork of the Spring and Autumn.
The twentieth year of Wanli
), the renchen year

I was forty-seven. In the seventh month of autumn I went to the capital and visited Master Daguan at Shangfang. In the Jin dynasty there was Master Wan, who, fearing that the three disasters would destroy the kalpa and leave no Buddhadharma, carved sutras in stone and stored them in a stone chamber. His pagoda court had been sold by monks, and the Master redeemed it, and thought that I should come and write a record of it. I happened to arrive, and the Master was overjoyed. As soon as we met we went together to Mount Stone-Sutra, and I wrote the Record of Master Wan's Pagoda Court and the Record of the Re-enshrining of the Relics, together with the Sea-Seal Drafts I had written before. At that time, facing Master Da and lingering with him forty days and nights, was the strangest thing of my life.
(Master Daguan, a second appearance.)

Zheng notes: in Fangshan county there is the Stone-Sutra Grotto. In the Sui dynasty Master Jingwan cut stone into slabs and carved one whole canon, storing it in the grotto and closing it with a stone door; through succeeding ages there were inscriptions. After Master Da took it in hand, a monk of the Stone-Lamp Hermitage in the capital, Zinan, collected funds to continue the carving, in the wuwu year of Wanli. Zheng, being in the capital for the provincial examination on the classics, did his utmost to assist the work.

I also heard it from an attendant of Wuru: 'In the renchen year the two Masters met in a garden in the western suburb of the capital and sat facing each other in stillness for forty days and nights without closing their eyes. They planned to compile a Record of the Transmission of the Lamp for the Ming dynasty, and therefore agreed to go and dredge Caoxi to open the Dharma lineage, and so on.' Here he says only 'the strangest thing of my life' without detail; perhaps this was not strange enough, and there was something stranger still.
The twenty-first year of Wanli
), the guisi year

I was forty-eight. In that year Shandong suffered a great famine, and the starving dead lay along the roads. All the provisions stored in the mountain I distributed to relieve the people near the mountain. When that was not enough, I took passage on a convenient boat to Liaodong and bought
dí
, to buy in grain)
several hundred shi of beans to relieve them. From this, among the people of the four communities of the border mountain, not one died of hunger.

Zheng: reading to this point, one heaves a long sigh! Thus lightly was the karmic bond of Sea-Seal on Mount Lao brought to an end. Yet in the twelve years before and after, his teaching spread and his relief was wide, and he was already within inconceivable merit.
The twenty-second year of Wanli
), the jiawu year

I was forty-nine. In the third month of spring, Lord Zheng Kunya, governor of Shandong, entered the mountain to visit and ask about the Dharma, and I spoke to him words of skillful means. In the tenth month of winter I went to the capital to offer congratulations on the imperial birthday festival, and was kept there over the New Year, and was asked to preach the precepts at the Temple of Compassionate Longevity. At that time, because of the matter of repairing my own temple, and knowing that the Sage Mother's reserves were already substantial, I asked that the work be begun. But the emperor, being then in council over the Japanese invasion of Korea and the sending of a punitive expedition, told me to wait, and so it was shelved.
(The Sage Mother saw him a ninth time, the emperor a fifth time, and Governor Zheng Kunya once.)

Zheng notes: to offer congratulations on the imperial birthday festival means that at the winter-solstice festival he congratulated the Sage Mother, not the emperor, and afterwards the word 'emperor' is specially used to distinguish him. The Sage Mother asked him to preach the precepts at the Temple of Compassionate Longevity, which closes the earlier case of 'in the jichou year the capital completed the building of the Great Temple of Compassionate Longevity.' The matter of repairing his original temple at Bao'en: the Sage Mother's reserves were already substantial, and the affair was on the verge of success when the conditions lapsed and it was not done, which closes the earlier case of his original intent in going north and restoring his own temple.

The first to set the meaning at the outset and the last to close it at the end: this is the brushwork of the Spring and Autumn. It was not for the repair of the temple that he entered the congratulatory audience and stayed in the capital. Had he not come and gone to the capital for three years, he would not have been drawn into the debates that brought disaster. I heard it from an attendant of the Mirror-of-Essence Hall in those days: 'When the Sage Mother asked him to preach the precepts, the gifts of ceremony were exceedingly grand
(the ceremonial gifts were extremely magnificent).

The Temple of Compassionate Longevity was also called the Tushita Court of Shangfang; the abbot's quarters were spread with nothing but felt and brocade. The fruit and viands offered to the Buddha were all rare things from the four quarters. The robes, food, and vessels the abbot's quarters required were sent by the grand master of rites, streaming along the roads morning and evening, and the onlookers were packed like a wall. Nobles and relatives
(meritorious imperial relatives and nobles)

and palace eunuchs made offerings beyond counting. Even children who rejoiced in it all received their share. Of the money and grain bestowed from the inner treasury he accepted not a fraction; he took only the begging bowls of the fifty-three pilgrimage-practicing monks. In one day every bowl came back empty, yet gold, coin, cloth, and grain had already filled the chests and overflowed the granaries. Thousands of people gathered daily, and none failed to eat their fill of the fragrant rice. On the eighth day of the twelfth month of that year the Sage Mother specially commanded the attendant Chen Ru to bestow a Vairocana cap, a purple kashaya of woven brocade, a Zhigong pair of shoes, and inner garments, all of thick wool above and below. The Hanshan Patriarch declined them all; only at the third bestowal did he accept — and having accepted, still did not wear them.'

At that time Master Daguan was dwelling at Mount Stone-Sutra. He opened the stone chamber, and beneath the Buddha's seat found a casket holding countless Buddha relics. When the Sage Mother heard of it she too sent attendants with offerings of food, bestowed a purple kashaya, and made great offering to the relics for three days, re-enshrining them in the stone cave. Master Da wrote a memorial declining the gift and yielding it to the Hanshan Patriarch. His verse said: 'Thirty years I have roamed rivers and seas; a single patch-robe has seen the seasons through. I am ashamed my poor bones cannot wear the purple; I pass it to a higher man, whose merit is the greater.' For since the Hanshan Patriarch was then in the capital and would not wear it, Master Da also would not accept, wishing to yield it all to the Hanshan Patriarch and have him wear it; hence he said the merit would be the greater. On the day the robe was bestowed, the Sage Mother commanded a eunuch attendant to convey her decree that she wished to invite him into the palace and ask his Dharma name to his face. The Master knew it was not the emperor's intent, and earnestly declined, saying that by ancestral rule monks do not enter the palace; so eunuchs were sent to paint his likeness, and a name was chosen and presented. The Sage Mother hung the portrait in the inner hall and made the emperor stand in attendance and bow to receive the Dharma name. The emperor served the Sage Mother with the utmost filial piety, and on that day he could not help his color changing. The Sage Mother's Dharma name is recorded after the chronicle; in the Dharma-lineage verse, 'virtue great, blessing deep and wide,' of its forty characters the second, 'great,' was used for her taboo-name; when the name was chosen and brought into the palace, the attendants were by no means allowed to hear it. But from that time the generation of 'great' was avoided, and all Dharma kin began with the 'blessing' generation. At that time the Sage Mother's reserves for repairing the temple were substantial; this excellent cause was a mere trifle. Had the issue registers been examined then, and the reserves come into his hands, he could not have cleared himself, and how could he have escaped disaster? Fortunately the matter was shelved and did not touch the donated funds. He gave thanks for the grace and returned; the disaster left him unharmed. And so I reflect that the bowl inscription of those days, 'lighter than ten thousand measures,' and the robe inscription, 'lighter than all under heaven,' are here greatly verified — how could they have been empty words!
Here end the three cases: Mount Lao, Compassionate Longevity, and the resolve to restore his own temple.
The twenty-third year of Wanli
), the yiwei year

I was fifty. In the second month of spring I returned from the capital to the sea, and straightway met with disaster. At first, because of the canon bestowed by imperial order, a eunuch envoy had been sent back with it. Earlier, the emperor had always detested the eunuchs, because their requests for Buddhist affairs were too frequent. When one of them first came to the Eastern Sea, the inner court happened for another reason to provoke the imperial anger, which was about to reach those around the Sage Mother, and the great ministers feared for them. It happened that among the powerful eunuchs there was one who envied the envoy who had carried the sutras and wished him dead; seizing the occasion, he stirred up trouble. He therefore made use of the earlier rumors among the Daoists and had a runner of the Eastern Depot
(the secret-police agency of the Ming)

disguised as a Daoist strike the Drum of Petition to bring the matter forward. The emperor read it and was greatly enraged, and ordered an arrest; and because of the affair of sending the sutras, I too was involved.
[The Drum of Petition]
A drum hung outside the court hall; when the people wished to remonstrate or to redress an injustice, they could strike the drum and have it brought up to the throne.

When I heard the report I gathered the assembly and said: 'The Buddha, for the sake of one living being, does not abandon the three evil paths. This Eastern Sea is the land of the mlecchas, where the names of the Three Jewels
(the Jewel of Buddha, the Jewel of Dharma, the Jewel of Sangha)

were never heard. Now I have taught and transformed here for twelve years: three-year-old children all know to invoke the Buddha. As for those who have abandoned the crooked and returned to the upright, they fill village after village and household after household. My vow is fulfilled; what regret is there in death? Only that my resolve to repair this temple remains unfulfilled — that is what pains my heart.' And when I left Jimo, the scholars and common people, old and young, of the city saw me off with tears, which shows how deeply men's hearts had been moved.
When I reached the capital I received the decree sending me down to the Zhenfu Office
(a subordinate office of the Ming Embroidered-Uniform Guard, which held the prison for those confined by imperial decree).
At the interrogation, the officers had first received the emperor's mind
(meaning the sovereign's will and intent)
and wished me to confess to having solicited, in former days
(previously),

the benefactions of alms that the Sage Mother had sent out to the famous mountains, no less than several hundred thousand in all. Under cruel torture I said: 'I am ashamed to be a monk and have no way to repay the state's grace; how should I now grudge a single death, and wound the emperor's great filial piety? To twist the truth and confess falsely in order to ensnare profit, and to serve the imperial will by damaging the cardinal bonds of morality, is by no means the heart with which a subject loves his lord. What would the historians write?' I resisted with all my strength to the death, and admitted only the seven hundred-odd taels previously given by the faithful, and asked that the emperor examine the inner issue registers. When they were examined, beyond the former relief there was indeed no trace, and the imperial mind was appeased; and from this mother and son were as before. Then, the imperial grace having been graciously made known, I was sentenced for privately founding a temple and sent into exile at Leizhou.

When I was thrown into prison in the third month of that year, all the temples of the capital chanted sutras and performed repentance rites for my protection. Among the monks there were those who burned incense on their arms and held spells to protect me the more. The son of Lord Zheng Fanxi, Grand Marshal of Ansui, an officer of the imperial guards
(a military officer charged with guarding the emperor and great ministers, with ceremonial escort, with patrol of the capital, and with public order),

who had never known me, specially made a banquet and gathered the court gentry to plead for me, weeping as he told of my innocence; and there was none who did not grieve for the Dharma. From this one may see how at that time men's hearts were set on the Dharma.
In prison for eight months, he who supplied me
(provided)

with food was only my attendant Fushan, one man. In the tenth month of winter I was sent south. Many of the court's scholar-officials, in plain clothes and riding donkeys, saw me off to the ferry crossing. On the day I left the capital, my attendant Fushan, with two or three monks, followed. In the eleventh month I reached Nanjing, and there beside the river took leave of my old mother, and wrote the Inscription of Mother and Son, and took with me my orphaned nephew Kejiu.
[In plain clothes riding donkeys to see me off to the crossing] In everyday dress and riding a donkey (
rather than in official robes, riding a horse or carried in a sedan, to show their grief), they came to the crossing to see me aboard.

Earlier, when I had passed Mount Stone-Sutra with Master Daguan, I had thought how desolate the Chan gate had grown, and said that Caoxi was the source, and its headwaters must be blocked; so we resolved to go together and dredge it. Because of my affairs it was not accomplished, and Master Da went first, waiting for me at Mount Kuang
(that is, Mount Lu in Jiangxi province).

When I met with disaster, the Master was then dwelling at Tianchi; hearing the report he was greatly shocked and said: 'If Master Hanshan is finished, then the vow for Caoxi is unfulfilled.' So the Master went first to Caoxi, and then to the capital to report it. In the end he hurried about and, returning to Liaocheng, heard that I was about to be released, and went back to Jinling to await me. When I arrived, we took leave of each other at the Traveler's Rest Hermitage by the river. The Master wished to do all he could to clear me of the false charge. I said: 'The command of lord and father, and the service of subject and son, are not two things; how much more is this settled karma. Pray, Master, say no more.' At the parting of the roads he grasped my arm and said: 'When I heard of your disaster at Tianchi, I at once vowed before the Buddha to recite the Lotus Sutra a hundred times to keep you from harm. My heart is your tongue.' I answered him and took leave, and the Master wrote the Essay on Expelling the Guest to see me off.

(The Sage Mother saw him a tenth time, the emperor a sixth time, and the son of Grand Marshal Lord Zheng Fanxi, officer of the imperial guards, once; the attendant Fushan a second time, his old mother a tenth time, and Master Daguan a third time.)

Zheng notes: in the yiwei year the crown prince was fourteen, yet the succession remained unsettled and the court's debates were in confusion. The Sage Mother's mind was with Taichang, and her party held for establishing the elder; the emperor's mind was with the Prince of Fu, and his party held for establishing the noble. Of the inner court's attendants, nine in ten took the side of Noble Consort Zheng; the powerful men of the outer court followed them, and the foundation of the state was nearly shaken. Those who mediated between them held to the doctrine of enfeoffing the three princes together. Those who stood firm — such as Grand Secretary Zhang Hongyang Wei, Grand Secretary Wang Jiapin, Supervising Secretary Zou Nangao Yuanbiao, and Vice-Minister of Rites Gao Jingyi Panlong — were no more than a few. At that time Taichang was also much afflicted with illness, and the heir of the Eastern Palace was not yet in the imperial heart, at the very moment of perilous and clashing odds. Those who understood said that 'the prayer for an heir at Mount Tai
(Mount Wutai)
and the protection of the heir at Compassionate Longevity
(the Great Temple of Compassionate Longevity)
involved a man who had left the world in the great matter of the state's fortune
(the realm's destiny and the throne),
and they feared greatly for the Hanshan Patriarch.
[The Three Princes Enfeoffed Together]
In the first month of the twenty-first year of Wanli (

), Emperor Shenzong hastened the process of changing the crown prince. He sent a handwritten decree to the Grand Secretary Wang Xijue, ordering that the eldest imperial son Zhu Changluo, the third imperial son Zhu Changxun, and the fifth imperial son Zhu Changhao be enfeoffed together as princes, and that afterwards the best of them be chosen as crown prince. At once the whole court was in an uproar.

From the first, one was at Wudang and one at Wutai; and so the Sage Mother stood with Mount Tai to the end, and the emperor stood with Wudang. Treacherous men within and without, spying out the emperor's momentary moods, then had runners of the Eastern Depot disguise themselves as Daoists, to work by innuendo and provoke a quarrel, so as to overturn the monks' position of stripping the branches and pulling up the root; and on that day it truly became a prairie fire, though it had nothing whatever to do with the Daoists of Mount Lao. Only, since the Daoists had no part in it, one may know that the palace was in great flood and fire. The Hanshan Patriarch had first heard within the palace of the matter of gaining an heir through the prayer at Mount Tai, and it had already become an embryo of disaster. Because he shunned fame, within half a year he had withdrawn and so escaped. This time, through the affair of the reserves for Bao'en, he could not forget the capital and came and went, lingering there nearly three years, and so was dragged into the great crux and the great dispute over establishing the heir. Moreover, his proposal that the Sage Mother daily reduce her table by a hundred taels and accumulate for three years was greatly inconvenient for the eunuchs, and a rift was easily bred. And by ancestral rule the empress dowager might not meddle in state affairs; no wonder that for a time, within and without, men seized the occasion to attack and frame him.
In former days the Second Patriarch calmly accepted what was unlawful
(Huineng's predecessor, the Second Patriarch Huike, was persecuted and nearly lost his life, and had no choice but to leave the capital of Ye and wander between Ye and Wei)

, and those who understood the truth called it paying a debt. This too was paying a debt — was it not great? The words in the prison record, 'only to serve the imperial will by damaging the cardinal bonds of morality, which is by no means the heart with which a subject loves his lord,' weigh more than nine tripods. The two words 'cardinal bonds' — were they spoken for the sake of donated funds alone? The naming of the Sea-Seal Temple was requested by the Sage Mother's decree, not by the emperor's edict, and so he was sentenced for the crime of privately founding it. Here it does not say the temple was destroyed; but in the Tower Inscription for Master Da he says outright that its temple was destroyed. Alas! The law officers' application of the statute was indeed excessive; and what of the thought of filial piety?

This account of parting from his mother is no longer given at length; after all, it is a mother letting her son go. Only the eight words 'beside the river at Nanjing he took leave of his old mother' dispose of the whole great case of serving one's parents. The preface to the Inscription of Mother and Son
gives it in detail, and is appended.
Qing
(Deqing; the Hanshan Patriarch's own name)

because of spreading the Dharma fell into disaster, and provoked the anger of the sage Son of Heaven, whose voice was like thunder. I thought to myself of my old mother, who on hearing it would surely be shocked to death. But I was graciously spared from death and sent into exile at Leiyang. Passing through my native place, I welcomed my old mother to a meeting beside the river. She was joyful, talking and laughing, her voice clear and bright, with not the least trace of stagnation in her breast. Then I asked: 'Old Mother, when you heard that your son stood between death and life, were you not grieved?' My mother said: 'Life and death are allotted; I do not grieve for myself — why should I grieve for you? Only, men's words differ, and since I had no settled view of the matter, it was doubt that troubled me.' We sat together in attendance until dawn, and there and then made our final farewell. My old mother charged me, saying: 'Do well, and cherish yourself by the Way; do not grieve for me. Now I too take my long farewell of you.' She set off joyfully on the road without once looking back. And I was moved that in all the world there are mothers such as this — would she not in a moment exhaust the feelings of birth and death? So I made an inscription for her, saying: The love of mother and son is the lodestone drawing the needle. The wondrous nature, naturally so, is from the first complete. I see my mother as wood gives out fire. The wood is already burned; the fire has never had a self. Living, not clinging; dying, as if unaware. Only then do I see my body is a barren woman's son.
[The barren woman's son] The child of a barren woman — a simile for what does not exist, like saying 'tortoise hair' or 'rabbit horns.' The Vimalakirti Sutra

the Chapter on Viewing Living Beings says: 'Like the tracks of birds in the sky, like the son of a barren woman.' In the inscription, 'only then do I see my body is a barren woman's son' means that my body is illusory. [A barren woman] is a woman who cannot bear children.
Appended: the four marks
(in prison)
reading the chapter on the four marks in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

Bells and drums, hand-bells and gongs, their sound never ceasing; sound upon sound, day and night, speak of the unborn. Pitiful are those drunk on dreams who wound their own life; gazing at one another in the mirror, their tears pour down. (The mark of self)

[The unborn] The truth of nirvana has neither birth nor death, and so is called 'the unborn.' Hence one contemplates the truth of the unborn to break the affliction of birth and death. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: 'All living beings, within the unborn, falsely see birth and death; therefore it is called revolving in birth and death.' The Sutra of the King of Supreme Victory says: 'The unborn is real; birth is delusion. The foolish drift and drown in birth and death; the Tathagata embodies the real, without any delusion, and this is called nirvana.'
Towering and jagged
cuán wán
, steep and high)

stands the iron city, its forest of knives and trees of swords cold as ice. Who would have thought the fire breaks out from the ice mountain, and when the ice mountain is burned away the fire is not born. (The mark of person)
The iron gate is shut fast and far
yǎo
, dim and dark)
and hard to open; bolt upon bolt — is it not misery too? How strange that the guest who groans through the long night does not know by what he came in here. (The mark of living beings)

One bloody staff is utterly without mercy; whoever it touches must have birth and death cut off. Only when the pain reaches the heart and stings the nose does one know the king's law is perfectly clear. (The mark of lifespan)
Four Poems Written Leaving Prison and Passing Through the Market of Chang'an say:
Chang'an's wind and moon are the same in every age; on the purple causeways and red dust the road has no end. What calls to a man most intimately is a single cock-crow and the fifth-watch bell.

The body, like empty space, is at ease of itself; not a speck of dust divides a thousand ranges. Pitiful are the guests of bright day and blue sky; eyes wide open, they sigh at the hardship of the road.
A whirlwind and sudden rain come in an instant; countless travelers cannot open their eyes. Then of a sudden the rain stops and the clouds scatter; the great void was from the first beyond all dust.
Men are a Gandharva city in the air, a wild horse of the plain; before the eyes they seem like a village in mist. One must go right into the city and look: sounds and forms were never real.

[The city in the air] The city of the Gandharvas, a city conjured by illusion. [The wild horse] A figure for illusion. The vapors steaming up in the fields look from afar like wild horses galloping through the sky, but in truth there are no wild horses. [Men are a Gandharva city in the air, a wild horse of the plain] Men are like a mirage in the sky and like wild horses galloping through the air — mere illusion.
In that year began the karmic bond with Caoxi.
The Twenty-Fourth Year of Wanli
Bingshen ●

I was fifty-one. In the first month of spring I passed through Wenjiang and visited Supervising Secretary Zou. Wang Xinghai, a grand herald of Luling, paid me homage on the river and asked me to annotate the Lankavatara. In the second month I crossed the Dayu Ridge, and at the ridge-head looked upon the place where Huiming seized the robe, writing a poem to mourn him; it has the lines, “Turning it over, I think of the traveler who walked by night — how does it compare with my heart crossing the ridge today?” Seeing the travelers sweating blood, I instructed a certain
(a Daoist layman: one who dwells in a Buddhist temple but keeps his hair and cultivates the Way)
to found a tea-giving hermitage at the ridge-head. Seeing the road rugged and hard to travel, I had the Daoist laymen urge its repair, and within a few years it became a level highway.

Reaching Shaoyang, I entered the mountain to pay homage to the Patriarch. Drinking the water of Caoxi, I made this verse: “A drop of Caoxi’s water from the spirit source, / flowing into the vast sea, its waves beat the sky. / How many fish and dragons have transformed therein — / yet the single vein at the source is still cool and clear
líng
, withered and spent)
and so.” Seeing the ancestral court in decline beyond words, I departed sorrowing.
Arriving at Wuyang
(Guangzhou)
in prison garb, I met the Grand General, who loosed my bonds, entertained me with a vegetarian meal, and lodged me at Haizhu Temple.
At that time the grand counselor
(an alternate title for a provincial administrator)

Lord Zhou Dingshi was expounding Wang Yangming’s teaching, and brought several dozen of his disciples to visit. In the course of the conversation Lord Zhou raised the phrase “comprehending the way of day and night” and posed it as a question. Among the company there was one called the Old Daoist Elder, who answered: “Everyone has awareness: when matters are met by day, it is this awareness; when dreaming at night, it is also this awareness; therefore it is said, comprehending the way of day and night.” Lord Zhou said: “That is how everyone explains it, but in my heart I am not so sure.” Then he asked me: “Old Chan master, pray instruct us.” I said: “From what classic does this saying come?” The lord said: “The Appended Phrases of the
(Book of Changes)

Book of Changes,” and he recited several lines in succession. I said: “This is the Sage pointing out to men that they must awaken to that one thing which is not subject to birth and death.” Lord Zhou clapped time and said: “Truly the old Chan master has pointed it out most intimately.” The assembly was wholly at a loss and asked again. Lord Zhou said: “Birth and death are the way of day and night. To comprehend day and night is to be no longer subject to day and night.” The whole company sighed in admiration.
[Wang Yangming’s Teaching]

The Yangming school, also called the Wang school or the school of mind, is a school of Confucianism, a Confucian doctrine developed by the great Ming scholar Wang Shouren. Because Wang Shouren once built a study in the Yangming Cave of his native place, he was known to the world as Master Yangming, and so his doctrine is called the Yangming school.

Earlier, certain protectors of the Dharma had written to the supreme commander Grand Marshal Lord Chen, who sent me post-station warrants and ferried me across. On the tenth day of the third month I reached Leizhou and was enrolled in the ranks, lodging at an old temple in the west of the city. On the first day of the fourth month of summer I set my hand to annotating the Lankavatara Sutra.
At that time the year was one of great famine, and pestilence
(plague)
broke out on every side; for a whole year no rain fell, and the dead and injured were beyond telling. I sat as though in the
charnel grounds
(where the dead are cast)
amid it all
and, by the power of the Dharma, was perfectly at ease
(untouched and unharmed)
In that time of drought the well water dried up, and only the attendant
(Fushan)

Shan remained with me. Every midnight he would obtain a single jar of water, and that served for the whole day. To a starving man a single drop of it was like sweet dew from heaven. Within and without the city, bones lay heaped and exposed. In the seventh month of autumn I and the provincial graduate Ke Shifu urged the people to gather and bury them, covering the
cī
, bones of the dead with flesh not yet fully rotted)

bones, ten thousand or more in number. Then I held a rite for their deliverance, and at once heaven sent down heavy rain, till the water stood three feet deep on the level ground; from this the pestilential air was dispelled.

In the eighth month the governor’s office summoned me back to Wuyang, and I lodged at the military drill ground. Coming and going, I wrote twenty poems, In the Army. Earlier, passing the Bitter Vine of Dianbai, the gateway of the mountain road, I composed an inscription and founded a tea-giving hermitage. Ding Youwu, grand counselor of Yuzhang, was exiled to the Guang sea on a false charge; when he arrived, having long admired me, we became
(sworn friends)
friends.

(Supervising Secretary Zou of Wenjiang; Wang Xinghai, grand herald of Luling; the Grand General, whose surname is unknown; Grand Counselor Zhou Dingshi; Grand Marshal Chen of the supreme command; the provincial graduate Ke Shifu; Grand Counselor Ding Youwu — once each. The attendant Shan is Fushan — three times. Supervising Secretary Zou was named Yuanbiao, styled Nangao, a native of Jishui in Jiangxi; he passed the metropolitan examination in the dingshou year of Wanli. When he argued at court that Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng ought not to be retained in office during mourning, he was exiled to garrison duty for seven years, then recalled to fill a post in the bureau of scrutiny, and rose to left censor-in-chief. Zhou Dingshi is Zhou Haimen, named Rudeng, styled Jiyuan, a native of Shengxian in Zhejiang. Lord Chen was named Dake, styled Sijin, a native of Yangzhou.)

Fuzheng observes: before Patriarch Han ever went up Mount Tai, he first entered Shaolin to pay homage to the First Patriarch. Here, before reaching Leizhou, he first entered Caoxi to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch. Dharma affinity is host; worldly affinity is guest. No Dharma affinity is too great: wherever he goes, he visits the Patriarch and annotates sutras. No Dharma affinity is too small: everywhere he gives tea and buries bones.
The Twenty-Fifth Year of Wanli
Dingyou ●

I was fifty-two. In the first month of spring, as there were many dead and wounded in the provincial city and bones lay exposed, I had people gather and bury them, several thousand in number, and held a Universal Relief rite for seven days and nights, with Ding Youwu himself assisting. Before this the men of Yue did not know the Buddha; from this time on they turned to him as one
xī
, yielding in obedience)
and took refuge.

In the fourth month of summer the Lankavatara Notes were completed. Because certain of the scholars who had taken refuge had not yet entered into Buddhist principle, I wrote Straight Pointers to the Doctrine of the Mean to draw them out. At first high and low alike, seeing me to be a condemned monk, made very light of me. At that time the supreme commander
(governor-general)

Grand Marshal Lord Chen Rugang enforced the law with the utmost strictness, and none dared visit him privately. Earlier, because someone had spoken of me, though I had not gone to see him, he sent people to inquire after me most assiduously. In the ninth month of that year I went with Youwu to call on him; when we reached his gate the runners reported us and we were turned away. On our return, that very evening he came in person to pay his respects to me on my boat, bringing tea and food, and sat talking until the third watch, to everyone’s astonishment. Afterwards he spoke of me to all the authorities in the highest terms, saying: “He is a qilin and phoenix among monks,” and instructed the three provincial offices
(the military commission, the provincial administration commission, and the surveillance commission)
to go and pay him homage. From then on all Lingnan knew that monks were to be honored.
(Ding Youwu and Lord Chen Rugang each appear a second time.)

Fuzheng records that the Outer Record of Hanshan says: when he first came to visit a certain garrison commander, he held his card below the steps, and for a long while was not told to rise and withdraw. He understood in his heart: should I not announce my own name and present myself? Yet he could not get the words out of his mouth; they weighed on him like a thousand catties, and there was nothing to be done. Then he summoned his courage, gave his own name, and announced himself, and only then was he allowed to rise and withdraw. The next day at the audience it was the same; for a whole year there was no respite. Others said: “How should a military man know to break convention in dealing with a man of knowledge?” At the last, on a day when they were to visit the governor together, the commander prepared a boat stocked with vegetarian food and fruit like a banquet for guests, invited him aboard, bowed and saluted him to the seat of honor, and said: “It is not that I could not have made an exception for you; I knew you had proud bones, and so I did but help you along.” They talked happily knee to knee before parting. And so one sighs that among magistrates there are many men of deep feeling — why ask about a mere military officer
biàn

Fuzheng suspects that this affair, had it occurred before Lord Chen Rugang’s condescension, would be a different matter; but in the days of Rugang and Youwu it was still the manner of a military officer. I have heard that in those days in the ranks he was known as Cai Deqing; he let his hair grow and kept a long beard, and at leisure wore the Dongpo cap. From the day of his exile at fifty until his sixty-ninth year, he then shaved before the Sacred Mother’s spirit tablet, removed beard and hair, and returned to the monk’s robes.
The Outer Record also says: while in Lingnan the people were not yet familiar with him, and he kept a lofty reserve
(grave and dignified)
about him, so that he could not put people at ease
(draw close to him)

and had no one close to him. There was a little child who wished to come near him, yet ever drew back in fear of him. One day he learned the lion’s way of taming its cubs, and forced himself to lie down and fondle the child, giving him fruits and melons; he fondled him one day after another, until at last the child no longer feared him, and from that time people no longer shrank from him but came daily to be near him. Fuzheng knows that this thought of a perfected man stooping to the world of children came from his own hard-won mastery. As it is said, “All under heaven are infants, and I too am an infant with them.” And our Confucian love of benevolence and the Buddha’s compassion are no different from this.

blocks.text: 17. Preaching the Dharma in Cap and Girdle

inline.s: The Twenty-Sixth Year of Wanli
Wuxu ●
I was fifty-three. In the first month of spring the censor Lord Fan Youxuan, for his stand on
(the establishing of a crown prince)

establishing the heir, was exiled to Leiyang. He first visited me at Wuyang while I was collating the Lankavatara draft, and asked me: “What is the scenery of Leiyang like?” I picked up a scroll of the sutra and showed it to him, saying: “This is the scenery of Leiyang.” He marveled and at once wrote a petition to raise funds for its printing.
[Establishing the Heir] The installing of a crown prince.
The Shenzong Emperor did not until the twenty-ninth year of the Wanli era

year, and only then under compulsion, establish his eldest son Zhu Changluo, already twenty by nominal age, as crown prince. Before that, whoever dared propose that the eldest son Zhu Changluo be made crown prince was a thorn in the Shenzong Emperor’s eye, and most of them suffered banishment.
When Lord Zhou Haimen held the post of salt intendant of Guangdong, he came and went asking after the Way, and as he also had charge of Nan-Shao he asked me to compile the Gazetteer of Caoxi.

The scholars of Yue had until then not known the Buddha. It happened that Lord Zhou was expounding the Yangming teaching and had gathered the scholars to ask me about the Way. There was a certain Long Zhang who, hearing my discourse, was struck by it in his heart; he went home and told his friends Wang Anshun and Feng Changli: “The Chan master who has come from the north preaches a most wonderful Dharma.” The two came to ask for instruction, and when I revealed to them the matter of the upward path they believed firmly without doubt and set their minds earnestly on investigation. These two were men who had long been of virtuous conduct, and those who came one after another to take refuge in the Dharma gate grew daily more numerous; from this time they first knew that there are Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Thereafter the Dharma teaching opened wide, and it was the strength of these three men.
I often recalled Master Da’s vow concerning the sutra
(his vow to recite a hundred fascicles of the Lotus Sutra)
and had no convenient way to repay it. That summer I first built a Chan hut among the ramparts, intending to follow Dahui’s example of preaching the Dharma in cap and girdle
(as Chan Master Dahui did when his monk’s registration was struck off: he wore the dress of a Confucian scholar while preaching the Dharma)

. So I gathered the disciples who had long relied on me from afar — Xingrong, Rugan, and others — and the disciples beneath the bodhi tree of Dharmata — Tong’an, Chaoyi, and others — several dozen in all, to recite the Lotus Sutra, and I expounded it for them up to the Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa, when I suddenly awoke to the Buddha’s meaning: he would point out that this Saha world, just as it is before each person’s eyes, is the Huazang ocean of worlds. Yet the three transformations are needed only for the dull-rooted, to show them a glimpse by degrees. So I wrote Beating the Measure on the Lotus Sutra.

Youwu was by nature impetuous and fierce, and bore himself with generosity; he knew to revere monks, but did not know the Buddhadharma. As he was about to return home I saw him off on his boat and brought down the hammer and tongs upon him once more, and the lord awakened with a great turning. So I gave him the style “Layman Juefei,” showed him an inscription, and wrote the Inscription on Clearing the Mind to warn him.

(The censor Fan Youxuan, once. Zhou Haimen is the former Dingshi, a second time. Long Zhang, Wang Anshun, and Feng Changli, and the disciples Xingrong, Rugan, Tong’an, and Chaoyi, once each. Master Da, a fourth time. Ding Youwu, a third time.)

Fuzheng observes: to know that praying for the heir, obtaining the heir, establishing the heir, and contending over the heir are one and the same criminal case and one and the same matter of the heart. Therefore he makes a point, for Lord Fan’s distant exile, of bringing out the scenery of Leiyang, and there is a deep feeling in it throughout.

And when he suddenly says, “I often recalled Master Da’s vow concerning the sutra,” it is that he had not forgotten the mind with which he vowed to recite the Lotus Sutra a hundred times. And so, preaching the Dharma for Leiyang, he wrote Beating the Measure on the Lotus Sutra; that is its origin.
The Outer Record says: the eye of the teachings and the eye of the Chan lineage are from the first not two eyes. Master Yongming, in setting forth the lineage, drew entirely on
zhí
, to gather up)

the words of the teachings to seal and confirm it, fearing that people would go astray along the road of no-meaning. If one does not gain the eye of the teachings, one falls into wrong views. My annotations of the Diamond, Lotus, Lankavatara, Surangama, and other sutras all pick out what bursts forth where feeling and consciousness cannot reach and where the road of no-meaning is cut off. Thus one seals the lineage with the teachings; students should gain it for themselves.

Fuzheng reflects that Patriarch Han, in bringing his disciples to accomplishment, applied the tongs and hammer without stint, prescribing medicine according to the illness and turning them suddenly to awakening. Men like Ding Youwu cannot be counted on more than one hand’s fingers. For though many followed him, shallow admirers were the greater part. If one examines throughout the chronicle the points to which he gave his mind, they can be numbered as clearly as by lamplight. The Inscription on Clearing the Mind says:
The true nature, deep and still, is like water settled clear. When hate and love strike it, the waves of affliction rise.
Wave upon wave, unceasing, the self-nature turns opaque. Affliction and ignorance but deepen unawareness.
To take the other with the self is mud cast into water. To let the other stir the self is oil upon the fire.
The other troubles my truth, yet the trouble is my own. If I do not arise, the kalpa’s fire freezes to ice.
Therefore the perfected man first empties the mark of self. If the mark of self is empty, from what can the other obstruct him?
The work of forgetting the self lies in unshaken patience. The moment habit-energy stirs, wake with sudden vehemence.
Where you wake, there is awakening; one thought turns back the light. Sweep away all traces, cut off every footstep’s print — instantly cool and clear.
Cool and still, standing straight and alone, tranquil and calm, gladdening the spirit: nothing can oppose it.

Afterwards the Gazetteer of Caoxi was completed in four fascicles, with prefaces and postscripts by Chen Dake of the supreme command, the vice-minister Yang Qiyuan, the grand counselor Zhou Rudeng, and the military commissioner Hou Jigao.
The Twenty-Seventh Year of Wanli
Jihai ●

I was fifty-four. In spring the printing of the Lankavatara Notes was completed. I expounded it once for the assembly, then had more than a hundred copies printed and sent them everywhere to men of knowledge in the Dharma gate throughout the land, and to the magistrates who protected the Dharma, that they might know that in the midst of adversity I had not forgotten the Buddha’s work. I also feared that if I died unheard of, I should leave words to show my purpose and hope to hand down something imperishable. There were those who did not understand and thought me presumptuous.
The customs of Yue were indeed fond of killing; at the Zhongyuan Festival

(the Zhongyuan Festival, on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month. On this day Daoist temples hold vegetarian rites, Buddhist temples hold Yulanpen assemblies, and folk custom also includes sacrifices to departed kin and the like)
all slaughtered animals to sacrifice to their forebears. At that time the market piled up livestock like firewood — a pitiful sight. So I held a Yulanpen assembly, expounded the
(the Filial Piety Commentary on the Buddha’s Yulanpen Sutra)

Filial Piety Commentary, and urged people on that day to feed monks, release living creatures, and use vegetarian offerings; many followed. From then on, for all great matters of funeral and sacrifice, or on parents’ birthdays, whether prayers to avert evil
ráng

or repentance rites, they released life and ate vegetarian. Before long, life-release assemblies appeared everywhere, and this was one of the turning points by which the Buddhadharma transformed the region.
[The Yulanpen Assembly]

A rite held every year on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month to deliver the ancestral dead, with activities such as feeding monks, repentance rites, and the offering of food to hungry ghosts.

At that time the Huizhou vice-minister Lord Yang Fusuo had long had a deep Dharma affinity with me, and had returned home for mourning. That autumn I went to visit him; on the day I arrived the lord had already died at his mourning lodge, and the next morning
(early morning)

as I was about to enter the mountains, his coffin had already reached the city. I went at once to attend the dressing of the body and sought a coffin and an outer coffin to see him properly laid to rest. It happened that Lord Ren, circuit intendant of Chaoyang, was accompanying the imperial inspector at Huiyang and invited me to tour West Lake; I climbed Dongpo’s White Crane Peak and returned. On returning I wished only to shut my gate and sweep no paths for guests.
