(The Huizhou vice-minister Lord Yang Fusuo and Lord Ren, circuit intendant of Chaoyang, once each. Lord Yang was named Qiyuan; Lord Ren was named Kerong.)

[Shutting the gate and sweeping no paths] To close the gate in retreat and decline guests. [Sweeping no paths] To sweep the path no longer to welcome guests. The meaning is: to shut the door and decline visitors.
Fuzheng notes: West Lake at Huizhou and West Lake at Hangzhou are two scenic legacies
(that is, “sheng gai,” fine scenery)
of Dongpo, and Patriarch Han made surpassing karmic ties at both. Fuzheng himself had the good fortune only at the Hangzhou lake, where he took part in the life-release assembly.

Fuzheng further notes: Lord Yang Fusuo wrote the preface to the Gazetteer of Caoxi for Patriarch Han; their Dharma bond was very deep, and he had long come to pay his respects. On the day of the visit the coffin happened to arrive — this too was a turning of Dharma affinity, and no mere accident.
The Twenty-Eighth Year of Wanli
Gengzi ●
I was fifty-five. At that time the tax commissioners had just been sent out
(the officials who collected the monopoly taxes had just left the capital to plunder the regions)

, and the region was shaken; added to this were alarms of Japanese pirates, and men’s hearts were in a panic. I therefore dismissed my disciples and shut myself away out of sight to avoid it all. The men of Yue had long suffered from the white-sailed boats of the
(the Fujian coast)
Fujian sea carrying rice
(cargo boats with white-painted hulls and holds)
, fearing that prices would soar
(fearing that the merchants would seize the chance to raise prices)
, and at that time they took it as a cause of disorder.

[The tax commissioners (officials who collected the monopoly taxes) first sent out] In the middle and late years of the Shenzong Emperor’s reign the finances were straitened, and so the emperor sent eunuchs throughout the land as mining and tax commissioners to fill the inner treasury; but most of these mining supervisors and tax envoys plundered the people’s property under false pretexts, running rampant everywhere and throwing the realm into disorder. [Alarms of Japanese pirates] At that time the Ming

government was politically corrupt, its coastal defenses lax, and it had adopted a policy of closing the borders to the sea; added to this, Japan was then plagued by war, and certain samurai and pirates joined forces with Ming merchants who had suffered from the closing of the borders, invading China, so that the Japanese pirates ran wild and plundered along long stretches of the coastal cities.
The new military commissioner
(governor-general)
was a man of Min
(Fujian)
, and the young lord’s boat was anchored at sea
(the military commissioner’s son’s boat lay at the seaside)
. It happened that the Grand General had asked leave and was about to depart
(it happened that he had taken leave of the Grand General and was about to go)
, and the tax commissioner was nursing designs against him
(the tax commissioner had long plotted to strike at the Grand General)
; he happened upon several white-sailed boats and straightway used them as a pretext that the Grand General was providing passage for the young lord
(and so on the pretext lied that this rice was the Grand General’s gift to see the young lord off)
. He stirred up
sǒu
, to incite)

the townspeople, and there was a great uproar. In a moment several thousand gathered, hurling bricks and stones, attacking the young lord’s boat until it nearly broke apart. They besieged the general’s headquarters, weapons leveled, and the situation was acute.
[White-sailed boats
cáo

)] Sea-going cargo boats with hulls painted white and holds for cargo. At that time sea-going cargo vessels were of two kinds, the white-sailed and the black-sailed. The New Discourses of Guangdong says: “Those that cross the oceans are called white-sailed and black-sailed; they are built of great iron-hard timbers, shaped like a trough, and so are called cao. Bow and stern are also shaped like the sea-whale (the right whale); the white ones have two black eyes, the black ones two white eyes, and when the sea-whale sees them from afar it takes them for its own kind and does not devour them.” [To provide passage] Originally it meant a dowry (the goods given by a bride’s family at her marriage); here it means to fund a journey (a euphemism for making a gift to one who is about to set out).

At that time the three provincial offices and the prefectural and county officials had all gone to Duanzhou to present the festival greetings, and there was not a single ranking official in the provincial city — in the end no one to rescue the situation, and the turn of events hung on a breath. The Grand General was in peril; at his wit’s end
(having no alternative)

, he ordered his central army commander to come before my gate to beg for help. I firmly refused, saying: “I have no magic art.” The commander knelt in tears and said: “If you, master, will not think of my general, will you not think of the living beings of this region?” Hearing this I was struck with alarm, and there was no help for it, so I opened my gate and went to see the tax commissioner, calmly persuading and transforming him and opening his understanding. When the commissioner heard my words he indeed awoke, and ordered that the people be pacified by his own proclamation, so as to disperse the mob.

At that time I went ahead of them and said loudly before the crowd: “What you gentlemen want now is cheap rice. But you are now violating the great law and will be put to death; and even if there were cheap rice, who would eat it?” Hearing this the crowd was dumbfounded; presently the order arrived, the siege of the general’s headquarters was at once lifted, and the provincial city was brought to peace. The elders were grateful to me and wished to make offerings to me as to a guardian spirit
(to sacrifice to)

At that time the three provincial offices were dining at the military commissioner’s yamen when they heard the report that the people had risen, and all threw down their chopsticks and rose. When they returned, the city was already at peace; yet all knew what my intent had been. At that time the circuit intendant Lord Ren heard of it and wrote to me, saying: “If Master Han had not come forth, what would have become of the region? And now that Master Han has come forth, what is to become of Master Han?” I too knew that from then on there would be no peaceful days.

In the seventh month of autumn Lord Zhu Xingcun, circuit intendant of Nan-Shao, invited me to Caoxi. I took him at his word and went into the mountains, and became a serving man of the Sixth Patriarch. At that time the new governor Lord Dai, knowing that I had pacified the rioters, was deeply grateful to me and wished to meet me, and instructed the Grand General to bring me. I went to call on him, and when we met he treated me with the greatest courtesy, keeping me at once to a vegetarian meal. When I took my leave to go to Caoxi, the lord then pledged himself as a protector of the Dharma, and told me to report to him whatever arose; only then could I set my mind at ease.

(The Grand General, whose surname is unknown, a second time. The tax commissioner, once. Circuit Intendant Ren, a second time. Lord Zhu Xingcun, circuit intendant of Nan-Shao, and the new governor Lord Dai, once each. Lord Zhu was named Yibin
bīn
a native of Haining, and rose to be prefect of Yingtianfu. Lord Dai was named Yao.)
[Knowing that I had pacified the rioters]

Master Yinguang says: “In the closing years of the Ming, the royal order was not upheld and the great ministers had no authority. Those who wielded power were all ignorant, unlettered eunuchs. The wicked leaned on their power to do wrong, and the well-meaning had no wisdom to devise remedies; and so the people were distressed and the state imperiled, past all saving. Hanshan, Zibai, Lianchi, and Miaofeng all arose in the world at this very time. How great were their secret aid to the way of governance and their unseen sheltering of the people’s livelihood! Hanshan, slandered for spreading the Dharma, was exiled to Guangzhou; his rescue of the men of Yue and his prolonging of the state’s life were deep and far-reaching. Had Hanshan not been exiled to Guangzhou, the people of Guangzhou would long since have taken to desperate measures and become a worry to the state. The withdrawal of the pearl-fishing boats, the settling of the civil unrest, and the great affair of reconciling Qinzhou were all settled by a single conversation. Who but one who came forth by vow to save the people from flood and fire could have done it?” (From the Preface to the Commentary on the Chronological Biography of Master Hanshan.)

Fuzheng wonders at this Grand General: he appears twice in the chronicle, with no surname or title. Could it be that he only knew to honor a famous monk, and did not know how to wield authority and trust in the region, so that a single provocation nearly became a great upheaval, and he had no choice but to rely on a teacher of goodness to lend a hand? A single phrase awakened the tax commissioner and dispersed the rioters. The old courtesy of loosing his bonds and offering a vegetarian meal — how heavily it was repaid! The way he settled the trouble that day — how it came off in a snap of the fingers, as if divine! Afterwards those in office, hearing the wind, rose up, and from that time Caoxi began to shine.
The Twenty-Ninth Year of Wanli
Xinchou ●
I was fifty-six. In the first month of spring I saw vagabonds from all quarters gathered at the mountain gate
(gathered at the mountain gate of Caoxi)

, opening butcher stalls and wine shops, exceedingly foul, a long-standing abuse of more than a hundred years. Graves routinely encroached on the Patriarch’s mountain, and monks’ property was much encroached upon. They colluded with outside ruffians to extort and swindle, and none of the temple monks dared look them in the face. I sighed and said: “This is a disease in the heart and belly. If it is not removed, the Sixth Patriarch’s seat of practice will in the end become a fox’s den, past all saving. What is to be done? There is no way to deal with it. Though I stay here, what use am I?” After long deliberation, having no alternative, I went to inform the governor Lord Dai. The lord said: “There is no difficulty. I will try to carry it through for you.” He at once ordered the county to take up station and within three days drive them all out, not leaving a single man, and to tear down every shop and stall, not leaving a tile. From then on the accumulated filth of Caoxi’s mountain gate was washed clean in a single day.

The lord then kept me to a vegetarian meal, and in the course of conversation said: “I have washed away the stench of the Sixth Patriarch for you. But now the living beings of this region are in misery — what compassion has the great bodhisattva to save them?” I asked: “What do you mean?” The lord said: “The thousand pearl boats are almost all great pirates of the sea. Now, under cover of the imperial pearl fishery, they are given power; when the fishery ends they do not return but run wild at sea, plundering without cease, and the law cannot stop them. That is one thing. As for the mines opened in the region, the conscripted laborers are violent and overbearing, digging up people’s graves and ruining their property; everywhere the common people suffer their poison, worse than plundering, so that none can sleep in peace. What is to be done about it?” I said: “This is not easy to speak of; let us take it up by and by.”
The mining commissioner Lord Li had a good measure of faith
(the mind of faith in the Buddha)

. In the autumn of that year he came to Caoxi to offer incense to the Sixth Patriarch and stayed in the mountain several days, greatly delighted to hear the Dharma. I therefore urged him to be the golden donor for the revival of the ancestral court, and he generously took it upon himself. I then quietly suggested to him: “The mining works harm the region grievously; this is not the sage Son of Heaven’s intent. As for the pearl boats, set a term of restraint at once, so that any who pass beyond the limit on their voyages are punished. Let the mines cease their working and all their conscripted labor be withdrawn, and let the responsible office merely pay in the annual quota; then not a hair of the people’s will be disturbed. May that be done?” The commissioner assented and carried it through with all his strength. From this the hill and sea regions were in a single day brought to peace.

The lord was deeply moved by this, and wrote to thank me, saying: “Now at last I know the vastness of the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ compassion.” For this he became ever more earnest in his resolve to protect the Dharma. And so I was able to set my mind at ease at Caoxi and open up the ancestral court. I altered the geomantic paths, selected monks and conferred the precepts, established a
(a charitable school, giving free schooling to the sons of the poor)

charitable school, trained and nurtured the sramaneras, set up the treasury office and the pure rules, audited the rents, redeemed the monks’ property, and recovered what had been encroached upon. Within a single year a hundred ruined works were all taken up.
(Lord Dai of the governor’s office, a second time. The mining commissioner Lord Li, once.)
Fuzheng, reading the Dream-Journey Collection

What Was Shown to Master Shan, found: “In the second month of spring in the bingshen year I crossed the ridge and came to Caoxi to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch. The monastery was wasted and the incense and lamps were dwindling; there was a monk, Haiyue Shan, who served as prior. In the dingyou year the demon winds vied to harass us, the bodhimanda was destroyed, and the monks had no support. Master Shan came to Wuyang to pay his respects and begged me to enter the mountain and confer the precepts. In the winter of the gengzi year I answered the invitation and came to the mountain.” Then he said: “Had the Patriarch not received and sustained me, I could not have come to Caoxi; had I not come, Caoxi could not have had the merit of restoring the monastery. Today, without pure sincerity, it is hard to attain the ultimate. From first to last it is always one great matter, and truly no accident,” and so on.

He also showed the origin of setting up the charitable school, saying: “In the gengzi year, when the authorities invited me to put Caoxi in order, the old regulations were wholly ruined. I therefore chose various sramaneras and set up a charitable school, inviting guest masters to teach them deportment and to have them recite the inner and outer scriptures. When they had come to some faith and aspiration, they were shaved, a Chan hall was established, and they were made to follow the pure rules, receive the precepts, and bow and recite day and night. I laboured with a bitter heart for ten years, and there was something tolerable to show. Later, in the bingwu year, when I was pardoned and returned to Nanyue, the sramaneras had all grown to manhood and were deeply attached to me; they gathered and begged for instruction. I said to them: If you let this day slip by and do not put your whole strength into your practice, then in the future, though you travel through the worlds of the ten directions to visit men of knowledge, it will always be another man’s living. This is the old man’s true instruction.

The Outer Record also says: “The sramaneras of Caoxi were for the most part woodcutters’ and herdsmen’s boys. Those among them young enough to be taught were chosen and made to study the scriptures. Scholars of faith were further invited to teach them the Confucian classics. Their worldly employments were broken off, they were shaved, and only then did they take up their proper work. In eight years more than a hundred were brought to accomplishment.”
Qian Muzhai says: “Master Han, after five years of garrison duty in Yue, was at last able to take up residence at Caoxi. He recovered the encroached fields, expelled the
jiù
, to lease)
hired dwellings and the butchers’ doors and wine shops, and made it flourish into a precious monastery. Black-robed and white-robed
gathered in crowds (
bèn
, to pile up)
, and he used both the winning and the subduing hand, so that the way of Dajian
(the Sixth Patriarch. The Sixth Patriarch Huineng was posthumously titled Chan Master Dajian in the tenth year of Yuanhe of Emperor Xianzong)
flourished and was restored.”

Fuzheng observes from this that this one great season and karmic occasion at Caoxi was truly inconceivable. At that time Patriarch Han, though he preached in cap and girdle, was still a condemned monk in the ranks. Moreover, the dispute over the heir was then perilous, the mining commissioners were going out in every direction, and the hill and sea folk were poisoned, worse than in nearby places; the times were utterly wrong, and the officials were helpless. Who would have known that the obstruction of local affairs would instead become the firm bond of pagoda and temple? In the days of shouldering spears and binding up the hair, he happened to meet with the benefits of mutual giving between monks and laity. The Caoxi opportunity came from the governor; the maritime opportunity came from the mining commissioner. Had the mining commissioner not offered incense and taken refuge in faith, how could the disorder of the pearl boats and the mines have been settled, the governor’s heart been bound as a protector of the Dharma, and the hundred ruined works of Caoxi accomplished? Had Patriarch Han’s power of practice not been complete, how could the mining commissioner, a man of power, have been brought into the mountain, secretly shown every courtesy, and with a single word have cleared the difficulty, letting the light of the Patriarch’s seat shine out over the edge of the sea? The sage precedes Heaven and does not contravene it; he follows Heaven and accords with the times. Heaven does it, and man does it too: this is called the concurrence of Heaven and man.
The Thirtieth Year of Wanli
Renyin ●

I was fifty-seven. That year I rebuilt the Patriarch’s Hall, banked up the rear dragon ridge, and altered the paths. I turned the butchers’ shops into a rest hall for pilgrims of the ten directions, opened up the spirit way, moved the monks’ quarters, and enlarged the Chan hall, establishing the regulations afresh.
[Rebuilding the Patriarch’s Hall, banking up the rear dragon ridge, and altering the paths.
] For details see (
Dream-Journey Collection
· Record of the Revival of Caoxi
Fuzheng reflects: in those days at Nanhua, within the ground of a single sitting-mat, the monks had all become Papiyas
(demons)

, and the Buddha-land had turned into a demon’s den. Had the Buddhas and Patriarchs not secretly charged him to restore it, how could he, in the midst of shouldering spears and bearing halberds, without waiting to don black robes and return to the monastic dress
(without waiting to recover his monk’s registration)
, have brought his vow-power to accomplish these new foundations! It was just as when Patriarch Lu preached among the hunters’ band
(just as the Sixth Patriarch did when he preached among the hunters)
: no small karmic occasion.
The Thirty-First Year of Wanli
Guimao ●
I was fifty-eight. In the eleventh month of winter, Chan Master Daguan, in the capital, met with the calamity of the seditious book; he was arrested and thrown into prison for questioning
(arrested, imprisoned, and interrogated)

, and it was thought to be on my account, and so I was implicated once more. In my heart I knew it could not be avoided, and I set my mind at ease and waited. Through the holy grace I was treated leniently, and the capital bureau issued a general order
(a document of notification)
(Master Da, a fifth time. His Majesty, a seventh time.)
Fuzheng observes: in that year Master Da passed into transformation in prison, yet the chronicle text
(the text of the Chronological Biography)
does not tell the whole story.
(Patriarch Han)
The epitaph for Master Da composed during the Eastern Journey, and what other records contain, I append one or two passages below.
The Stupa Inscription
(the Stupa Inscription for Chan Master Daguan Ke of Mount Jing)
says in brief:

The Master’s taboo name was Zhenke, his courtesy name Daguan, his sobriquet Zibo. His disciples called him Venerable, out of reverence for the Dharma. His surname was Shen; his forebears were men of Juqu, and moved to live on the lakeshore of Wujiang on Lake Tai. At five the Master could not speak. A monk came to the gate, stroked his crown, and said to his father: ‘If this child leaves home, he will be a teacher of gods and men.’ Having spoken, he suddenly vanished, and the Master at once could speak. In his childhood his nature was generous and ardent, and no woman dared come near him. At seventeen he wished to travel north with a sword at his side. Reaching the Chang Gate of Suzhou, he met with heavy rain. He fell in with the monk Mingjue of Huqiu; seeing that the youth was uncommon, Mingjue marvelled inwardly, and so they shared an umbrella and returned to the temple, where he ate and lodged. At night the Master heard the chanting of the Sutra of the Names of the Eighty-Eight Buddhas
(the Great Repentance Text of the Eighty-Eight Buddhas)
, and at dawn
(early in the morning, when the sky is just growing light)
, he untied from his waist more than ten pieces of gold, asked to be shaved, and took Jue as his master, thereafter going to and fro among the three Wu
(a general term for the lower Yangzi region)

regions. One day he took leave of Jue and departed. Hearing a monk recite Zhang Zhuo’s Verse on Seeing the Way, he came to the lines ‘To cut off deluded thoughts only adds to the sickness; to incline toward suchness is likewise wrong,’ and was thrown into great doubt. Wherever he went he wrote these two lines on the wall; his doubt grew until his face and head swelled. One day, in the midst of a meal, he suddenly awakened, and the swelling of face and head vanished at once. From then on he
(surpassed)

trod down the various quarters. Passing Mount Kuang, he plumbed the profound meaning of the Consciousness-Only school. One day, having walked twenty li, his feet hurt; the Master ground his soles with a stone, until he could walk two hundred li a day, and only then stopped.

He travelled to Mount Wutai and came to the capital, where he called on the great elder Bianrong and was allowed to lodge there. He visited all the men of knowledge, such as Xiaoyan and Xianli. He met Lord Run of Daqian, and saw him ascend the hall to expound a public case, taking what was heard with the ear as the mind-seal and a handkerchief as the true transmission. The Master sighed and said: ‘Is the meaning of the coming from the West indeed like this?’ And so he did not enter the assembly. Returning south, he came to Jiahe, where there was Mizang Daokai, a native of Nanchang, who cast off his
(the dress of a Confucian scholar)
scholar’s gown, left home, and relied on the Master as his attendant. In the prefectural city there was the Lengyan Temple, the place where
(Chan Master Changshui, who composed the commentaries on the Surangama Sutra and other works in the Xianshou school, all of which circulated in the world)
Changshui had expounded the sutras; it had long been abandoned. The Master, in heartfelt accord with the grand minister
(the minister of personnel)

Lord Lu Wutai Guangzu, first proposed its restoration and built a Chan hall of five bays. On the day it was completed, the Master pricked his arm with an awl until the blood filled a bowl, and wrote a couplet: ‘If you do not fathom the mind, sitting in Chan only adds to the misery of karma; if you can guard the thought, even scolding the Buddha furthers true practice.’ He reflected that the canon was bulky in fascicles and heavy, so that in far places and remote corners there were those who would never hear so much as the name of the Buddhadharma. He wished to carve it in folded volumes, easy to circulate, so that all who saw or heard might plant the diamond seed. Even should there be those who slandered him, he would take their guilt upon himself; and so he called for donations. At that time Grand Minister Lu, with the education official Feng Mengzhen, the judicial officer Zeng Tongheng, and the assistant equerry Qu Ruji, gathered workmen
(assembled craftsmen)
at the Jizhao Hermitage on Mount Jing. Masters Mizang Kai, Huanyu Ben, and Danju Kai took turns in directing
(supervising and managing)

the work. Later Wu Fangbo Yongxian of Tongcheng turned Huacheng into a storehouse for the blocks. The Master, having settled the plan for carving the canon at Jiahe, then returned to the Wu gate. He went to visit
(to call on)

his former ordination master, the Venerable Jue, who had already returned to lay life and made a name as a physician. So he concealed his name, claimed illness aboard a boat, and invited Jue to attend him. When Jue saw the Master he was greatly astonished. The Master wept and urged him to shave his head. Jue, ashamed and moved, resumed the rites of a disciple.

At that time the Shen and Zhou clans of Wujiang, and the He, Sun, Jin, and Yu clans of Qu’a and Jinsha, gathered their kinsmen to pay him homage. At Yu Garden the Master copied out the Lotus Sutra to repay his two parents. Hearing that Master Miaofeng was building an iron stupa at Luya, he sent the sutra to be placed within the stupa. He came to visit me at the Eastern Sea; I was then at Chang’an to give thanks for the imperial favor. The Master brought Master Kai with him to Jiaoxi, where they met the autumn floods rising; the company judged that they could not possibly cross. The Master took off his clothes and waded in first, the water up to his shoulders, calling urgently to the others to follow. Having crossed, he said: ‘At the barrier of birth and death, one must go straight through, and that is what counts.’ I was in Chang’an when I heard from Lord Yu that the Master was travelling east; I hurriedly packed, travelled day and night, and likewise braved the flooding waters, racing as far as Jimo — but the Master had already left the mountain. When we met there was great joy; we returned to the mountain and stayed ten days, and from that time pledged ourselves as lifelong friends.

The Master returned to the capital and restored the ancient temple of Tanzhe. Then he went by way of the three Jin, through the Guanzhong region, along the plank roads to Shu, visited Mount Emei and paid homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. He followed the current down through Qutang, passed Jing and Xiang, climbed Taihe, reached Mount Kuang, passed Anqing, and visited Mount Wangong and Mazu’s Hermitage. The layman Ruan Zihua sought ordination, and so the Master shaved him in the mountains, naming him Fakai; he is Danju.

The Master travelled north again, to the Stone Sutra Mountain, and restored the stupa court of Duke Jin Wan. Opening the stone seat, he found a casket containing a quantity of Buddha relics, whose light illuminated the crags and gullies. When the Sacred Mother heard of it, she bestowed a purple kashaya and sent out treasury gold to enshrine them anew. It happened that when I heard the Master was travelling west, I galloped at once to the capital and waited for him at the Shangfang Doushuai Court. The Master drew me along to see the stone sutras, and so I wrote a record of it. We left the mountain together and stayed in a garden in the western suburbs, facing each other in talk for forty days and nights without closing our eyes. I believe it was the happiest thing in my life.

When the Master was at Tanzhe he would not eat before making his reverence to the Buddha. One day a guest arrived and he mistakenly ate first; he ordered the officer of affairs to punish him severely with thirty blows, and the Master knelt before the Buddha to receive the staff, until both his thighs were black as ink. Then he said: ‘The beginningless habit-energy of living beings is like oil poured into flour, so firmly set that nothing can break it. If one does not cut off feeling with pain, it is not easy to tame and subdue.’

In the yiwei year the Master was at Mount Kuang, about to go down to the capital to save me, when he heard that I was to be exiled to the south. So he waited on the riverbank, and we met at the Lübopo Hermitage below the pass. The Master took my hand and sighed: ‘You bear the great Dharma as a burden even unto death. For the Dharma, the ancients had the hearts of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu
(see the story of the Orphan of Zhao)

; what am I? If you do not return alive, I shall have no birthday to keep.’ I consoled him again and again. As I was about to set out, the Master charged me: ‘If I should die before you, my affairs after death are yours.’ And so we parted for ever.
In the fifth year after I crossed the ridge, because I had not returned to my former dress
(had not resumed the monk’s robes of former days)

, the Master would often sigh and say: ‘There are no men left in the Dharma gate. If one sits and watches the Dharma-banner broken, then where should one who would continue and prosper the Three Jewels set his mind? If old Han does not return, that is one great debt of my coming into the world. If the mining taxes do not cease, that is my second great debt of saving the world. If the transmission of the lamp is not continued, that is my third great debt of the wisdom-life. If I could discharge these three debts, I should never again walk to Rājagṛha
(a figure for the capital)

In the autumn of the guimao year I was at Caoxi, and sent a flying letter by one of my disciples who was going up to the examinations, inviting the Master to enter the mountain. His reply said simply: ‘I will part with this one poor bag of bones.’ Before long the affair of the seditious book suddenly broke out and shook the court and the country. At that time those who begrudged him seized the occasion and impeached the Master with a memorial, and in the end it was on this that he met his calamity.
[In the end it was on this that he met his calamity]

In the late Ming the eunuch faction monopolized power, levied harsh taxes, and the people could not live. Wu Baoxiu, prefect of Nankang, rose up to resist the taxes and was arrested and thrown into prison; his wife, née Chen, in grief and fury took her own life. When Great Master Daguan heard the news he went at once to the capital to protect Wu, and thereby offended the eunuch faction and the powerful. Afterwards he was falsely accused of connection with the “seditious book,” and thrown into prison.
Earlier,
His Majesty (the Shenzong Emperor)
with his own hand wrote the Diamond Prajñā
(the Diamond Sutra)

and it happened that sweat fell and stained the paper. He thought it should be replaced, and sent a palace attendant to consult the Master. The Master presented a verse: ‘One drop of the imperial sweat, a ford and bridge for ten thousand ages; the infinite Dharma-treasury from this sends forth its light.’ When His Majesty read it he was greatly pleased. When the memorials of impeachment came, the rescript said: ‘Let him but be questioned.’ When the imperial guard interrogated him, he answered only with the matter of the three debts
(the three “I do not know”s)

[The outbreak of the seditious book affair] The Shenzong Emperor’s empress, of the Wang clan, had no son; Consort Gong bore the eldest son, Changluo, who by the rites ought to have been established as heir, but the emperor favored the son of Consort Zheng, Changxun, and so was unwilling to establish the heir, and the matter became the talk of the whole city. In the eleventh month of the thirty-first year of Wanli

year, someone wrote A Continued Discussion of Hidden Perils, which was widely spread through the capital in the form of handbills, so that overnight it was everywhere, from the palace gates down to the streets and lanes. The piece said that the Shenzong Emperor had been forced to establish Changluo as crown prince, and that the position of the crown prince was in danger; it sharply criticized the chief grand secretary Shen Yiguan and the grand secretary Zhu Geng. When the Shenzong Emperor learned of it he was furious, and ordered the Eastern Depot, the imperial guard, and the patrol offices of the five city districts to arrest people at once, “to get at the name of the one who made the book”; and from this arose the “seditious book case.” Thereupon Shen Yiguan of the Zhejiang faction seized the chance to falsely destroy the Donglin men Guo Zhengyu, Shen Li, and others. Great Master Daguan too was falsely accused of connection with the seditious book, arrested and thrown into prison, and after severe torture sentenced to death.

In prison there was the memorializing censor Lord Cao Xuecheng, who asked him about the Way, and the Recorded Sayings of the Prison were made. At that time the chief ministers wished to put the Master to death; when the Master heard of it he said: ‘The world’s law being thus, what use is it to remain long?’ Then he asked for a bath, and when he had finished he sat upright, spoke a verse, and passed away. When Lord Cao heard of it he hurried to him and, stroking the body, said: ‘The Master has gone well.’ The Master opened his eyes again, smiled, and took his leave. It was the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the guimao year
year, and his worldly lifespan was sixty-one years; his Dharma-age
(also called the precept-age, the years since a bhiksu received the precepts)
was more than forty
(upwards of)
. Ah, the Master’s conduct through life left doubt and faith in equal halves. Yet at this last, easy, swift stroke, all who heard of it, high and low, were filled with admiration.”

Fuzheng, in attendance on Patriarch Han during his Eastern Journey, saw the great world-transcending writings that came from his own hand, and none equal the two stupa inscriptions for Yunqi Lianchi and Jing Daguan. In the reigns of Shizong and Shenzong the land produced three great patriarchs
(Master Lianchi, Master Daguan, and Patriarch Han)
. Patriarch Han’s karmic bond with Master Lian was shallow, with Master Da deep. Half of the stupa inscription for Master Da is in truth half a stupa inscription for himself
(his own)

. Their involvement in the palace succession was the same, their repute and their courting of trouble were the same, their mastery of the teachings and the Chan lineage was the same, their unifying of Confucius and Mencius was the same. With one Eastern Journey Patriarch Han settled the three great public cases of both sides.

At Mount Jing he gave the Essentials of Chan Investigation; at Yunqi he gave the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation. Gathering the great accomplishments of the two Masters, he laid bare the three teachings for all ages. Dharma upon dharma was complete; never was there a greater flourishing than in the days of the Eastern Journey, when he cremated Master Da and mourned at Master Lian’s shrine.
The end of the Stupa Inscription says:
At first the disciples brought the Master’s reliquary back to Mount Jing, and divined a day in the

the eleventh month of the bingchen year, the nineteenth day, for the cremation, and on the twenty-third day the relics were returned and a stupa was built behind the stupa of Dahui on the Mañjuśrī Terrace. I was then still in the ranks; when I heard the news of the Master’s death I wished at once to go in person to mourn, but through delays a whole twelve years passed
(because I was still in exile and could not leave the place, the matter was put off for twelve years)

, and I could not fulfill my original wish. Of late I have come thousands of li from Nanyue, with no thought of meeting on an appointed day, and yet I foreknew the day of the sacrifice — surely it was the mutual response of spirit, and strange indeed. The Master’s affairs after death I was fortunate enough to witness, and so I could do my poor best of reverence.”

Fuzheng saw with his own eyes that the memorial text sent a thousand li did not miss the day by even one day from the opening of the scroll; yet he still always said that he regretted he could not weep face to face over Zibo, and the mutual knowledge of these two Masters’ hearts lies wholly in the inconceivable power of spiritual penetration.
He also recorded:

Raising the fire he said: Fire by nature is empty, true emptiness is true fire; when they meet on a narrow road, there is nowhere to hide. I reverently address the Venerable Zibo, the Great Monk Daguan, who came by chance into the human world and fell into it by mistake. Bare and unadorned, he stripped off the shirt his mother bore him in; blazing with light, he revealed his original face. Shouldering the true Dharma, his shoulders were forged of pure steel; working utterly for others, his liver and gall were cast of pig iron. On the road of birth and death he comes and goes straight; at the gate of present affairs he half opens and half closes. For more than sixty years his breast held the wind in the pines and the moon in the water; for seventeen hundred cases his staff was a hare’s horn and a turtle’s hair. Though he had his last
(that last easy, swift stroke)

flourish of style, he could not help hiding his head and showing his tail. He threw down his stolen goods, and who would have thought they would fall into the hands of the man of Hanshan? Today, before the assembly of gods and men, I pick them up on the spot. Does the great assembly see them? (Drawing a circle in the air with the firebrand, he said:) The staff pries open the clouds of the twin paths; the whole body gushes forth the treasury of light. Take care, all of you, to look well: this time at last you may believe there is no covering or hindrance.”

Fuzheng has heard that when Master Da met his calamity, the crown prince had but lately been established and the Prince of Fu had not yet gone to his fief. Someone threw an anonymous letter to the cabinet and the ministries, entitled A Continued Discussion of Hidden Perils, saying that the imperial consort would endanger the crown prince. When His Majesty heard of it he was furious and sent soldiers to arrest people rigorously, weaving
(trumping up charges to entrap)
a net of accusations. The grand minister Shen Li and the master of rites Guo Zhengyu both nearly met disaster; afterwards Jiao Shengguang was torn apart
zhé
, the cruel punishment of old in which the limbs were torn apart)
alive to settle the matter
[Jiao
hé

Shengguang] This man was originally a licentiate of Shuntian prefecture; he was made the scapegoat of the seditious book case and executed by slow slicing, and his family was sent into exile on the frontier to serve as soldiers.

Fuzheng further notes: the Remaining Affairs of Master Da says: when the Master was interrogated, the chief imperial guard asked in a stern voice: ‘As to the affair of the seditious book, you certainly know of it.’ The Master replied: ‘Your servant does not know.’ The guard said: ‘Why do you not know?’ The Master said: ‘Your servant is but a common monk; he does not know.’ When he was questioned further, he only related the words about the three debts, and had no other words at all. In prison, one day before his passing, Lord Lu Wutai’s son, Lord Danyuan, who was then in the Water Bureau, received a handwritten note from the Master: ‘It is exceedingly dark here; quickly buy seven glazed lamps and send them in, as an excellent work of light.’ Danyuan sent them as bidden. A day later the Master lit the lamps; on the table he sat upright and spoke a verse: ‘A single smile has always had its own cause; who knew the great clod would not abide a speck of dust? From now I gather up the feet my mother bore; the iron post blooms and does not wait for spring.’

Fuzheng further notes: Master Da’s deeds of forgetting himself for the Dharma were not one only, but the initiating of the carving of the folded-volume canon seems, beside the calamity he met in prison, all the greater and more enduring. For only this folded-volume form spreads the Dharma’s course, makes study convenient, and can circulate with anyone, in any place. Otherwise the Sanskrit volumes, stately as they are, are bulky in fascicles and heavy in price, current among monks but not among layfolk; and the faithful in distant lands, though they hear the Buddha’s name, can hardly see a single word of the Dharma treasure. Since Master Da opened up this surpassing cause, it has spread throughout the seas, within and without; among those of the Buddhadharma in heaven above and on earth below there is none who has not heard of it.

[Initiating the carving of the folded-volume canon, all the greater and more enduring] In ancient times the canon carved in our country was always bound in the accordion-fold style, and so the fascicles were vast and cumbersome, bringing great inconvenience to circulation. Seeing this, the Master redesigned the carving of the Great Canon and changed it to the light, thread-bound book form, from which time reading became convenient for all and circulation flourished. At the same time the Master also gathered a great many extracanonical works — commentaries, repentance texts, recorded sayings, and the like — into the Continued Canon and the Further Continued Canon, greatly enriching the content of the Great Canon; the merit of this can hardly be overstated. Great Master Daguan’s carving of the “folded-volume canon” spread the Dharma’s course, made study convenient, and could circulate with anyone, in any place, opening the eyes of gods and men for long ages; its service to the propagation of the Buddhadharma was very great and very enduring. The so-called “folded-volume canon” is the carved edition of the Great Canon that later generations called the Jing Mountain Canon or the Jiaxing Canon.

In Jiaxing prefecture there is the Lengyan Temple, with a permanent endowment for the scripture workshop. The origin of the carving of the canon lay with Master Da’s eminent disciple Master Mizang, who, by order of the Empress Dowager Cisheng, gathered workmen at Mount Wutai; but the final accomplishment was at the Jizhao Huacheng on Mount Jing and at the two places of the Lengyan Prajñā Hall in our own prefecture.
Master Da’s Dharma words of that day were fixed as an ordinance: ‘The blocks kept at Mount Jing may not issue scriptures; the Lengyan
(the Lengyan Temple)

may issue scriptures but may not keep blocks’ — as if he foresaw that later men in other prefectures would recklessly make changes. When Patriarch Han passed through Jiaxing prefecture, the master of the Lengyan Hall, Lord Maozhu, invited him to a vegetarian feast in the temple and asked for instruction. Patriarch Han’s words recounted the rise and fall of the Lengyan
(the Lengyan Temple)

, and he also praised Lord Mao as upright, cultured, kind, and forbearing, urging him on to the great Dharma and to the endless, imperishable Buddhist work of circulation. Thereupon, seated there, he charged me face to face: ‘Master Da and I were of one heart in the Dharma gate and shared in one another’s sorrow and joy; the carving of the canon is my own affair, and this is the thought I have not finished — do not you forget it.’ Afterwards the workshop was moved and copies were printed privately, and there were repeated upheavals.
From the guihai year, when the Jiangxi lineage monk Baifa Zong was invited to be abbot of the Lengyan
(the Lengyan Temple)

, affairs were somewhat set in order. But the monk Qingyin of Huacheng, in the years bingyin and dingmao, again fabricated tales of upheaval. Thanks to Lord Bai’s upright conduct and meticulous management, shrinking from no resentment, in the end it could not be shaken. To this day, more than twenty years on, the merit rests with the Lengyan
(the Lengyan Temple)

, whose gates, halls, images, and the various provisions of the fragrant kitchen have been brought to no small completion. But his greatest turning of the tide lay in circulating the folded volumes and opening the eyes of gods and men for long ages. Mr. Li Jiuyi called Lord Bai ‘a true son of Zibo
(Great Master Daguan)
and a younger brother of Mizang
(Master Da’s eminent disciple Master Mizang)
,’ and he was not wrong. In the intercalary sixth month of the yiyou year, when the fire of war
xiḿn
, burning in the midst of soldiers’ chaos)

brought great disorder, Lord Bai sat in charge of the scripture workshop while blades were brandished and he was beaten and plundered four times over, yet he stood unshaken. With his very head, eyes, marrow, and brain he guarded the scriptures of India, and kept them whole as in ordinary times; the power of the Buddha, the power of the Dharma, and the power of the Sangha here showed forth great marvels. Now though Lord Bai has left the Lengyan
(to open the eyes of gods and men for long ages)

, yet at Yingquan, at Louze, and at Dongta, wherever his staff and bamboo hat have reached, all has been made new and set in order. And as for the one great karmic occasion of the scripture workshop, I, Fuzheng, ought to follow it from first to last, and not fail the charge left by the Patriarchs Da and Han.
The Thirty-Second Year of Wanli
Jiachen ●
I was fifty-nine. In the first month of spring, on account of Master Da, a general order
(a document of notification)
went to the censorate, and I was directed by writ
xí
, to proclaim)
to return to my garrison
(the place where I was exiled and stationed)
, and so I left
(and so departed from)
Caoxi for Leizhou.

Remembering that Master Da had said: ‘The Surangama sets forth the causes and results of the seven destinies, and no worldly book has a matching explanation.’ I said: ‘The Spring and Autumn is precisely a book that makes causes and results clear,’ and so I wrote the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals.
(Master Daguan, a sixth time.)
[The seven destinies]

The destiny of hell, the destiny of hungry ghosts, the destiny of animals, the destiny of humans, the destiny of immortals, the destiny of gods, and the destiny of asuras. “Destiny” here means the direction toward which one tends.
Fuzheng reads the passage above: “on my account, and so I was implicated once more”; and here: “on account of Master Da, I was directed by writ to return to my garrison.” For the affair of Master Da
(in)
and the tearing apart of Jiao Shengguang belonged to the time when the heir was in peril: the two men were in truth one man
(in the “seditious book case” and the matter of endangering the imperial heir, Patriarch Han and Great Master Daguan were in truth one man)

, the two affairs in truth one affair, the two perils in truth one peril. Hence one general order from the capital bureau, and again one great crisis; suspicion and right and wrong were mingled. Yet he had leisure of mind to write a book — and not a Buddhist book but a Confucian one; not any other book but the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary — because in the Spring and Autumn, from the reigns of Yin and Huan onward, states such as Lu, Wei, Qi, and Jin were led, through the confusion of consorts and spouses, to depose or set up heirs and to the decline and peril of their dynasties
(it was always bewitching consorts who wrought confusion, deposed or set up the heir, and brought the state’s fortune to decline and peril)

. Citing antiquity to mirror the present, the Yin mirror is not far off. The speaker is guiltless; the hearer is warned enough. The heart-method of Zuo was received from Confucius, and the heart-method of the Patriarchs was received from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. In the world and beyond it, no meaning is greater than that of the Spring and Autumn.
[The Spring and Autumn]
The history of the state of Lu, recording the years from the first year of Duke Yin of Lu (722
BC) to the fourteenth year of Duke Ai of Lu (481

BC). As the chronological history of Lu, it was compiled and revised by Confucius. The language of the Spring and Autumn is extremely terse, yet almost every sentence contains an implicit praise or blame, and later ages called this “the brush-method of the Spring and Autumn.”
[Zuo]

Zuo Qiuming of the state of Lu in the closing years of the Spring and Autumn period. Because the text of the Spring and Autumn is very terse and its record of events most summary, he annotated it, and the book he wrote is called the Zuo Commentary, the first chronologically arranged history in China to narrate events in detail.
[The Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals] Patriarch Han
wrote the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals to set forth the principle of cause and effect. (For details see
Dream-Journey Collection
· Preface to the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals
The Thirty-Third Year of Wanli
Yisi ●

“I was sixty. In the third month of spring I crossed the Qiong Sea and visited Dongpo’s Betel-Nut Hut and the White Dragon Spring, seeking traces of Chan Master Juefan, but could not find them. I lodged at the Mingchang Pagoda Court and wrote the Preface to the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals. I journeyed to Stone Mountain and wrote A Record of Wonders Explored in the Qiong Sea and A Record of the Golden Millet Spring. At night I climbed the prefectural wall: it was so desolate it seemed that no human smoke remained; only in the western quarter of the city was there a little life. I therefore said to my disciples: ‘Qiong city is about to meet with calamity; quickly perform rites to avert it
ráng
, to pray for the removal of disaster)

’ People thought this false. Yet when I crossed the sea, only half a month later, there was a great earthquake: in the eastern part of the city the wall and gate collapsed, and the government buildings in the city were all thrown down. The Mingchang Pagoda fell and crushed the upper storey where I had been lodging to pieces. When I left, the gentry of the prefecture had pressed me hard to stay, but I would not remain; had I not gone, I too would have been dust. At the time people thought it strange.
So it was that I crossed the sea by moonlight and saw the finest prospects of Qiong
(the same as “gai”)
, which I took to be a fairy capital, one of the ten isles
(the ten famous mountain paradises where the immortals dwell in the great sea)

. In the fourth month of summer the governor directed me by writ to return to Wuyang. In the seventh month of autumn I reached Caoxi. When I left, the Patriarch’s Hall had already been pulled down for rebuilding and the work was not yet stopped; on my return, six or seven tenths were complete. The debt for materials and labour came to nearly a thousand pieces of gold, with no means of meeting it. I converted the two palace eunuchs to give, and paid it all; I also repaired the Changchun Hut at Qingmen in Wuyang, to be an administration court of Caoxi
xiè
and a place for making offerings on behalf of the Sixth Patriarch.
(Lord Dai of the governor’s office, a third time. The two palace eunuchs are the former mining commissioner Lord Li and his colleague, a second time.)

Fuzheng wonders: the two palace eunuchs were the mining commissioners who were able to prove loyal to the Sacred Mother; hence, on the writ returning me to the garrison, they were able at once to give and pay off the thousand pieces of gold owed for the Patriarch’s Hall, material and labour. How could this have been easily brought about by begging for alms? The eunuchs’ gift was also a karmic fruit of the Sacred Mother’s former fame.
To look at the air and know a calamity, like Confucius
(Confucius)
and the shangyang bird
(a bird of legend. It is said that before heavy rain it often dances on one foot)
that knows the rain, or the halo round the moon that foretells fair weather, is of itself an ordinary matter for a man of clear understanding who knows the first signs
(who knows the subtle beforehand)

; it is not to be called strange talk. In the spring of the third month of the yisi year before, the Mingchang Pagoda of Qiongzhou city fell and crushed the upper storey in which he lodged to pieces, yet Master Hanshan happened to have left, and he said he had escaped being ground to powder; people thought it strange. Twelve years later,
dài
, to wait until)
in the summer of the bingchen year

, on the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month, in the Chunshu Lane of the north city of Jiaxing, the five-roomed hall and upper storey in which Fuzheng lodged collapsed entirely, and Fuzheng was crushed beneath it; three great beams fell astride and propped it up. Bricks and tiles more than a foot across struck his body like the paper goods used in funerary offerings; he felt no pain and was not hurt at all. He came out from among the piled rubble like a clay figure, and after bathing a while was clean, feeling no difference whatever in his movements. The whole city was astonished, taking it for a rare thing even among those born twice. At that time Fuzheng had long believed in the Buddhadharma, and when the building gave way with a great crash, the whole household heard a single “Namo Guanyin Bodhisattva” filling the air. On the first of the seventh month he entered Mount Jing and paid his respects to Chan Master Xueqiao, telling him of it; Xue was calm and did not think it strange. Then on the first of the eleventh month, at Mount Jing, he met Patriarch Han and told him of it, and the Patriarch was startled and did not take it as ordinary. So he named him Fuzheng, styled him Liangsheng, and showed him a verse. Now, reading in the chronicle the words about the shattered tower at Qiong city, I recall the former affair. The Patriarch, by knowing the subtle signs and being godlike in it, escaped being ground to powder by crossing the sea, and people thought it strange. Fuzheng, by holding that birth and death are fated, escaped being ground to powder from amid the powder and dust, and his heart never forgot it. So, moved, I append this note.
The Thirty-Fourth Year of Wanli
Bingwu ●

I was sixty-one. In the third month of spring I crossed the ridge to Nanzhou, to wait upon Ding Youwu and to thank the grand minister Lord Zhang Hongyang. When I was in trouble, the lord was then assistant minister and knew the whole course of my case most thoroughly; he joined with others to do all in his power to save me, and my heart was grateful. Now the lord was living at home, and so I went to thank him. The lord was delighted to speak of old times, gathered his sons, and set out a vegetarian feast for me at the Idle Cloud Tower on the river. In the midst of the gathering the lord said: “Everyone knows that Master Han is a great teacher of goodness, but they do not know that he has done great hidden service to the state.” Hearing this the company was awestruck and asked the lord to explain; the lord told the whole account
(the same as “gai”)
, and the whole table was moved
(everyone present was deeply moved)
. At that time I wrote six poems.

Returning, I passed through Wenjiang and visited Supervising Secretary Zou, staying several days. At Zhanggong, General Chen Ershi kept me in his headquarters; I was ill for a month, and wrote twelve poems on lying ill, then returned to Caoxi. In the eighth month of autumn the imperial eldest grandson was born, and there was a gracious amnesty: all those in garrison who were old or ill, and those who by error
guà
, to err)
had offended, were to be heard, cleared, and released; I was among them. So I went to inform the military commissioner, who permitted a review of the case
(granted a retrial)
, and I returned to the Leizhou circuit; the review made clear that I should be pardoned, and the surveillance commission drew up the papers to await the memorial, and so I left the ranks
(and so departed from the soldiers’ ranks, ending the life of exile)

(Ding Youwu, a fourth time. Grand Minister Zhang Hongyang, once. Supervising Secretary Zou, a second time. General Chen Ershi, once. The imperial eldest grandson, once. Hongyang was named Wei, a man of Xinjian in Jiangxi; he led the proposal to settle the succession under Taichang, and with Grand Minister Shen Li and the Master of Rites Guo Zhengyu did great service.)

Fuzheng notes: what Lord Hongyang spoke of — the great hidden merit he had wrought for the altars of state — and the outline he gave of it, which stirred a whole table to a change of countenance, was nothing other than praying for an heir and obtaining one, protecting the heir and establishing him, and so courting taboo and disaster in matters within and without the palace that may not be spoken of. Hence his words were half revealed and half concealed, and in the end could not be transmitted. The Hanshan Master began with this exile and ended with this pardon, and so he wrote it in large letters: “In the autumn, the eighth month, the imperial eldest grandson was born.” Following the precedent of the renwu year, when he wrote that in the eighth month the crown prince was born, and the example of the special brush of the Spring and Autumn Annals, this is why the Spring and Autumn Zuo Commentary: Mind-Method came to be written. Who was the crown prince? It is the title given after Taichang came to the throne. Who was the imperial eldest grandson? It is the designation used at his birth in the early Tianqi reign. Tianqi too was born of Consort Wang, a lady of Taichang's household, later posthumously titled Empress Xiaoduan. For the two Consorts Wang, one after another, gave birth to
(the character used is a variant of “to bear”)

two emperors. Though the Hanshan Master stood within the grace of the pardon, his meaning was not directed to the pardon alone; his brush goes straight to the point where the affinity of praying for an heir at Mount Tai is tied together. The great pivotal matter of half a lifetime, the great public case, lies in the four words “the imperial eldest grandson was born.” From this one knows that the whole course of the chronicle, from beginning to end, is nothing but the mind-method of the Spring and Autumn and the Zuo Commentary.
The thirty-fifth year of Wanli
, dingwei ●
I was sixty-two. In the third month of spring I petitioned to return to my native place
(to have my monastic register restored)

, and the governor-general directed the prefecture of Shaozhou by writ to settle me at Caoxi. While I dwelt in the mountain I was able to preach the Dharma for my disciples. In my youth I read the Laozi, and because its language is ancient and its meaning deep, I found it hard and knotty. Searching its purport to the utmost, I gained something; my lay disciples asked me to write a commentary on it, and I began in the renchen year. I set my mind upon it, and only when each point had been investigated through and through did I set down my brush. If a single word was doubtful and would not come clear, I never let it pass lightly. Thus I labored fifteen years, carrying it with me on my travels, and only now is it finished.
(Lord Dai of the governor-general's office, fourth appearance.)

Fuzheng notes: the Outer Chronicle of the Hanshan Master says: “The commentary on the one scripture of the Dao and its Virtue took thirteen years before the draft left his hand. As for the purport of the Supreme One's words, he must have tried them on himself before he saw them; they cannot be called stale words on paper, without true savor. Whenever I write on a scripture, I must gather my spirit and enter contemplation, and only when my body tallies with the Buddha-mind and a subtle opening suddenly bursts forth of itself do I commit it to paper. If deliberation enters in, it is of no use at all.”
The thirty-sixth year of Wanli
, wushen ●

I was sixty-three. We discussed repairing the great hall of Caoxi. In the second month of spring, Lord Feng Yuancheng of Wuzhong took up the post of circuit intendant of Lingxi. He came into the mountain to visit me and stayed the night, and dreamed that a great bodhisattva appeared; he was moved by it. At dawn
(early morning)

he entered the hall to worship the Buddha, and coming before the three great bodhisattvas he saw that two of the great beams were rotted through. Startled, he said to me: “Why do you not repair this?” I said: “The work is great and the cost heavy; my strength does not reach to it.” He asked: “How much would it cost?” I answered with a certain sum. He said: “That is no difficulty; let me try.” He returned and reported it to Lord Dai of the governor-general's office, who said: “How perilous! If one sees a child about to fall into a well, one must crawl to the rescue; how much more when the Buddhas and bodhisattvas stand in such a perilous place — to be unmoved would be no man at all.” He then asked what the cost would be, and was told what I had said. The Lord said: “That is not yet enough.” He at once sent the Nan-Shao circuit to survey and estimate, and told them to ask me to deliberate on it. I went and saw the Lord, who in his ardor wished to build it out of his own funds. I told him: “If it draws on public money, I fear it will not be proper. If we follow the old precedent of the Dharma gate
(if we follow the custom of the Buddhist order)
, it may perhaps be done
(in that way it can be accomplished)
. The Lord said: “What then
(what is to be done)

?” I asked that it be done by appealing to the many: “Let Your Lordship instruct the Lingxi circuit to prepare twelve subscription books; let the three offices, the circuits, and the prefectures each keep one, and let each give according to his wish; let all be gathered in the prefecture and remitted as one, without passing through the monks' hands. In this way it will be no burden and will soon be collected.” The Lord followed it, and in less than a month nearly a thousand gold pieces were gathered. I went in person to western Yue to choose great timbers, and when I reached Duanzhou the governor-general kept me to repair the Treasure Moon Terrace, and appointed other officials to purchase the timber in my stead. In winter the Treasure Moon Terrace was completed and I wrote its record; the timber was all piled on the bank of the Duan River and carried up in due order.
In the eleventh month of winter the Annamite bandits breached Qinzhou; Lord Dai asked that the imperial troops be sent on a distant punitive expedition, and was thereupon impeached and dismissed.

(Feng Yuancheng of Lingxi, first appearance. Lord Dai of the governor-general's office, fifth appearance. Yuancheng, whose personal name was Shike and whose style was Wensuo, was a man of Huating, a jinshi of the xinwei year of Longqing, and rose to be assistant administrator of Zhejiang.)
[Dismissed after impeachment]

In the eleventh month of winter the Yao and Zhuang of Annam attacked and breached Qinzhou. The Master, with banners and jeweled canopies for his insignia, majestic as a heavenly being, entered their caves and talked them into surrender. The bandits then withdrew and the region was made secure, and the million living souls of Qinzhou were saved (Master Yinguang says in his discourse: “His withdrawing the timber boats, settling the popular uprising, and bringing peace to Qinzhou — such great matters he settled all with a single talk. Had he not been one who came forth by his vow to save people from fire and water, who could have done it?”). Lord Dai then memorialized the throne asking that the imperial troops be sent to punish the crime, so as to cover up the loss of Qinzhou. Because the Yao bandits had already withdrawn and the city was safe and sound, the court, after deliberating, issued its decree: Lord Dai was merely dismissed from office, and escaped arrest and interrogation.

At the Zongjing Hall Fuzheng heard from an attendant: “Lord Dai held the staff of office in Guangdong for nine years; bandits and rebels on the mountains and the seas stirred several times, and the reason he could hold his post so long without mishap was wholly the Hanshan Master's strength. Therefore he gave so generously to Caoxi that a hundred ruined works were all set afoot; only the great hall was not built. He planned to use ironwood for the beams, and had it all brought from western Yue to the site; the price already came to three thousand gold pieces. Had Lord Dai stayed another year in office, the work at Caoxi would have been accomplished beyond thought.” On the day he was dismissed he left the Master to repair the Treasure Moon Hall. At that time the Yao and Zhuang of Annam had breached Qinzhou and the affair had already collapsed. When the emperor heard of it, he was nearly arrested. The Master, by reason of his great name, went in with banners and jeweled canopies and talked the bandits into surrender. When the bandits had withdrawn and the region was pacified
(settled)

, the million living souls of Qinzhou were saved. Lord Dai then submitted a memorial asking that the imperial troops be sent to punish the crime, so as to cover up the earlier failure; hence he was only impeached and dismissed, and escaped arrest and interrogation. The Master's repayment of Lord Dai's merit in restoring Caoxi was likewise exceedingly
(utmost)

great. Yet he did not make much of his own merit, nor expose Lord Dai's fault; with a mere ten or so characters he closed the case of the governor-general's departure from office — this too is the mind-method of the Spring and Autumn Annals, which conceals the faults of the worthy, and the utmost of loyal and generous righteousness. At that time there was a book, The Palm-Pointing of the Wonderful Gate, written at Lord Dai's request.
The thirty-seventh year of Wanli
, jiyou ●

I was sixty-four. In the second month of spring, as I was bringing timber back from Duanzhou, the wind blocked us at the Antelope Gorge; I visited the Duan Stream and wrote A Dream Record of Visiting the Duan Stream. When the timber had been brought to the Meng River I entered the mountain and was just gathering the assembly to set the work going. At that time several unworthy monks among them
(of vicious character)
did mischief and opposed it
(that is, they worked mischief to ruin me)

, and they stirred up the assembly to riot like rebellious commoners. I saw it and sighed, saying: “This is my own grave offense against the Buddha's teaching; it is the fault of grasping at appearances.” While the crowd was still clamoring, I sat alone in the hall, burned incense, and recited the Diamond Prajna
(the Diamond Sutra)

, until I came to the Buddha's words “the four views are precisely not the four views,” and suddenly I was greatly awakened; I then wrote the Diamond Doubts Resolved. When the draft was finished, the crowd fell silent.
[The four views are precisely not the four views] The Diamond Sutra

reads: “The World-Honored One speaks of the view of self, the view of a person, the view of sentient beings, the view of a life-span; these are precisely not the view of self, the view of a person, the view of sentient beings, the view of a life-span; therefore they are called the view of self, the view of a person, the view of sentient beings, the view of a life-span.” (For detailed annotation see
The Diamond Sutra Explained in Detail
These
unworthy ones
(the wicked men)
, did not trust my mind
(saw that I would not be swayed)
, but were misled by wicked men
(deceived again by villains)
, and grew the more fearful
(all the more afraid)
, and so brought suit before the regional inspector
(another name for the Ming regional inspecting censor)
, who approved the case being passed to the judicial officer
(directed that the judicial officer handle the case
. The judicial officer was the official in charge of litigation and punishment
At that time I calmly left the mountain and went to answer the charge, living on a boat on the Hibiscus River for two years, until my traveling funds were exhausted. Then the assistant prefect
(assistant to the prefectural governor)
Lord Xiang Chudong was guarding the pass on the Han
hán

River and invited me to come. On the river journey we met a wind and the boat was wrecked. When I arrived I fell gravely ill and nearly died; the Lord brought physicians and had me treated with all his strength. When I returned to the prefecture I lay ill in an inn, approaching the full year
(nearly a year)
(The judicial officer: no surname given. Lord Xiang Chudong, assistant prefect, whose personal name was Guifang, a man of Jiaxing; each appears once.)
Fuzheng notes: he gave the Diamond Doubts Resolved to the block-carvers at the Lengyan
(Monastery)
scripture workshop; it came to forty-eight leaves. How, amid all that turmoil and clamor, could the draft have been finished in a moment? It was truly
xún
, indeed)
a hand answering the mind; it is not to be sought in the words.
The thirty-eighth year of Wanli
, gengxu ●
I was sixty-five. That year I lived on a boat on the river. In the seventh month of autumn the regional inspector came on his circuit to the prefecture
(the regional inspector came on his tour of inspection to this prefecture; the regional inspector was the official charged solely with inspection and with handling local government affairs)
, and inquired after me
(came to visit me)
. When the judicial officer heard of it
(when the judicial officer heard of this)
, he had only then begun to hear the case
(only then began to try it)
, and turned about and judged me guilty
(and instead found me guilty)
. The regional inspector strongly disapproved, and rebutted him, saying: “A certain man
has done great service for the Sixth Patriarch
(Master Hanshan has done great service for the Sixth Patriarch)
. Those who formerly gave for the sake of the permanent endowment
(previously took great pains to plan, raise funds, and build for this monastery)
, now
(now)
the wicked monks get the benefit, and instead he is judged guilty — is this what you call the dharma gate of equality?” He again instructed the local circuit
(and again instructed the local circuit and prefecture)
to investigate strictly. Thereupon
(thereupon)

the prefecture came in person into the mountain, and taking the charges the monks had lodged, examined them point by point: all were baseless words with nothing to them. They falsely accused me of misappropriating more than eight thousand in gold from the permanent endowment. I had, when I first took charge, established clear rules for the endowment's treasury office and issued numbered receipts. For every receipt and expenditure of money and grain there were supervising monks and scribes
(who recorded it in writing)

, and each smallest item that passed in or out was supported by a numbered receipt and never paid out at random. Now the monks who had held office over the years were examined and reckoned before the officials; the numbered receipts were the standard, and not a fraction of it touched me. Then high and low, within and without, believed that I did not act recklessly, and the matter was cleared
(the false accusation was thus made plain to all the world)

. The authorities were greatly angered at those monks, and I did my utmost to intercede for them. They begged me again and again to stay in the mountain, but by then my heart was weary, and I firmly declined. I handed the Chan hall over to my disciple Huaiyu, and at once calmly departed, lodging at the Changchun Hut in Wuyang.
(The regional inspector: no surname given, first appearance. ○The Chan hall is the Baolin Hall.)
Fuzheng notes: I suspect that Lord Dai of the governor-general's office had but just been dismissed
(had just been removed from office)

, and yet those few unworthy monks dared to raise such a great storm of trouble. What monks were they? They must have been the old abbots of Caoxi. What money and grain was it that they falsely accused him of misappropriating? It must have been the permanent endowment of many years, which by the old rule of Caoxi was received and paid out before the officials and reckoned before the officials. Ever since the high authorities invited the Hanshan Master into Caoxi, the old monks could no longer be masters there and had long lost the profit of embezzlement; therefore, seizing the moment when the censorate had no intimate friends to turn to, they bought over
(bribed)
the judicial officer to overturn the case. But his foresight
(prescience)

, which saw the workings beforehand, had long since prevented the trouble; the mischief of a sudden moment could vent its poison without doing harm. Yet after two years of hearing the case from a boat, in the blink of an eye the timber for the hall came to nothing — a great stinginess in the karmic affair of the Sixth Patriarch; happily the Hanshan Master's far-reaching plans made good what came after. Looking back at the earlier matter of the request to examine the inner expenditure registers and the unverifiable donations falsely entered, though the troubles differed in size, the solution was one dharma. A gruel-and-rice ground for a thousand monks, a single mat of pure white ground. The Chan hall was handed over, and going and coming were free. The public case of Caoxi was from then on closed — and yet truly not closed. On the point of departure, his Ten Poems to Encourage the Disciples of Caoxi says

A thousand monks in concord, as on Vulture Peak; / no common thing, this refuge that the assembly seek. / Had you not once received his personal charge, / how could you ever enter the patriarchs' gate?

The flesh-body stands before you, living as of old; / morning and evening tea and broth are offered in sincerity. / Bell and drum ring out clear — that is the Dharma preached; / no need for a bitter tongue to warn you again.

Sow deep the seeds within the field of merit; / cause and effect stand clear as a bright mirror-stand. / You have come to the jewel mountain a thousand times; / this time, do not go back again empty-handed.

Take up your labors, and shrink not from toil; / remember the stone that hung at his waist of old. / One breath that fails to come is a thousand kalpas; / if roots of goodness are not planted, suffering is not dispelled.
[The stone that hung at his waist in that year] In that year the Sixth Patriarch pounded rice with a stone tied at his waist. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The Patriarch
(the Fifth Patriarch)
stole to the pounding shed, and seeing Huineng
(Huineng)
pounding rice with a stone tied at his waist, said: ‘One who seeks the Way forgets his own body for the sake of the Dharma — should it not be thus?’”

[Pounding rice with a stone at the waist] In old times, when rice was pounded in quantity, the principle of the lever was used: a pounding mallet at one end, a man treading at the other. Huineng tied a great stone at his waist to add to his weight, so that the counterweight at the pounder opposite could be increased, and in this way the efficiency of the pounding was raised.

Do not let this life pass lightly by; / time flies like an arrow — truly a fearful thing. / I only fear that when the breath leaves these three inches of throat, / when will you walk the jewel mountain again?
The garden of merit must not be taken lightly; / every step of the foot must be clear and sure. / Do not let it slip and go along with the rest, / lest the blind man walk again in the night.

An inch of rafter, a shard of tile — all come of many causes; / the fat and marrow of faithful gifts must not be taken lightly. / Never covet another's dung-caked peg, / and lightly trade away your pair of eyes.

The fat and blood of the faithful weigh heavier than Sumeru; / a grain of rice, a stalk of firewood must never be misused. / Only look at those who wear fur and carry horns: / they repay their former debts in the bitter niraya
(Sanskrit for hell)

Blessed to be born in the Middle Kingdom and early leave the dust; / wearing the kashaya, far from the six kinds of kin. / You enjoy the pure blessings of the empty gate — / how will you ever repay the patriarchs' grace?

If from youth you can hold fast the mind that reaches upward, / a tiny sprout will grow at last to a thousand fathoms. / You have only to pass through all the bitterness of ice and frost / before you can become timber and come forth from the Deng Forest
(the Deng Forest of ancient myth, a figure for a gathering place of the outstanding)
Again, his Ten Poems Written on the Eve of Going to Nanyue, Taking Leave of the Brethren of the Lingnan Dharma Society, says:

Once fallen into the dust of the world, twenty years; / that we meet at all, know it for a former bond. / Ever since the robe and bowl came south, / today I take up once more the Chan of direct pointing.

The matter is clear within your own person; / no need to ask outside whether you prosper or fail. / Only turn the light back wherever you meet a thing, / and let not the toil of dust trap the master within.

[The matter] This matter. [One's own person] To practice it oneself (to carry it out in person). [Dust-toil] The mind toiling over objects of dust; another name for affliction. [The master] The master within, meaning one's own nature.

The great Way has always cut off the original and the true; / it is discrimination that forces the near and the far apart. / You must see right through the face your mother bore you with, / and then you are one set apart amid the dust.

I have drunk all the miasmic mists, and my teeth still ache with cold; / I no longer recall how hard the road has been before. / Now I go to the deep, close places of ten thousand mountains, / to watch the five-colored clouds from my seat.

Twenty years I galloped through the land of miasma; / these years past, unawares, my temples turned to frost. / Now I take a single leaf of a boat and go; / my traces shall be hidden in ten thousand ravines.
Long have I roamed the toil of dust, blending my light
(blending light with dust)
, busy only with raising up this matter
(the upward path)
for others. Of my thousand-foot fishing pole, almost all is cut away; / looking back on sea and sky, more boundless still.

Ever since I took refuge and circled the Dharma altar, / I have begged at every hour for this mind to be at peace. / Say not that we part three thousand li apart: / the bright moon at mid-heaven meets us face to face.
Sometimes I take up my fishing line
(fishing pole)
and see my plain and simple heart; my bamboo songs
(bamboo-branch songs — here meaning his own poems, writings, and all his various instructions)
are sung out — how few are the true listeners! / I go back in a small boat on a frosty night; / the bright moon and the reed flowers — where shall they be found?

In the cold sky, clear and distinct, a lone wild goose cries; / from today my traces fall among the Five Lakes. / Boundless mist and waves carry my sorrowful thoughts; / a single sail on the horizon is my road home.
For the Dharma, would I shrink from a long road
(long, drawn-out)
? How could one call the miasmic sea the end of the world? Again and again I take a drop of Caoxi's water to nourish the West-coming
(Bodhidharma's coming from the West)
five-petaled flower.
[The five-petaled flower] After the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, the Chan school branched into the five houses of Caodong, Linji, Yunmen, Guiyang, and Fayan; hence the saying, “one flower, five petals.”
In the first ten he sets forth the teaching, in the latter ten he sets forth Chan; this in itself is the robe and bowl.
The thirty-ninth year of Wanli
, xinhai ●

I was sixty-six. In the third month of spring I was living at Dinghu Mountain in Duanzhou, nursing my illness.
