At first, when I received the pardon and awaited the memorial, there was never any reply from the regional inspector, and so it was delayed until now; then, examined and cleared once more, the case was at last cancelled and I was left to do as I pleased
(to be a free man)
. At that time several scholars attached themselves to me and asked for instruction, and so I set forth the Doubts Resolved on the Great Learning.

Fuzheng notes: reading the chronicle, in the dingyou year he wrote the Direct Pointing at the Doctrine of the Mean. Fifteen years later, in the xinhai year, he first set forth the Doubts Resolved on the Great Learning. That the Mean comes first and the Great Learning after follows the Book of Rites, where the Mean is the thirty-first chapter and the Great Learning the forty-second. The Master, at the Zongjing Hall, said to Fuzheng face to face: “The Great Learning tails
(follows upon)
the meaning of the Mean.” Fuzheng took this and so completed the book.
The fortieth year of Wanli
, renzi ●
I was sixty-seven, dwelling at the Changchun Hut, where I expounded the Awakening of Faith for my disciples, the Eight Consciousnesses
(the Verses on the Rules of the Eight Consciousnesses)
, and the Hundred Dharmas
(the Treatise on the Door of Understanding of the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahayana)

, and was asked to set forth a direct exposition. Previously, because the Lotus Sutra: Beating the Beat had its text and meaning so linked together as not to be divided, so that students found it hard to grasp, I wrote the Chapter Divisions
(the General Exposition on the Chapter Divisions of the Lotus Sutra)
The forty-first year of Wanli
, guichou ●

I was sixty-eight. I kept the summer retreat for my disciples at the Changchun Hut and expounded the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment. Halfway through, a carbuncle broke out on my back and was very grave; the physicians could not cure it and I was near death. The Great General Lord Wang Hanchong had already made arrangements for my last affairs. At that time a Cantonese named Liang Xingshan, a wine-drinker
(a lover of wine)
, had long been renowned for doctoring sores
yáng
, the general term for boils, abscesses, carbuncles, and furuncles)
(that is, he was famous for it)

. He happened to come, looked at it, and said: “It is grave; a little delay and it could not be saved. Be at ease, there is no harm.” He then gathered nothing but herbs and applied them, and success followed at every touch as if he were juggling balls, the effect coming at the appointed time. By winter I was healed, and I wrote a piece to thank him
(for details see
A Preface for the Good Physician Mr. Liang Xingshan, in the Dream-Journey Collection

[Keeping the summer retreat] Also called the rainy-season retreat: during the three months of summer, monks may not go out at will, so that they may devote themselves to sitting in meditation and practicing the Buddha-Dharma.

This carbuncle had its origin at the time when I first sat in Chan. I knew it to be a debt of resentment, and I asked leave of it by reciting the Avatamsaka; whenever I was copying, reciting, or reading the Avatamsaka, it would secretly break out, and as soon as I prayed it would stop. Even here in Guangdong it twice failed to come to a head. This trouble has been in my body for forty-eight years. When it first arose I happened to forget it, and did not know that it was a carbuncle, and so it became a grave illness. So it is that the requital of karmic resentment was tried upon his own body, and proved true.
In the tenth month my illness was healed. Earlier I had become a friend beyond the world
(a friend who has no part in worldly affairs)
with Zeng Jinjian, a secretary of the Ministry of Rites at Hengyang, and we had long had a pact to spend our old age together at Nanyue
(Mount Heng, in Hengyang, Hunan)

. Letters had passed between us more than ten times, but it could not be done. Now he specially wrote, sending his own man Xuanzhan to welcome me, and so I took up my staff and went, and left Guangdong
(and so departed from Guangdong)

. When I first came to Guangdong, several dozen disciples of the Dharma-nature followed me; in time they gradually scattered, and only Tongjiong and Chaoyi, through every storm, hardship, and illness, followed me and never left my side. Tong'an came and went constantly. Now that I was about to set out they could not bear to part, and so An
(Tong'an)
and Yi
(Chaoyi)

carried their rain-hats with all their strength and followed me. I brought with me my attendants Fuhui, Guangyi, and Guangcheng, and crossed the ridge. In the eleventh month of that year I reached Hudong and there took up my dwelling. Earlier, my disciple Fushan had taken the attendant Shenguang north to visit his family. By this time, within a few days, they too caught up with us.

(The Great General Lord Wang Hanchong, the sore-doctor Liang Xingshan, the Ministry of Rites secretary Zeng Jinjian, and the disciples Xuanzhan and Tongjiong: each first appearance. Chaoyi and Tong'an: each second appearance. Fuhui, Guangyi, Guangcheng, and Shenguang: each first appearance. Fushan: fourth appearance. Jinjian, whose personal name was Fengyi and whose courtesy name was Shunzheng, was a man of Hengyang; he retired from the post of bureau director in the Ministry of Rites, styled himself the Mountain Elder of Nanyue, and wrote the General Understanding of the Lankavatara in eight fascicles.)

Fuzheng notes: looking at the patriarchs, there is not one who does not speak of following the times, and not one who does not speak of repaying debts. Can it be that the fixed karma accumulated through lives — even the great Dharma of the Avatamsaka — may be prayed away and borrowed against, but can never be escaped? That a body which for forty-eight years suffered again and again from this grudge-born carbuncle should in the end become an imperishable flesh-body: therein is seen the spiritual efficacy of the great Dharma. The Hanshan Master went back and forth east, west, south, and north, and the monks and laity who took refuge in him could not be counted even by relays of servants. Yet what the chronicle records is as sparse as the morning stars. Even great and famous lords of the time are often not given their names, titles, or native places. Of Lord Zeng, for instance, the record is somewhat complete, yet even he is for the most part not named.

From the yiwei year, when he entered Guangdong, to this time is eighteen years, and only now does he write the two words “left Guangdong.” In between: exile to Leiyang, entry into Nan-Shao, the revival of Nanhua Monastery at Caoxi, the Baolin Hall, the Pilgrims' Lodge — such great public cases, all closed with the two words “left Guangdong.” And yet the karmic affair of Caoxi was in the end neither closed nor gone.
Fuzheng further observes that Patriarch Lu
(the Sixth Patriarch)
, from Huangmei to Caoxi, hid himself from danger among the hunters for seventeen years and only then shaved
(a variant of “shaved”)

his head under the bodhi tree. The Hanshan Master's six years of wearing his hair bound up and following the army — even at Caoxi he preached the Dharma in cap and kerchief. Patriarch Lu, at the invitation of the prefect of Shaozhou, first sat on the seat with the four assemblies, twelve hundred in all, and preached prajna; from that time his light flowed beyond the eight directions
(the farthest reaches beyond the eight directions)
, and his Way covered all within the realm
(that is, the whole world)

. The Hanshan Master, exiled in Guangdong, was permitted, in compliance with the requests of the governor-general and the various high officials, to move his staff to Caoxi, and at once made butcher shops and wine houses bloom into jeweled monasteries; monks and laity gathered in crowds, and he used both the gentle and the stern. The seed of Dajian's Way sprang up and flourished in a revival.

Patriarch Lu's flesh-body at Baolin. He showed his cessation in the second year of Xiantian of Emperor Zhongzong of the Tang. Down to the bingshen year, the twenty-fourth year of Wanli of the Ming, the Hanshan Master first crossed the ridge and came face to face with Patriarch Lu. Down to the third year of Tianqi, when the flesh-body showed its cessation at Caoxi, and again down to the guiwei year, the sixteenth year of Chongzhen, when he was brought again from Wuru, crossed the ridge once more, and the reliquary was opened, and the two faced each other closely — counting in round numbers, exactly a thousand years. Bright mirroring bright, before and after, fitting together like the two halves of a tally: the earlier sage and the later sage, their measure is one.

All the tales handed down in the world — such as those of Chen Yaxian, the Young Master Xiao, and Mao the Debt-Defaulter — were checked for error against what the attendants at the Zongjing Hall said. Only the matter of administering the precept against wine to the attendant Lingtong was heard in especial detail and verified in especial truth, and is worth recording.

The attendant Lingtong was the crown prince of the kingdom of Champa. His father the king sent five great ministers with the prince to Caoxi to invite the Sixth Patriarch to come and receive offerings there. The Sixth Patriarch did not go, and the prince and the ministers all stood and passed away in transformation at the seaside, and did not return. The five ministers became spirits and manifested their powers in Shaoyang. The people set up a Shrine of the Lords outside the mountain gate of Nanhua Monastery, and beside it is the Lords' Bridge. After the prince had passed away in transformation, by his spiritual nature he appeared as an attendant of the Sixth Patriarch, and he alone did not keep the precept against wine; the Sixth Patriarch permitted it, and he received the transmission of the Dharma and departed. One bowl remained in the monastery, and the monks cast a bronze image of him standing in attendance beside the Sixth Patriarch's flesh-body. On the image's head there is a cloth cap, and the villagers who live near the monastery each day fill a bowl with wine and offer it; the wine at once turns to water. After the wine is offered, the cap tilts askew. When the Hanshan Master first entered the mountain, he intended to give the precepts to the great assembly, and the assembly said: “The attendant Lingtong drinks wine; it is not fitting that we receive the precepts.” The Master then wrote a text and announced it before the seat of the Sixth Patriarch, first administering the precept against wine to the attendant Lingtong, and he smashed his bowl. In the announcement are the words: “Smash the vessel of wine, and make of it a vessel of Dharma.” From that time the attendant Lingtong received no offering of wine; when wine is offered to him, the cap does not tilt and the wine does not turn to water.
Further note: Lord Zeng Jinjian wrote the General Understanding of the Lankavatara, and in his own preface
(the author's preface)

says: “He was on terms of perfect friendship with Master Hanshan. He first visited him at Mount Lao; later, when Master Hanshan entered Guangdong and passed by Luochuan, I respectfully entrusted the Lankavatara to him, and at Leiyang he wrote his Notes
(the Hanshan Master, on reaching Leiyang, wrote the Lankavatara Notes)
.” Fuzheng has now seen Lord Zeng's General Understanding, which harmonizes the three translations
(harmonizes the three Chinese translations of the Lankavatara Sutra)
. Weighing it against the Notes
(the Lankavatara Notes)

, it would seem that the Hanshan Master, on reaching Leiyang, sent the Notes to Jinjian, and so discharged his former promise. Yet in the earlier part of the chronicle, for the two years bingshen and dingyou, it says: “Began annotating the Lankavatara,” and again: “The Lankavatara Notes completed.” And its origin is given as “Wang Xinghai of Daxing worshipped on the river and asked for the annotation” — which does not belong to Jinjian. I do not know what to make of it. Could it be that both asked at the same time, and so it was quickly finished?
The above concludes the public case of the revival of Caoxi.
The forty-second year of Wanli
, jiayin ●

I was sixty-nine. When I left Guangdong, those disciples who could not follow me felt their longing grow the keener. At that time the scholar Feng Qinan and others sent letters inviting Fuhui to take my seat in my stead. That year I sent Fushan to escort Hui back to Guangdong.

In late spring I travelled to Mount De to pay homage to the Patriarch and wrote four poems. I visited Lord Feng Yuancheng at Wuling and wrote two poems. I met the assistant administrator Lord Long at Zhuling, received the vegetarian feast of Prince Rong, and the monks of Dashi Monastery asked me to expound the precepts. Lord Feng and his fellow followers of the Way each contributed funds to repair the Tanhua Retreat.
Returning to Hengyang, my boat passed Xiangtan, where I met Bao Yifu. In the fourth month of summer I returned to Huguang and heard that the Sacred Mother had departed to heaven
(the term used for the death of a sovereign)
, and I at once established a Dharma assembly of requital. An edict of grace came, and so before the spirit tablet I had my head shaved, gave thanks for the grace, and put on the monk's robe again.
[Putting on the monk's robe again] The Master, in
, recovered his monastic register, and only in

, when the Empress Dowager passed away and the assembly of requital was established, did he face the Empress Dowager's spirit tablet, shave his head, give thanks for the grace, and put on the monk's robe again. His gratitude was too deep for words.

As for the Surangama Sutra: from the time I was at the Eastern Sea I had resolved to write the General Exposition, and it lay long in my mind without leisure to set it forth. This summer, in the fifth month, I took up my brush, and in fifty days the draft
was finished. In the eleventh month the retreat was completed, and there are poems on dwelling in the mountains; at that time my disciples Wuxin and Zhuanyu came to inquire after me.

(The Sacred Mother: eleventh appearance. The scholar Feng Qinan: first appearance; Fuhui: second appearance. Fushan: fifth appearance. Feng Yuancheng: second appearance. The assistant administrator Long, Zhuling, Prince Rong, Bao Yifu, and the disciples Wuxin and Zhuanyu: each first appearance. Yifu, whose personal name was Hongkui, was a man of Xiushui, a jinshi, magistrate of Xiangtan, and his family had long believed in the Buddha.)

Fuzheng observes: that the Guangdong disciples came to invite the attendant Fuhui to take the seat at Baolin in his stead — this was the origin of his return to Caoxi. It was before the Sacred Mother's spirit tablet that he was willing to shave his head, give thanks for grace, and put on the monk's robe again. Before this, when the grace of pardon came, when the case was examined and cleared, when he was released from the ranks, for eight years he would not lightly put on the monk's robe again of his own accord. In the end he waited for the Sacred Mother, and for the requital assembly that crowned it, to repay the grace of the Sacred Mother's compassionate long life at Mount Tai; and in the matter of the reserves laid up at Bao'en Monastery, the two were bound up together with especial care. An extraordinary tribulation, an extraordinary requital of grace, an extraordinary edict of grace, an extraordinary shaving of the head: truly an extraordinary turning point accumulated over lives and ages.

The Sacred Mother was the Empress Dowager Cisheng, née Li, an imperial consort of Longqing, who gave birth to Shenzong and to the Prince of Lu. When she became Empress Dowager her faith was deep and she delighted in giving; everywhere she was called the Old Buddha Lady. By the regulations of the Ming, where a consort's family had given birth to the heir apparent, the father was enfeoffed as marquis for one generation only and the sons merely inherited the brocade guard; but the Empress Dowager's father was enfeoffed as Duke of Xuanguo, and her nephew Li Chengming inherited the title of Marquis of Wuqing, unbroken for three generations, and the family produced many examination graduates. Their wealth and honor were without compare, and people took it as the reward for the Sacred Mother's lifelong service of the Buddha.
In the twelfth year of Chongzhen, Guochen, the eldest son by a concubine of Chengming, quarreled with his half-brothers over the succession to the title and the family property. The emperor
(Emperor Shenzong of the Ming)

was angry, saying that hereditary titles for consort families were not in the ancestral statutes, and moreover, disliking the family's great wealth, he had it proposed that the property be confiscated; those who carried it out went too hastily, and the Li family could not bear it.

Suddenly one day the fifth imperial prince fell ill and died, and after a while came back to life, and said to the emperor: “I went and saw the Empress Ancestress; she is now a Buddha, called the Nine-Lotus Bodhisattva. She said the estate of the Marquis of Wuqing was bestowed by me while I lived. Tell your father
(tell your father)
that it is without crime and may not be confiscated. National calamity is not far off; you go and come back at once.” Having spoken, he soon died. The emperor
(Emperor Shenzong)
heard it and was greatly alarmed, and so agreed to a judgment of
(to try and decide)
the consort clan
(the family of an empress or imperial consort)
's case, and stopped
(halted)

the earlier proposal, and built the temple of the Nine-Lotus Bodhisattva north of the palace. This showed forth the portent of the dynasty's fall, and the more proved the efficacy of the Buddha-Dharma.

I also heard: “When the Sacred Mother departed to heaven, she charged the Wanli Emperor that it was her regret not to have had Daguan and Hanshan build a Dharma assembly, and hearing that Hanshan was still in Guangdong, she urgently summoned him to return, and so forth.” This Fuzheng heard when he held office at the capital in the military supply depot, where he worked often with the palace envoys, and so came to hear the outline
(the general outline)
of the matter.

The draft of the General Exposition on the Surangama was finished; that it was completed in fifty days, twenty-seven years after the case at Haiyin in the wuzi year, seems also to have been bound up with the affairs of the Sacred Mother.

At that time there was the poem “Seeing Off Wuxin Rong, Chief Seat, on His Return to Jingkou”: “In the empty mountain I meant to spend my last years; / who would have thought you would go east and board the Dharma boat? / Wait until the lone moon rises over the sea gate — / then round off a huatou for this old monk.” And the poem “Inquiring After the Illness of Zhuanyu Heng”: “Long have I contemplated the four elements as a bubble, a shadow; / where can the demon of sickness hide? / The ancients had their own way of resting at ease: / it lies only in the single thought of the unborn.” Reading these, one may know the true conduct and capacity of Masters Wu and Zhuan of old, and may also imagine the karmic bond that led the two to travel together to distant provinces.
In that year began the karmic occasion of the Eastern Journey from Nanyue to Mount Kuang.
The forty-third year of Wanli
, yimao ●

I was seventy. In spring I expounded the General Exposition on the Surangama for the assembly. In the fourth month of summer I wrote the General Exposition on the Lotus Sutra. Because, though there were two sections, the full text was not yet thoroughly unified, I expounded it again, and the draft was likewise finished in fifty days. I lectured on the Awakening of Faith and compiled a Brief Commentary on the Awakening of Faith. In the seventh month of autumn I travelled to Nanyue and climbed Zhurong
(the highest peak of Mount Heng)
, and wrote poems. On the Double Ninth, Lord Feng, transferred from Wuling to be prefect of Hunan, again invited me to travel with him to Fangguang
(a term for a Buddhist monastery)
. Returning to the prefecture, the Lord, together with the circuit intendant Lord Wu Shengbo, came to visit me at Hudong, and in the course of talk touched upon the Surangama
(touched upon the General Exposition on the Surangama)

, and Lord Wu was delighted; he and his subordinates at once contributed funds to print it. On worshipping the portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs, Lord Wu was loud in praise, and had painters copy the small portraits into an album, asking me to write a life and eulogy for each
(the Lives and Eulogies of the Portraits of the Eighty-Eight Patriarchs)
. Lord Feng had not long been in office when he asked me to travel to Jiuyi
(that is, Mount Jiuyi (
yí
. In the tenth month of winter I reached Lingling and stayed the winter at Yuxi.
(Lord Feng Yuancheng: third appearance. The circuit intendant Wu Shengbo: first appearance. Shengbo, whose personal name was Zhongwei, was a man of Haiyan, and rose to be vice minister of justice.)
Fuzheng observes: this old man of seventy, expounding the classics of India
(India)
, the ancient books
(a term joining the Three Graves and the Five Canons, later a general name for the ancient classics)
, writing expositions and compiling commentaries, had not a day's leisure — this is the place in words and letters where the waters run out and the mountains end.
Sakyamuni
(Shakyamuni Buddha)
taught for forty-nine years and bequeathed five thousand and forty-eight divisions, yet said he had never spoken a single word. Confucius
(Kongzi)

edited the Odes and Documents, fixed the rites and music, praised the Zhou Changes, and compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals — all of it the work of a few years after he was sixty-eight and before he was seventy-three. He forgot to eat and forgot his cares, unaware that old age was coming on. In the end he said: “I wish to be without words” — what words has Heaven? And as for the First Patriarch's four fascicles of the Lankavatara and the Sixth Patriarch's one fascicle of the Diamond Sutra — are these speech or no speech, a staff or a shout, the same or different? O my Master, my Master! And so I was moved.
The forty-fourth year of Wanli
, bingchen ●

I was seventy-one. In the first month of spring I returned from Lingling. In the year following Chan Master Daguan's entry into cessation, my disciple Dayi asked that his reliquary be brought south, and the monks and laity enshrined it at the Jizhao Hut on Jingshan — that was a full twelve years ago. I could not forget my obligation in the Dharma gate, and had long wished to go in person to mourn him; even incense I had not sent. Now, hearing of the burial date, I was determined to go. Moreover there was an invitation from the East Chan Monastery at Jinsha, and so I set out in high spirits. As I was about to leave, the monks of the Huayao Monastery asked me to a vegetarian feast and to continue the Dharma lineage. I passed the Plum-Snow Hall and mourned the Chan Master Xun'an.
In the fourth month of summer I left Hudong,
and wrote the poem “Laughing at Myself on Leaving Nanyue.”

On the Double Fifth I reached Wuchang, paid homage to the Great Buddha, visited the Nine Peaks, and paid homage at the stupa of Chan Master Wunian. In the sixth month I reached Xunyang, visited Donglin, and wrote poems on the past. I climbed Mount Kuang
(that is, Mount Lu in Jiangxi; it is said that in the time of Yin and Zhou seven brothers of the Kuang clan built huts here, and so it is called Kuanglu)

, mourned Chan Master Chekong, took refuge from the heat at Jinzhu Ping, and annotated the Zhaolun. Because I found the mountain secluded and lovely, I had thoughts of retiring there, and surveyed all its fine places. In the seventh month I visited Guizong
(Guizong Monastery, at the foot of Mount Lu in Jiangxi)
, climbed the Golden Wheel Peak, paid homage at the relic stupa, and wrote poems. Just then a certain monk offered me Wuru
(Wuru Peak)

as a place for a quiet hut. When I climbed up to look, I saw that the ground was not broad but the situation was quite secluded, and so I accepted it. At that time Xing Laici, a licentiate of Jiangzhou, wished to be the donor who spreads gold, and at once contributed fifty gold pieces to buy the mountain for me; and so my wish to spend my old age there
(to retire in old age)
was fulfilled. Presently Chen Chishi, assistant administrator of Fuliang, heard that I had come and also came to the mountain to visit me. Hearing that I had thoughts of Mount Kuang
(that is, Mount Lu in Jiangxi)
, he made a vow to be my protector of the Dharma.
In the eighth month of autumn I left the mountain and came to Huangmei
(Huangmei county, present-day Hubei)
, where I paid homage to the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs
(the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin and the Fifth Patriarch Hongren)

. I visited Lord Wang, the master of horse, and entered the Purple Cloud Mountain, staying ten days; Lord Wang wished to be the donor for the building on Mount Kuang, and drawing in the Prince of Jing, Prefect Yuan, and others, formed the Society of Seven Worthies before I took my leave. At Tongcheng I visited the grand scribe Wu Guanwo and the assistant censor Wu Benru, who wished to build a hut to keep me. I visited Mount Fu and wrote a song. I crossed the river and climbed Mount Jiu. In the beginning of the tenth month I reached the East Chan Monastery at Jinsha, where I met the gentlemen Yu, Wang, and Sun.

Soon after, leaving Jinsha, I went to Shuangjing. Passing Qu'a, the magistrate Lord Wang of Dongli asked the Dharma at Guanyin Mountain. The He family of Jiangshu welcomed me to their country retreat and kept me several days, providing a boat to send me on. Passing Liangxi, I visited Hui Mountain, and Lord Gao Jingyi, a secretary of the Ministry of Rites, and others feasted me in the Zou family garden. The licentiate Wang of Loudong and the laymen Zhang Jiufu and others welcomed me at the pass and lodged me in their home
(kept me at his house)

, respectfully asking for the essentials of the Dharma. Passing Wujiang, I met the gentlemen Zhou and Shen at the Reception Court. The layman Yan Shengsheng of Shimen awaited me at Songling and welcomed me to his home, providing vegetarian provisions to accompany me on the road.
On the full moon of the long-day month
(the fifteenth day of each lunar month)
, I reached the Jizhao Hut. On the nineteenth day I performed the cremation
(cremation by fire)

rites for Master Daguan. At that time the Master's disciples, monks and laity alike, all gathered; I first wrote a text to sacrifice to him. The day had been fixed beforehand, and there was no divergence. On the twenty-fifth I gathered the sacred bones with my own hands and deposited them at Manjushri Terrace. My disciple Fakai built the stupa accordingly, and I wrote the inscription for it, thus fulfilling the obligation of a lifetime in the Dharma gate.
And so I stayed in the mountain to see in the new year
(to pass the New Year)

, gave informal instruction to the patch-robed monks of the Chan hall, and wrote the Essentials of Investigating Chan. Lord Kai asked for instruction on the school of characteristics, and I set forth the General Explanation of Nature and Characteristics. To each who asked for instruction I gave a Dharma talk, and I wrote the Song of the Pole-Carrier. The laymen Zhu Baimin and Wang Jie'an of Wumen talked with me morning and evening, taking Dharma joy as their delight. At that time the grand scribe Qian Shouzhi of Yushan and the palace secretary Yan Tianchi sent letters inviting me; the censor Jin and the Ministry of Personnel official Yu of Wulin, and various gentry, all sent letters of welcome. Because it was the end of the year, I did not accept.

(Master Daguan: seventh appearance. The disciple Dayi, the Chan Master Xun'an, and Chan Master Wunian: each first appearance. Master Chekong: third appearance. The licentiate Xing Laici, Chen Chishi the assistant administrator of Fuliang, and the master of horse Wang: no style-names given. The Prince of Jing and Prefect Yuan: no style-names. The grand scribe Wu Guanwo, the assistant censor Wu Benru, Yu of Jinsha, and the gentlemen Wang and Sun; the He family of Qu'a: no style-names. The magistrate Wang Dongli, the Ministry of Rites secretary Gao Jingyi, and the licentiate Wang of Loudong: no style-names. The laymen Zhang Jiufu and the gentlemen Zhou and Shen of Wujiang: no style-names. Yan Shengsheng of Shimen, Master Da's disciple Fakai, the laymen of Wumen Zhu Baimin and Wang Jie'an, the grand scribe Qian Shouzhi of Yushan, the palace secretary Yan Tianchi, the censor Jin, and the Ministry of Personnel official Yu: no style-names, each first appearance. Chishi's personal name was Dashou; he rose to be minister of the imperial stud. The master of horse Wang, styled Jingfeng, was a man of Huangmei, and served as governor-general of Miyun. Prefect Yuan is Lord Yuan Jiuji, later prefect of Nankang. Guanwo's personal name was Yingbin; Benru's was Yongxian; both were of Tongcheng. Wang Dongli's personal name was Zhidao, a man of Quanzhou, who rose to be chief censor. Jingyi's name was Panlong, a man of Wuxi, who rose to be left chief censor. Baimin's name was Lu, a man of Suzhou, famous for painting bamboo. Jie'an's name was Zaigong, courtesy name Mengsu, a man of Kunshan, who became a magistrate through the licentiate examination and soon gave up office and left. Shouzhi's name was Qianyi, a man of Changshu, who rose to be the grand minister of rites. Tianchi's name was Ne, a man of Changshu. The censor Jin's name was Xuezeng, styled Xingwu. The Ministry of Personnel official Yu's name was Chunxi, styled Deyuan; both were men of Qiantang. Deyuan wrote the preface to the Eastern Journey Collection.)
Fuzheng notes: this year
(the bingchen year, the forty-fourth year of Wanli,
CE)
, the first half of the chronicle
(the first section recorded in this year's chronicle)
gives the origin of Fayun Monastery on Wuru Peak. The latter half of the chronicle
(the latter section recorded in this year's chronicle)
gives the faithful and Dharma companions of the time at Jinsha, Qu'a, Wumen, and Wulin.
It was then that Fuzheng came to take refuge in the Master, who gave him the name Fuzheng
(this is the year in which Fuzheng, the author of these annotations, took refuge in the Hanshan Master)
, and the courtesy name Liangsheng, and so completed the Origin of the Eastern Journey Collection.

In the whole chronicle, the great turning points are: first paying homage to the First Patriarch, then to the Sixth Patriarch, and here to the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs — each one following the karmic occasion of the time, verified face to face, with the flesh-body succeeding to the patriarchs. How marvelous, how great!

When the Master reached the Jizhao Hut at Shuangjing, Fuzheng was lodging at the West Lake reading in the Liaozhai studio. Because a great building had collapsed and three beams had sheltered him, giving him a second life, he hastened to Jingshan to pay his respects to Chan Master Xueqiao. In the Qianzhi Hut that had been built there, he was pressed to lead the bowing and worship of the Liang Emperor's Repentance for seven days, and at once gained ease of body and mind. He vowed to press on with diligence and did not return from the mountain, and it happened that at the Jizhao Hut he met the Master, who had come up the mountain to perform the cremation of Master Daguan, on the very day, fixed beforehand without divergence, when the mourning text sealed at Nanyue was to be opened.
Yan Shengsheng was a man of Tongxiang county who lived at Shimen. He and Fuzheng were classmates
(men who passed the provincial or metropolitan examination in the same year)
, and he was the father of Kaimei, whose personal name was Junyan
(father)
. One evening he had a dream beforehand of the monastery's guardian spirit, who commanded him to welcome Pindola
(Pindola, the first of the sixteen arhats; these sixteen great arhats received the Buddha's charge to remain forever in this world to save living beings)
. He saw one seated in the principal place in the central hall, with others seated in attendance at his side, all of them famous worthies of the time
(people of long-established reputation)

, masters of Dharma and discipline, those he had known in the past — all were there; and he woke with a start. The next day he heard that the Master was coming east, and sent a boat to welcome him at Songling, and accompanied him through Shuangjing, Yunqi, and the mountains about the lake. Wherever they went, Fuzheng attended him longest, and was given the name Fujian. Later, when the Master was returning and passed through Shimen, Shengsheng invited him to his home. There was a troupe of players, and the Master had them perform The Pavilion of Moon-Worship, and set out a great offering; only those attendants who had received the full precepts were chosen to sit at the feast, and all others were excluded. Among those seated at the time were such famous worthies as Chaosong, Yiyu, Zhihe, Wengu, Gude, Foshi, Dezong, Xinzong, and Xuanjin, and others. Shengsheng told Fuzheng of this at the feast, clear in every detail: it was the very scene and company he had seen in his dream on the day of Pindola.
The next day, on the Dharma boat, Fuzheng asked: “Does watching a play hinder the precepts?” The Master sighed and said: “
Very (in ancient usage the same as “tài”)

hard to say. Another man, if he does not break the precepts for a day, is for that day one who does not break the precepts. I do not break the precepts every day, and every day I am one who breaks the precepts.” When Fuzheng heard this, he could not help but be utterly overturned; to this day the words are still in his ears. The Essentials of Investigating Chan and the Song of the Pole-Carrier were both expounded for the assembly in the great hall of Jingshan. It is widely said that the Song of the Pole-Carrier was written for the Chan Master Xueqiao, but that is a great error. Master Xue stood out steep and lofty, and was out of tune with many of the famous Chan masters; only with the Master was he without any gap
(in ancient usage, a variant of “gap”)

. The Master wrote for him the True Eulogy of the Abbot of Xueqiao and the Six Wondrous Inscriptions of the Qianzhi Hut. On the point of leaving, he also received Master Xue's offering of an iron ruyi and wrote an inscription for it; all are in the Eastern Journey Collection, and reading them one may know the karmic occasion of their meeting. I therefore record the Song of the Pole-Carrier, to resolve the doubts of the Dharma gate.
The Song of the Pole-Carrier, with a Preface, says:

The Dharma cavern of Jingshan: ever since Dahui revived the way of Linji and the wisdom-life was continued in succession, no generation has lacked its men. Of late the Chan gate has been desolate and its echoes have long ceased. Just now a whole company of students investigating Chan have come to sit filling the mountain. There are even some who at a single thought glimpse the ground
(see their nature)

and have it appear before them, and attain great freedom. Yet alas, they sit down on that pure white ground and will not let it go, taking it for something extraordinary, unaware that it has instead become a Dharma obstruction; in the teachings it is called the obstacle of the known. Hence the ancients said: “Even if you reach the point where
(even if you attain)

‘the cold pool and the bright moon, the bell in the still night, sound without loss when struck and are not scattered when they meet the waves’ — that is still a matter on the shore of birth and death.” As it is said: it is easy to set your foot down in a thicket of thorns, but hard to turn your body under the bright moon's curtain. This is called clinging to the pole-top, or sitting still in dead water. Even that is not permitted to abide in — how much less for those who have not yet reached the glimpsing of the ground, who chance upon a lightning-flash samadhi and at once think they have attained, and play with the shadows of the consciousness-spirit? This is the common disease of all ages in investigating Chan: to be content with a little. I feared it would spread as a worldly teaching and mislead many, so when someone asked for instruction I smiled and gave him the Song of the Pole-Carrier.

[Pole-carrier] A Chan forest term. Originally it means a laborer carrying a plank on his back; because he can see only in front and not to either side, the Chan gate uses it for one whose views are one-sided and cannot penetrate the whole. Here it means those who investigate Chan and are content with a little: they reach “returning all to nothing” and think it the ultimate, mistaking the conjured city for the jewel treasure-ground. To cling to “returning all to nothing” is like carrying a plank on the back: you see one side only and do not know the whole. And so the song says:
“Alas, they sit down on the pure white ground
(they stagnate in the state of returning all to nothing)
, and will not let it go, taking it for something extraordinary, unaware that it has instead become a Dharma obstruction.” “I urge you, do not carry
(do not cling to the state of returning all to nothing)

[The conjured city] A phantom city. It comes from the parable of the conjured city in the Lotus Sutra. The parable says: the place where all living beings attain Buddhahood is the jewel treasure-ground, but the road to that treasure-ground is perilous and far. The Buddha, fearing that travelers would grow weary and turn back, conjured a city midway, so that they might rest a while, gather their strength, and then press on straight to the treasure-ground. The Buddha wished to bring all living beings to the fruit of Buddhahood, but because beings are timid and weak and cannot bear it, he first taught the small-vehicle nirvana, so that they might gain that nirvana and rest a while, and from there arouse the greater mind and advance toward the true treasure-ground of the great-vehicle nirvana (the fruit of Buddhahood). (For detailed annotation see
Annotations to the Song of the Pole-Carrier
The song says:
Pole-carrier, pole-carrier, how are you so bitterly taken in
You only want the shoulder to be light, / and never mind the stumbling at your heels.
Even if you carry it back to before your birth, / it has long since blocked half of you from view.
This plank, a cangue on your neck: / all the flesh and bone of your body belong to it.
If you do not quickly throw it off, / through a hundred thousand kalpas it is your true enemy.
Sitting, it wearies you; walking, it wearies you — / it is plainly an obstruction: why can you not see it
It is only because at the first you took the false for the true / that ghosts and goblins haunt your pure and quiet house.
Open your eyes and you see it; close your eyes and you see it: / in the bright day, lightning flashes in the empty sky.
A gandharva city's image appears in the void; / the foolish child takes it for a heavenly palace.
If you would be light, you must let it go. / A stinking dead toad — what price can it fetch?
To trade a black bean for an eye — / in a fish's eye you must tell the true from the false.
There is a road, the best of roads to walk, / broad and level as a balance-beam.
Only do not linger by the flowers and willows, / and you are sure to enter the imperial capital one year.
Give up body and life as though they were the great earth; / ox, horse, camel, donkey — you need not shun them.
If you can truly cast it over Mount Sumeru, / the sword-trees and knife-mountains are a child's game.
If you love it, you are harmed by it; / burdens pile up mostly from all the fuss and care.
One morning you shatter the crystal bottle, / and the great earth and its rivers and mountains are all ground to dust.
I urge you, do not carry it; / the sweat on a skull dries on the spot.
You divide your body and scatter your shadows into hundreds of thousands of millions; / from today you no longer enter the gate of death.

Further note: in the Master's chronicle, what he himself narrates sets down only the outline and has no leisure to write the details. What Fuzheng has set forth in these annotations likewise takes in only one part in ten of what he saw and heard, and leaves nine parts in ten aside. Thus in this year he writes “wished to be the donor for building on Mount Kuang,” and the next year again writes of “Lord Wang, who had already provided the funds to build a quiet hut, and such donors and officials” — giving only the title master of horse Wang, without his personal name or his native place. Reading it in the past, I supposed it might be the earlier master of horse Wang Boyu; but the years are far apart, and Chu
(Hubei)
and She
xī
, Anhui)

are separated by distance, which I could not understand. Recently I met the Master's Dharma kinsman, Master Rongcheng, and learned that it was Lord Jingfeng, who lived at Huangmei and held the post of governor-general. So for the other omissions among the faithful who took refuge, they are surely too many to count on the fingers.

Again, in this year, when he reached Jinzhu Ping on Mount Kuang, the four words “surveyed all its fine places” embrace how many deeds of monasteries, no one knows. For instance, at Jiujiang there is the monastery of Master Yuan of Shimen, the place where the Master settled his staff and preached for a whole month; the one he appointed as abbot there was Master Rongcheng. He had first been a stipendiary student of Xiuning, of the Cheng family by birth, personal name Keyu; he studied at Shimen together with the layman Bi Guanzhi, and at the first sight of the Master he abandoned his home, took refuge, had his head shaved, and was given the Dharma name Guangshe, and was then appointed to preside over the Shimen monastery. Later, when the Master was at Wuru, he repeatedly sent letters by hand, charging him to manage the affairs of Shimen, with earnest and detailed instruction; this was his closest Dharma heir at the time, yet the chronicle has no leisure to record it.

One day Master Rong, together with Shao Shisheng, brought various writings in the Master's own hand and came to lodge with me at the Rain-Flower Terrace; we burned incense and unrolled them to read, and so I write this to record it. Another day Master Shaoxuan, whose Dharma name was Ciyi, came from Jiangyin to visit me. He was the Dharma grandson of Master Zhiwei and the Dharma heir of Master Cimen; he had once lived at Fayun, later at the One Bowl Chan Grove in Xunyang, and had also restored the Xiujing Monastery at Hongshan in Wuchang. In the midst of the military turmoil, wherever he went he buried the bones of the dead, and twice established land-and-water Dharma assemblies. He was by birth a son of the Lu family of Jiangyin; after the dynastic change he returned to his village and is now restoring the Ten Thousand Buddhas Chan Grove. He says himself that the disciples he has saved, such as Renda and Liangming, are very many; but he never had the chance to receive the Master's own personal instruction.

Of the foremost disciples whom the Master most approved, there was none like Master Zhiwei, whose personal name was Fushan. At first he shared good and ill fortune alike, appearing six times in the chronicle of the Master's approaching cessation; at the end he hurried about and steadied the reliquary, and wrote in detail the karmic circumstances of the Master's later affairs. He was the worthy son of Wuru.

Again, there was Master Xuzhong, whose name was Guangyi: at the Baolin assembly he personally witnessed the nirvana, begged the Master to let down his foot, and transmitted his dying words, all clearly attested; he was a dharma-grandson of Caoxi.

Now Master Zhiwei's great-great-grandson Renxi, styled Mingji, studies the Dharma at Changgan; and Master Xuzhong had a disciple Ciren, styled Jianru, who was abbot of Qixia. It was these too whom Fuzheng, after the chaos, met by karmic chance while lodging in the old capital of Nanking, and who brought the chronicle and commentary to completion. Among these, the circumstances of the Master's last affairs, as heard from Kuanju, whose name was Guangyong, are especially detailed and accurate. Of the many later accounts none is trustworthy, and I dare not set them down rashly. I regret that he passed away so suddenly at Qixia and did not live to see the chronicle and commentary completed.

Kuanju was in truth the heir of Zhiwei and the grandfather of Mingji. Again, at one time, going back and forth to the Patriarch's Hall and the Bao'en Temple, there was one whom Fuzheng met when Master Su of Lingfeng was preaching: Master Huaibai, whose name was Hengdao, who had lived at Fayun for more than two years, attended our Master closely, and received the full precepts from him. And the prior of the Patriarch's Hall, Zhanchi, whose name was Xiuru, was a grandson of Great Master Xuelang and the direct heir of the revered elder brother whom our Master often remembered. All these gentlemen, together with Master Su of Lingfeng, had deep Dharma bonds; by rule they are recorded here after the Dharma lineage.

Fuzheng notes: from taking refuge in that year onward, in all matters of attending closely on our Master, he began to call him "our Master." At first he enshrined and honoured his Dharma image at the Dragon-Tree Altar of Mount Yao, and later at the Ou-xie Dwelling of the Rain-Flower Terrace, this when the monk Juelang was preaching in the Three Treasures Hall, and he specially led the assembled attendants to do reverence at the feet of the one who presided there. Now that Master Su is again preaching in the Three Treasures Hall, Fuzheng has been able to take counsel with him and bring the excellent work of the chronicle and commentary to completion; the whole origin of it is recorded here.
Master Su was of the Zhong family; in his youth he lived at Sumen and studied the Confucian classics, firmly believing in Confucius
(Confucius)
, whom he often saw in dreams. At seventeen, reading the writings of Master Lian
(Master Lianchi)

, he first awakened to the Pure Land. At twenty-two, through Master Xueling Jun's Key to the Contemplation Hymn he came into accord with our Master, went to Mount Kuang to consult him, and there, offering a stick of incense, asked about the Dharma. The verse our Master showed the layman Zhong runs: 'The West lies only in your own heart's head; when afflictions are empty, deluded thoughts are stilled. Then you shall see Amitabha's true face: he comes of old, from the sea of suffering, sailing his boat of compassion.' Two years later he relied on Master Xue, abandoned his home, and was shaved. From then until our Master's passing into cessation there were four occasions of dream-karma. Now he expounds the Tiantai school and points the way to the Pure Land, the Dharma milk that Fuzheng witnessed with his own eyes.
[Dharma milk] that which nourishes people's wisdom-life

blocks.text: 22. A Bodhisattva Comes into the World

inline.s: The forty-fifth year of Wanli
Dingji ●
I was seventy-two. On the first day of the first month of spring I expounded the precepts for the assembly. I went down from Shuangjing to mourn at Yunqi
(to mourn Master Lianchi)

; more than a thousand black-robed and white-robed disciples had long been waiting in the mountain, and I stayed twenty days. Every night I gave informal instruction and answered questions on the Dharma; each was filled with joy, and I set forth the secret practices of Master Lianchi's life. Some disciples wept to hear it, saying that I had revealed what others did not know, and they asked me to write his stupa inscription
(see
Inscription and Annotation for the Stupa of Master Lianchi
When I left the mountain, Master Xuanjin and the scholar Tan Mengxun

(Fuzheng; a later passage of this commentary says: "At that time Fuzheng was twenty-seven; together with Master Xuanjin he went up Mount Jing and invited the Master of Hunan to open the hall at Jingci")
, with the gentry and laymen of the same prefecture, invited me to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci; for days thousands of fingers were raised around me
(one man has ten fingers; a thousand fingers describes how many people there were)
as I expounded the great precepts, and I wrote the Record of the Zongjing Hall
(Record of the Zongjing Hall of Jingci Temple on West Lake)

. At that time all the famous worthies of every quarter gathered about the lake, and with the scholar Tan they asked about the Dharma, each pressing his own hard questions; it was called the greatest Dharma assembly of the southeast, such as had never been seen before.

Then I visited Lingyin, the Three Zhu, and the Western Hills, all famous places, and praised the three ponds of releasing life, and so departed. At that time the officials and laymen of the city provided boats to release living creatures and gave me a farewell feast on the lake, and moreover drew up a petition asking me to stay at Yunqi; so there was a promise of three years.

Passing Zuili, the vice-minister Yue Shifan and the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong, old acquaintances of mine, met me at the Lengyan Chan Cloister. It happened that Shen Lübo of Linxi welcomed me to his home, and in the midst of the gathering he suddenly asked where the stupa of the former Master Yungu was, saying he did not know its whereabouts. The layman told him at once: 'Near, quite near, about a li from Qizhen.' I was overjoyed, and that evening I went to the temple and did reverence at my late master's stupa. I saw that the temple was most secluded and lovely, while the stupa court was rather desolate; I was sad for a long while. Regretting that my journey was hurried and I could not set it in order, I respectfully asked Mr. Shen to repair it in my stead, and charged him to establish a long-life field to support the incense and lamps
(to provide for the costs of incense and lamps)

. Of all that I passed by on that journey, the writings I made at the time were collected by Master Xuanjin He and the scholar Tan Mengxun into four fascicles and printed under the title Eastern Journey Collection.

Returning to Wumen, the two masters Chaosong and Yiyu invited me into Mount Hua and to visit Tianchi, Xuanmu, and Iron Mountain, all famous places. At Cold Mountain the gentlemen Zhao Fanfu, Wen Wenqi, Yao Mengchang, Xu Zhongrong, and Xu Qingzhi asked about the Way at Guanyin Mountain. The two officials Feng Yuancheng and Shen Xuanzhu entertained me at their homes. As I was about to set out, my disciples Dongwen and Hanyue, the grand historian Qian, Wang Jihe, and Qu Wanchu welcomed me to Changshu, and so I came to Mount Yu and lodged two nights. The grand historian of Fushui escorted me to Qu'a, where He Zhiren and his sons and nephews waited at the Sanli Hut at Benniu and asked me to stay in their garden for the summer retreat. I firmly declined.

Returning to the mountain, the layman He Zhiren gave me the Portraits of the Eighty-Eight Patriarchs, painted by the great gentleman Ding Yunpeng, and I accepted them. He escorted me to Jingkou, where I received the vegetarian feast of the black-robed and white-robed of Three Mountains, and in the Dache Hall expounded the precepts for the assembly.

When it was done I at once set sail for Mount Kuang, and on the first day of the fifth month passed Baixia, spending a night on the river and seeing one or two old friends. On the fifth I reached Wuhu, where Liu Yushou of the works ministry was supervising the customs barrier and detained me, asking me to write A Discourse on Strange Dreams. The ministry official Cui Helou met me on the river. On the sixteenth day of the fifth month the boat reached Xingzhu, and I arrived at Guizong and lodged there. At that time Minister of War Wang had already provided the funds to build me a quiet hut, and on the fifteenth of the sixth month I ordered my disciple Fushan to begin work at Wuru; by the tenth month one room was finished, and I was able to dwell in peace.

(Master Lianchi of Yunqi, Master Xuanjin, the scholar Tan Mengxun, and the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong, a second time each. The vice-minister Yue Shifan and Shen Lübo of Linxi, once each. The monk Yungu, a third time. The two masters Chaosong and Yiyu, and Zhao Fanfu, Wen Wenqi, Yao Mengchang, Xu Zhongrong, and Xu Qingzhi of Cold Mountain, once each. Feng Yuancheng, a fourth time. Shen Xuanzhu, Dongwen, and Hanyue, the two masters, once each. The grand historian Qian Shouzhi, a second time. Wang Jihe, Qu Wanchu, the layman He Zhiren and his sons, the works official Liu Yushou, and the ministry official Cui Helou, once each. Minister of War Wang, that is the former Jingfeng, a second time. The disciple Fushan, a sixth time. Master Xuanjin was named Dahe, a disciple of Great Master Xuelang, abbot of the Zongjing Hall of Jingci, and a colleague of Fuzheng. Shifan was named Yuansheng, a man of Jiaxing, and served as junior minister of war. Fanfu was named Yiguang, famed for cursive seal script. Wenqi was named Zhenmeng, a first-place graduate who became chief minister. Mengchang was named Ximeng, an official of the palace secretariat. Qingzhi was named Rong, a secretariat drafter. Xuanzhu was named Yongmao and served as chief minister. All the above were men of the city of Suzhou. Jihe was named Yuchun, and Wanchu was named Chunren, both famous scholars of Changshu. Yushou was named Xixuan, a man of Suzhou, and served as assistant administrator.)

Fuzheng observes: in the one age of the Great Ming, the great monks of the Dharma gate who appeared together in the Wanli reign and whose fame overflowed were none other than Lianchi of Yunqi, Daguan Zibo, and Hanshan of Caoxi, the three great elders of the world at that time. He who was the flesh-body heir of the Sixth Patriarch was our Master alone. Our Master, an old veteran of seventy, made one Eastern Journey, and the two stupa inscriptions for Yunqi and Zibo stand as imperishable biographies; the sacrificial texts and likeness-praises fill many leaves with splendour, like the three great elders gathered in conversation. That Fuzheng was able to move among them with staff and sandals was a rare encounter of his life and a good cause from former lives.

In the Eastern Journey Collection that Fuzheng copied out with his own hand, the Essentials of Chan Practice was spoken in the Dharma Hall of Mount Jing, the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation in the Dharma Hall of Yunqi, and the Essentials of Holding the Cundi in the Zongjing Hall of Jingci. For going west and coming east, and for the various secret gates of mantra-holding, these three instructions leave nothing unstated.
[Holding the mantra]
Ming is another name for dharani; to hold the mantra means to receive and uphold the true words.

Master Da was our Master's first and greatest Dharma friend in life; he always regretted that he could not weep face to face for him, and the origin of the Eastern Journey lay precisely in settling this first great public case.

The karmic accord with Master Lian at Mount Wutai was forty-one years before; the karmic occasion of Master Yungu's sitting in Chan at the Tianjie Temple was fifty-two years before, at the very beginning. These other two great public cases were also settled within the half year of the Eastern Journey.

On the day he mourned at Yunqi, more than a thousand black-robed and white-robed pressed him to stay in the mountain. He did not grant their request, but had his portrait painted and left it to be honoured, in expectation of the future, asking that they write a praise themselves. The one who, hearing of Master Lian's secret practices, wept aloud was Lord Song Huaqing, a disciple of Yunqi. He lingered long at the Zongjing Hall, yet the chronicle omits his surname, for the Dharma occasions of that time were so
ta
thronged, interchangeable with "ta", meaning numerous and crowded

that its light could not be counted through every crack. And so Fuzheng reflects that in all the chronicle's course, from Bao'en in Nanking to Jingci by West Lake, the places are so many li apart and the times so many years apart. Of the black-robed and white-robed worthies who took refuge in him in a lifetime, no more than one or two in a thousand are preserved. Yet within its words there is a deep import of its own, which the clear-eyed will be able to fathom for themselves.

That which the chronicle says, that Master Xuanjin and the scholar Tan Mengxun, with the gentry and laymen of the same prefecture, invited him to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci, where for days thousands of fingers were raised around him as he expounded the great precepts, and that he visited Lingyin, the Three Zhu, and the Western Hills and all the famous places, was all a matter of a hundred days. At that time, because the Sacred Mother's gracious Master
(at that time, because Empress Dowager Li had shown favour to Patriarch Hanshan)

had been persecuted for spreading the Dharma, and after long garrison duty had returned alive, his fame was truly loud and wide. From the provincial grand coordinators and the regional commanders down to officials great and small of the prefectures and counties, and the faithful of every quarter, officials and laymen, and the elders and younger men of the three gates of Dharma, Vinaya, and Chan, all gathered at Wulin
(an old name for Hangzhou, taken from Mount Wulin)
, truly a day worth a thousand years.

At that time those who first proposed inviting him from Yunqi and then brought him to Jingci at Nanping were the Renhe magistrate Zhou Jihou, the provincial grand coordinator Jin Xingwu of this region, the ministry official Yu Deyuan, the education commissioner Ge Qizhan, the provincial graduate Wen Qixiang, the official Song Huaqing, the literatus Yan Yinchi, the literatus Zou Mengyang, and other faithful donors. The one who set in order the rules of the cloister and managed the various affairs of providing for the assembly was Master Xuanjin He. At first he put his name to the invitation, and afterwards he followed at his heels to carry out his commands, serving as guest-master and secretary and toiling with the morning lamps: for Fuzheng this was, from first to last, the one great public case of our Master's Eastern Journey through the Three Wu.

At that time, attending him day by day, there was no day when I did not tremble in awe amid dragons, gods, and ghosts. I saw that our Master, wherever he went, carried no fly-whisk or staff, and his jade countenance was fair and bright; in the heat of summer he did not sweat, and morning and evening when he washed, the water in the vessel was perfectly clear. He always sat cross-legged without troubling his hands to arrange his legs. Closing his eyes he entered samadhi, opening them he left it, at dawn and by lamplight, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. At a single request his gaze was like lightning, with not a speck in his eyes and no need to wipe them with his hand. After his ordeal his feet were slow to walk; he could not stand long, and a few paces required support, a hundred paces a carriage. There were four faithful bearers, two from Caoxi and two from Nanyue, who gave up their bodies to serve him over thousands of li, and for years did not leave him.

From the day in the tenth month of the winter of the yiwei year when our Master received the decree of garrison exile in Guangdong, he let his hair and beard grow, his long beard reaching a foot, and taught the Dharma in cap and gown for twelve years. In the eighth month of the autumn of the bingwu year, when the imperial great-grandson was born and an amnesty released him from the ranks, he had not yet been shaved. Nine years later, in the jiayin year, he left Guangdong, and in the fourth month of summer reached Hudong; hearing that the Sacred Mother had passed away, he established a bodhimanda of requiting kindness, and in obedience to the gracious edict was shaved before the spirit tablet and changed into monastic dress. Before that, in Guangdong, he had gone unshaved for fully twenty years. From his shaving to the day in the eleventh month of the winter of the bingchen year when he travelled east to Shuangjing, when Fuzheng first saw our Master's perfect form, only three years had passed since the shaving, not long at all.

When he ascended the hall and taught the Dharma, he might utter thousands of words without swallowing a single one, like a great bell sounding, heard even outside the hall. When he took up the brush to write an instruction, he did not change his usual cross-legged posture, and spread out
(paper)

for thousands of characters without his brush ever pausing. The attendants who took down his words were worn out running to and fro, and the day was not long enough for them. With his left hand he turned his prayer beads, with his right he held a white bamboo folding fan; winter and summer it never left his hand, raised but not waved, closed but not opened. When some great affair of command among humans, gods, and the three realms arose, one rap on the desk and nothing failed to respond. The bamboo clapper and the staff, the shout and the blow, could not match the working of that one fan. It could make demons retire and obey more swiftly than thunder. As for the reaches of his meditative power and spiritual penetration, Fuzheng witnessed a hundred kinds, and records here only the greatest.

At the Zongjing Hall one day, just as he had ascended the seat, two monks came supporting a third between them up the steps, raving without cease. His two fellow practitioners begged our Master to rescue him, saying: "This monk has recited the Great Compassion Mantra for five years and has never committed a bad act; we do not know why he has become possessed like this." Our Master said: "This illness can be cured." He at once ordered an attendant to inquire throughout the hall, and three who had practised the recitation of the Ucchusma Vajra Spirit Mantra were found and brought forward. Our Master then recited it himself from the seat and had the practitioners pass on the teaching. At first the transmission did not take; our Master struck the desk with his fan in a display of awe, and lifting up a single line and handing it on, the transmission answered like an echo. The practitioners then passed on every line to the end, and the raving monk awoke as from a dream, bowed in homage, and withdrew. Our Master sent him into the Fragrance-Accumulating Quarters, and he was as if nothing had happened. Among those seated that day were the provincial administration commissioner Wu Xingke of this province, the Renhe magistrate Zhou Jihou, the Chu education commissioner Ge
tu
ji
Qizhan and his colleague Yin Liang, who had never been deeply convinced; by now their countenances changed, and the great assembly was of one voice
(unanimously praising)

Another day a monk came to bow in homage. Before he had risen, our Master struck with his fan and shouted: "Murdering thief, what do you want with me?" The manager of affairs hurried him out. The monk went off without a word, and the assembly stared in astonishment, not understanding. The next day it was heard that he had been arrested for theft. Penetrations of this kind could not be counted.
Flying staff
(travelling about from place to place)

for two months: every day some donor would provide a hundred taels of gold to feast the assembly at Jingci, in a great cauldron boiling ten piculs of rice. Whether he stayed or travelled, there was no day when the fire was not lit. On the day he reached Jiaxing, the assembly welcomed him into the Chan Hall of the Jinming Temple. Our Master ordered Fuzheng to inquire of his old associates, and the two lords the minister of war Yue Shifan and the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong both came to pay their respects. When Chudong was serving his commission in Kuangzhou, he had lingered long and warmly with our Master, providing medicines and care, and had settled a certain demon affair that troubled the judicial officer for a time; our Master was deeply grateful to him. Of their exchanges at that time, the Dharma words and handwritten notes were the most numerous. Shifan, wont to turn the joy of Chan into playful talk, had been in the ministry of rites when our Master was persecuted for spreading the Dharma, and spoke out boldly to save him. Now they met and were greatly delighted. They had scarcely sat down and exchanged greetings when Yue asked: "Just now I am puzzled by the four lines on 'according to one's station'
(When in wealth and honour, act as befits wealth and honour; when in poverty and low station, act as befits poverty and low station)

how does the Great Master explain them?" Our Master answered: "Plainness is a blank sheet of paper: paint a gauze cap on it and it becomes a gauze cap; paint a beggar on it and it becomes a beggar." For in the Ming dynasty officials were called gauze caps. They laughed heartily, and after a while took their leave.

At that time, when the meal was over and candles were set out for tea and informal instruction, the hall door was already closed. Suddenly there was a man carrying a staff who shouted outside the door. Someone recognized him as a runner of the grain office named Qian, and took him for a drunken madman, but driving him off did not work; his voice grew shriller, and mixed with Buddha-words he cried: "Today the living bodhisattva has come down; I ought to be delivered. Do not block the way." Fuzheng thought his words strange and reported them to our Master. Our Master said: "Call him in." He entered with palms joined in homage, possessing the dignity of a son of the Buddha, and all marvelled at him. He knelt with both knees on the ground and made the prostration of a son of the Buddha.
The ghost spoke through him, saying: "I am the one possessed by Qian the Elder; my name is Zhong Yueren
(also written Yueren)

, and I have borrowed this body to seek deliverance. In life your disciple kept a long fast and practised the Pure Land for eight years; now I have died and the fifth seventh-day is at hand. Not going to the underworld, I should be born in the Western Heaven, and I beg the bodhisattva in his compassion to guide me." He lay prostrate, tears falling, weeping without cease. Our Master summoned six elders of the assembly
(senior, long-practising, and greatly revered)

who specialized in Buddha-recitation to stand in attendance, and himself unfolded the prayer beads. He gave the man a string of beads and had him recite the Buddha's name a thousand times, and through the possessed body he could recite it. The whole hall was solemn and silent. When the recitation was done, our Master accordingly expounded the Mengshan Text for Feeding the Hungry Ghosts, and when he came to "one should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: all is made by mind alone," he raised his fan, struck the desk, and cried aloud: "Be swiftly delivered!" The man answered at once: "Delivered indeed!" Three calls and three answers, quicker than echo or shadow. He rose, made the prostration of a son of the Buddha, and gave thanks for rebirth in the Pure Land. Facing east and west he bowed to the great assembly, saying: "Let each of you strive; we shall meet again at the Dragon-Flower Assembly." By then it was past the first watch, and the assembly had not dispersed; some wept, some sighed, some even laughed secretly, and some
slandered (
zi

through it all. As a rule he would always mount his carriage and return to the boat; the man followed the carriage as far as the cliff, bowed in homage and gave thanks, and then returned to the gate of the Chan Hall, saying, "Thank you, Elder Qian; through you I have gained deliverance," and fell to the ground and woke, once more the runner Qian as before. The bystanders then said: "Yueren was the father of the scholar Zhong Xiangshi
(another name for a provincial graduate)
(another name for a provincial graduate)

, whose name was Wenshao; in life he practised the Pure Land with great devotion, and such a response was fitting." Fuzheng answered: "That was my friend of the Wall-Scripture Society, Zhong Shengfu." He went at once with several faithful men to knock at the door and drew him over to the Dharma Boat to give thanks. Then they knew that on that very day the dead man's fifth seventh-day mourning period had fallen, and Qian the runner, coming to press for grain-tax, had entered before the spirit seat, and in his drunkenness had drawn the soul to deliverance. Later, in the xinyou examination, Shengfu passed the provincial examination
(became a provincial graduate)

That day a relative and friend, the layman Xu Taiwei, who had long believed in the Buddha, saw our Master's spiritual power and invited him to his home to set up a spirit seat for his father Lord Xianfu and beg him to speak the Dharma. Every word our Master spoke revealed his father's secret deeds
(things that could not be told to others)
, and all who heard were awed into submission.

Within a day or two the word of the living bodhisattva spread, and the sound of recitation ran through the streets; the elders, children, and women of the prefecture city craned their necks as if mad. Fuzheng attended our Master to Qizhen to do reverence at the stupa of Master Yungu, and returning prepared carriage, canopy, and full ceremonial to go to the Eastern Stupa, so that the crowds who thirsted to see him might have one chance to bow. Presently black-robed and white-robed swarmed together, from the mountain gate to the abbot's quarters shoulder to shoulder and heel to heel; for a time the long causeway and broad terrace had nowhere to set a foot. So he took counsel with Mr. Yue Shifan to lead the way for our Master, and they climbed the steps to the stupa and fastened the stupa door. Our Master's body was massive, and they could only support him to the southern railing of the second storey; the four assemblies looked up, bowed in homage in rows, rising and falling to the ground like rising mist and cloud, and only dispersed at nightfall. Lamps were lit as he entered the abbot's quarters, and ascending the seat he spoke the Dharma; after a few brief words the meal was served. When the meal was done he at once boarded the boat, and those who came bearing incense, cloth, fruit, and cakes to present them pressed the boat down with their weight. The master of the Eastern Stupa hall at that time was Master Jingxiu. The next day the Lengyan Cloister invited him to a meal, and the master of that hall was Master Maolin. He examined the scripture workshop and inquired into its regulations in full, and especially charged Fuzheng with the matter of printing the canon, talking on without wearying. That day the men and women of the city who came to share in the joy also surged in crowds. Yet another day passed, and the boat crossed Songling.

The chronicle also says: "The famous worthies of every quarter all gathered about the lake, and with the scholar Tan asked about the Dharma; the splendour of that southeast Dharma assembly had never been seen before." It also says: "Of whatever writings he made at the time along the way, Master Xuanjin He and the scholar Tan Mengxun collected four fascicles and printed them under the title Eastern Journey Collection." This was because our Master, at the nirvana assembly, let down his foot as a sign and gave his charge earnestly, singling out the one word "with", attributing the surpassing cause of the Eastern Journey directly to Fuzheng himself; nowhere in the whole chronicle is there a comparable stroke of approval. In his youth Fuzheng, at the bidding of the late assistant equerry Lord Fantong, was given the courtesy name Mengxun. Afterwards, when his own body lay beneath the collapsed hall and he was saved by the shelter of three beams, it happened that in that very year he met our Master, who gave him the Dharma name Liangsheng. Later he styled himself Sao'an, and people no longer knew him as Mengxun. The verse our Master showed Liangsheng runs: 'The roof-beam fell and crushed the scholar Tan; being crushed, why did the scholar not die? If the beam had reached the body, the body would be shattered; if the body had reached the beam, the beam would not avoid it. Both have reached, why do they not touch? Ask yourself the reason they do not touch. The illusions before you are not to be compared to a beam; why should the scholar Tan first panic so? If you would not panic, watch a dog driven to leap the wall.' This was the instruction given at their first meeting. Afterwards there were earnest Dharma words given him on holding the Cundi and on the awl-piercing, all recorded in the Eastern Journey Collection.

And so he recalls those days: from Shuangjing to Yunqi, invited to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci and to open the hall, then journeying about the lake, Lingyin, Tianzhu, and the various mountains, and to Zuili, Jinming, and the Eastern Stupa, where the light shone greatly; then crossing Songling and Wumen, straight to the Eastern Chan Temple at Jinsha, where he did reverence at his feet and took leave. From spring through summer he attended him with the morning lamps, with no idle day. As the boat was about to be loosed, our Master stroked Fuzheng's back with his hand and said with a smile: "The affairs after my death I entrust to you." This was a matter of his twenty-seventh year. Fuzheng's feeling for our Master was no less than an infant's craving for the breast; our Master's care for Fuzheng was no different from a tender mother's rearing of her child. At that time Fuzheng's father was at court and his mother in attendance, and our Master, seeing the first signs early, foretold to him the unfinished karmic causes of standing in the world and entering society, and firmly stopped him from following him to Wuru; yet in his gazing and leaning, in dream and sleep, he never forgot him for a moment. From that parting to now his years have reached sixty-two; he is old. All along since receiving the prediction he has held the Cundi, four twelve-year cycles as one day. He sent offerings to Fayun, and the letters that went back and forth fill his boxes. At the Stone Lamp bodhimanda in the capital of Yan he mourned in silence and longing. Only now, face to face with the Dharma image, does he expound the chronicle in commentary, drawing out the instructions of former days and the records he was shown, in hope of settling one day the public case of entering the canon and requesting a posthumous title; and only now does he know that the words of the charge about affairs after death belonged to this very day. Alas, our Master loved Fuzheng as though there were no second in his eyes at the time; and Fuzheng's service of our Master has perhaps answered to him in some small part.

blocks.text: 23. Pointing the Way to the Pure Land

inline.s: The forty-sixth year of Wanli
Wuwu ●
I was seventy-three. The laymen of Wuxia contributed funds to build me the Yilao Hut. That year I began to build the Buddha Hall and the Chan hall at Wuru
(Wuru Temple)

. In the third month Lord Chen Chishi, assistant administrator of Fuliang, came into the mountain, and with Lord Bao Zhongsu, ministry official of Xin'an, and Lord Xia Woqi, ministry official of Xingzi, formed a society of ten friends to help with the cost of building; by the long-day month the halls were complete.

(Chen Chishi, a second time. The ministry official Bao Zhongsu and the ministry official Xia Woqi, once each. Zhongsu was named Ying'ao, a man of Huizhou, and served as chief of the court of imperial sacrifices.)

[Wuru Temple] It stands below Wuru Peak on the southern side of Mount Kuang and is also called the Wuru Cloister; it was first built in the Song dynasty. When Great Master Hanshan came here from Caoxi he took a liking to its mountains and waters and enlarged and rebuilt it. After the rebuilding its fame rose sharply, its incense flourished for a time, and pilgrims and visitors came in an unending stream. In the temple are kept portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs of Buddhism, the masterpiece of the Xin'an painter Ding Yunpeng, with a record written by the poet Tan Yuanchun of the Jingling school.

In the fourth month of summer of the dingsi year, when Fuzheng took leave of our Master, he was charged to collect funds to make an image of the three holy ones of the West. For Amitabha, Guanyin, and Mahasthamaprapta are the lords of the six-period Buddha-recitation bodhimanda, in imitation of Master Yuan's Lotus Society. This image is rare among the world's temples, and it happened that a master craftsman of Jiangxi had inherited the art, and the sandalwood carving was exquisite and uncommon. It also happened that a single coiled root of a natural seat was obtained, on which the three holy ones were seated in a row; and again that five ancient bronze censers, vases, candlesticks, and offering vessels were found. In that spring it was completed, and the attendant Master Xuzhong Yi, as the Buddha Hall was about to be finished, came to welcome it, and Fuzheng that same day bought a boat and sent it. At the first sight of it our Master was joyful and praised it, and to this day it is honoured and complete. The halls built at Wuru stand in the prefecture of Jiujiang, county of Dehua, on the shady side of Mount Kuang; at first it was called the Wood-and-Stone Hut, and now it is called the Fayun Temple. The abbot, Master Zhizheng, has passed away; it now belongs to Master Ciyan, styled Runhong.
The forty-seventh year of Wanli
Jiwei ●

I was seventy-four. In the first month of spring I began a long term of reciting the Avatamsaka Sutra and expounded the General Exposition on the Lotus Sutra for the assembly. In summer I expounded the Surangama, the Awakening of Faith, the Diamond, the Perfect Enlightenment, and the Consciousness-Only, the sutras and treatises. In the seventh month of autumn I charged Lord Yuan, prefect of Nankang, to write a record, making Wuru a permanent endowment for the support of the aged of the ten directions. On the fifteenth of the eighth month I shut myself in retreat and cut off all ties, imitating Master Yuan, burning incense at the six periods in place of the water-clock, and gave my mind wholly to the pure work. I often reflected that the Avatamsaka school was about to lose its transmission: men feared that Qingliang's subcommentary was too vast and their minds could not reach it, so most in the world set it aside and relied only on the Combined Treatise
(the Combined Treatise on the Avatamsaka Sutra).
And so I reflected that Qingliang
(National Master Qingliang)

was the ancestor of composition in this land; if he were abandoned, the school would lose its lineage. I resolved to take only the subcommentary text and set forth its great purport with the brush, so that readers might easily understand it, entitling it the Essentials
(the Essentials of the Avatamsaka)
; and in the retreat I began to read, revise, and cut it
(to revise a text)
(Lord Yuan is the former Prefect Yuan; Lord Yuan Jiuji, a second time.)

Fuzheng observes: in the chronicle the Qingliang public case appears five times, and in the end it is closed with the Essentials of the Avatamsaka. Three years later, in the renxu year, the draft was done, and the karmic occasion of Qingliang was accomplished, and the karmic occasion of Caoxi likewise. Can it be that our Master was Qingliang come again?
