Moreover, at that very time our Master took the burning of incense in place of the water-clock and made the pure work his whole aim, and yet he could again revise the subcommentary of Qingliang and the whole Avatamsaka school into the Essentials and hand it down to later men: this is what is called the Pure Land as mind-only, the ten thousand dharmas returning to one.
The forty-eighth year of Wanli
Gengshen, the change of reign-title to Taichang
(the Tianqi Emperor succeeded to the throne, with the reign-title Tianqi, in the year
I was seventy-five. In spring, outside my lessons, the attendant Guangyi asked me to set forth the Perfect Enlightenment and the Awakening of Faith in direct explanation
(the Direct Explanation of the Perfect Enlightenment and the Direct Explanation of the Awakening of Faith)

, and to annotate the seven inner chapters of Zhuangzi. In summer I was ill with a foot ailment. In the eighth month of autumn Lord Chen Wuyi, ministry official of Macheng, Lord Xu Mingheng, ministry official of Anyi, Lord Wu Xunshang, ministry official of Xingzi, Lord Lu Jingye, prefect of Jiangzhou, Lord Yuan Jiuji, prefect of Nankang, and Lord Li Zhongda, the judicial officer, came into the mountain to ask about the Way. The former circuit intendant of Hunan, Lord Wu, now transferred to the Guangdong judgeship, entered Caoxi to do reverence to the Patriarch and asked the disciples in the mountain to send him biographies and praises of the Patriarchs. In my illness I compiled more than seventy short biographies, each with a praise attached, and wrote them out with my own hand.

It was already eight years since I had left Caoxi for Nanyue and dwelt at Mount Kuang. The monks of Caoxi longed deeply for my return and sent inquiries again and again, wishing to invite me but unable to. It happened that Lord Wu, going to his post, came into the mountain by the way and saw the work of my restoration, and sighed over it a long while. The monks then told him the whole matter, how they longed for my return and could not obtain it. Lord Wu gladly became their protector of the Dharma and at once sent letters to invite me. The whole assembly of the mountain, with the gentry, elders, and scholars of the province, jointly drew up a petition and came to Mount Kuang to beg me with tears. The Guangdong disciple the censor Wang Xingdong came into the mountain in person three times to invite me, but I firmly declined on account of illness.

(Guangyi, a second time. Chen Wuyi, ministry official of Macheng, Xu Mingheng, ministry official of Anyi, Wu Xunshang, ministry official of Xingzi, Lu Jingye, prefect of Jiangzhou, Li Zhongda, judicial officer of Nankang, and Wang Xingdong, censor of Guangdong, once each. Yuan Jiuji, that is Lord Yuan, and Lord Wu, that is Wu Shengbai Zhongwei, a second time each. Jingye was named Menglong, a man of Shanyin in Zhejiang, chief examiner of Guangdong, and served as assistant administrator of Guizhou. Zhongda was named Yingsheng, a man of Jiangyin, an official censor, who was arrested and died in the time of the eunuch Wei.)

Fuzheng observes: in the chronicle the first entry is that in the eighth month of autumn of the tenth year of Wanli, the renwu year, the crown prince was born; the second entry, that in the eighth month of autumn of the thirty-fourth year the imperial eldest grandson was born; the third entry, the forty-eighth year, gengshen, which is the change of reign-title to Taichang. For on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month of that year the Shenzong Emperor died and Taichang ascended, and an edict decreed that the next year should be the first year of Taichang. On the third day of the ninth month of that year the Guangzong Emperor in turn died, and on the sixth day Tianqi ascended. The supervising official Li Ruogui and the investigating censor Zuo Guangdou petitioned that from the first day of the eighth month to the end of the twelfth month the reign-title Wanli be dropped and the days be styled the first year of Taichang, borrowed from the late emperor; in the end it was not approved. This too failed in the meaning of a proper beginning and a proper ending, and came of a moment's groundless expedient, closing the matter in haste. To borrow from the late emperor and so diminish the calendar years, which is unfilial toward the one who died later, is worse than to borrow from the later emperor and so make plain the first year of sacrifice, which is filial toward the newly ascended. Moreover, to take the first year of Tianqi as the first year of Taichang is precisely to believe that the edict of Taichang's accession was no borrowing. The second year of Tianqi was in truth the first year of Tianqi. Now the first year of Taichang can only be appended in a side-note under the forty-eighth year of Wanli. Our Master feared that this change of reign-title would be buried, and therefore writes it large and twice under the forty-eighth year, gengshen: "the change of reign-title to Taichang." These five characters are the greatest instance of the brush-method and heart-method of the Spring and Autumn; how could they have been met with in the chronicles of former Patriarchs? The prayer for an heir at Mount Wutai, the protection of the heir at the Cishou Temple, and even the interrogation at the Zhenfu Office and the garrison service beyond the Dayu Ridge, what Chancellor Zhang Hongyang called his great hidden service to the altars of state, all come to one great conclusion in these five characters.
[The first year of Taichang]
On the twenty-first day of the seventh month of the forty-eighth year of Wanli (
), the Emperor (the Shenzong Emperor of Ming) passed away; on the first day of the eighth month (
), Zhu Changluo ascended the throne with the reign-title Taichang. The Taichang Emperor reigned only one month, and on the first day of the ninth month (
) he passed away, known to history as "the one-month Son of Heaven." Because the year was then reckoned as the forty-eighth year of Wanli, the forty-eighth year of Wanli (
to
was fixed as the forty-eighth year, and from
to the end of that year was fixed as the first year of Taichang; thus the Wanli reign-title still stands at forty-eight years, while the Taichang reign-title covers only five months.

In the intervals of the incense-clock and Buddha-recitation at Wuru, to expound, annotate, and compose, preaching ardently without an empty day, how could that be within the power of an old man of seventy-five, and ill at that? The work of Wuru was unfinished and the work of Caoxi revived: this is what is called "Heaven's movement is strong; the gentleman strengthens himself without cease."

My friend Wang Jiyan, whose name was Qilong, wrote A Debate on the First Year of Taichang and Doubts Raised, examining back and forth in detail the regulations of reign-changes in ancient and modern times, some two thousand characters with all his strength, and truly he first spoke my own mind. His main point is that a change of reign-title after the year has passed is the constant rule for all ages, and that changing it with the month is the error of a moment, two phrases cover it. He also says that if a year can be divided into two sections, then since Wanli, Taichang, and Tianqi all fall within one year, why can it not be divided into three? That is a forced and disjointed argument, making the Guangzong temple a mere wart. These words open the eyes and pierce the heart still more; my poor view had not reached so far. Moreover, the Guangzong Emperor's sagely virtue was lofty and generous, and he was a lord not to be produced in a generation: in the month of his accession the Yellow River at Lingong in Shaanxi ran clear for three days. He early stopped the mining taxes by decree, recalled all the tax eunuchs, and sent out treasury gold to reward the frontier to the amount of a million; he summoned back the outspoken officials who had offered advice, as though he had no leisure even to eat, and this is only what the new government accomplished. As for his nurturing of virtue in the Eastern Palace, his benevolence and filial piety were exhaustively devoted, when within there were the forms of flourishing and withering and without the provocations of partisans; to stand in such a place was truly hard. When the Shenzong Emperor was about to die he decreed that the Honoured Consort Zheng be made empress and charged him to carry it out; the court officials disputed it, yet in the end he could not bear to take it from her. These forty days of filial thought and benevolent grace reached to three reigns, the way of Heaven may still be asked about. So, because in the Patriarch Hanshan's chronicle there stand the five characters "the change of reign-title to Taichang," Fuzheng was moved and noted it.
In that year there was a letter showing Fuzheng his intention of going to Caoxi, and he wrote beforehand an inscription for the layman Tan, provincial graduate.
The first year of Tianqi
Xinyou ●

I was seventy-six. In summer, at the request of the assembly, I expounded the Surangama Notes. In the tenth month of winter my disciples, the provincial graduates Liu Qixiang, Chen Dixiang, Chen Dichun, and Liang Sixiang, came to inquire after me. At that time the former observer of Shaoyang, Lord Zhu, now transferred to the Guangdong sea circuit, together with Lord Wu, sent letters and came again to Mount Kuang, and I again declined on account of illness.
(Liu Qixiang, Chen Dixiang, Chen Dichun, and Liang Sixiang, once each. Lord Zhu, the former Xingcun, a second time; Lord Wu, the former Shengbai, a third time.)

Fuzheng notes: Lord Zhu Xingcun and Lord Wu Shengbai, two elders of his own district and both men of Yanguan, were in the end able to bring about the gathering of the flesh-bodies of the Sixth Patriarch and the Patriarch Hanshan, so great a karmic occasion. In this year, though he had not yet returned to Caoxi, the first signs of return had already stirred and the momentum of return was decided. Had he not returned to Caoxi again, then even though his flesh-body came forth from Wuru, without coming face to face with Patriarch Lu there would have been no great marvel.
The above closes the public case of the Fayun Temple at Wuru on Mount Kuang.
The second year of Tianqi
Renxu ●

I was seventy-seven. I pressed on with the Essentials of the Avatamsaka, and the draft was done. The assembly asked me to expound the Surangama, the Perfect Enlightenment, the Diamond, the Awakening of Faith, and the Zhao Lun, and the various sutras and treatises. When Lord Wu returned from his audience at court
(chao jin: going to the capital to have audience with the emperor)

he sent letters again, his meaning the more urgent; and Lord Zhang Sanxing, prefect of Shaoyang, sent a special letter and dispatched the hall master Ben'ang to me. My feelings left me no choice, and I resolved that I must go. On the tenth day of the eleventh month of that year at the winter solstice
(the eleventh month of the lunar calendar)

I left Mount Kuang and crossed Lake Peng, and wrote poems. Before long Lord Zou Nangao, the chief of the academy, returning north, sought me in the mountain. By then I had reached Jizhou, and met the grand historian Xiao Zhuoxiu, Ma Jifang, Zeng Yaochen, Liu Shaoye, He Keshang, and Liu Zhuanhua, who asked about the Way at the Ziyan Mountain House. On the eighth day of the twelfth month
(the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month)
I crossed the ridge, and on the fifteenth
(the fifteenth day of each lunar month; here the fifteenth of the twelfth month)
entered Caoxi.

(Lord Wu Shengbai, a fourth time. Lord Zhang Sanxing, prefect of Shaoyang, and the hall master Ben'ang, once each. Lord Zou Nangao, chief of the academy, a second time. The grand historian Xiao Zhuoxiu, Ma Jifang, Zeng Yaochen, Liu Shaoye, He Keshang, and Liu Zhuanhua, once each. Sanxing was named Yizhen, a man of Huating in Songjiang, who rose from prefect of Shaozhou to assistant commissioner of Guangxi. Zhuoxiu was named Yunju, styled Xuanpu, registered in Xuanhua of Guangxi, a man of Taihe in Jiangxi, and served as junior minister.)

Fuzheng observes: Lord Nangao and those after him were all men of Jiangxi of firm principle and of the Dharma, noted in the last leaves; they were chosen out of many and only a few taken, and in the end he never gave his approval to any one of them. Confucius at seventy-two, in the tenth month of winter, composed the Spring and Autumn, laying down his brush at the capture of the qilin in the western hunt; the next year, at seventy-three, he dreamed of the offerings and sang his last song. The Patriarch Hanshan at seventy-seven, on the fifteenth of the twelfth month, composed the chronicle, laying down his brush at the crossing of the ridge and his entry into Caoxi; the next year, at seventy-eight, his flesh-body passed into cessation. The sage before and the sage after fit like the two halves of a tally, how should one speak of Confucian and Buddhist appearances? still more marvellous: our Master, during his former stay in Guangdong, twenty-one years from first to last, was never shaved. Only when he came to Chu did he assume the perfect form and return to the monastic dress. Had he not returned again to Caoxi, then the black-robed and white-robed of Guangdong would never in their lives have seen our Master's perfect form in monastic dress. Yet whether with hair or without, in monastic or Confucian dress, wherein the sages differ and agree does not lie here at all.

Fuzheng was able to see the works of our Master: the Surangama Notes, the Essentials of the Avatamsaka, the Beating the Beat on the Lotus, the Hanging Mirror on the Surangama, the General Exposition on the Surangama, the General Exposition on the Lotus, the Explanation of the Awakening of Faith, the Explanation of the Consciousness-Only Treatise, the Direct Explanation of the Perfect Enlightenment, the Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, the Explanation of the Classic of the Dao and its Virtue, the Explanation of the Seven Inner Chapters of Zhuangzi, the Hanshan Preface, the Direct Pointing at the Doctrine of the Mean, the Doubts Resolved on the Great Learning, the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Palm-Guide to the Qimen, the Dream-Wandering Collection, and the Gazetteer of Caoxi. Those that Fuzheng copied out with his own hand and sent to the block were the Eastern Journey Collection; and printed, the Doubts Resolved on the Diamond. His writings are many more. As he said face to face, there are the Treatise on the Three Teachings, the General Explanation of the Analects, and the Palm-Guide to the Qimen. And as Jianru said, there are the Complete Recorded Sayings in a certain number of fascicles, which after our Master's passing were stolen and sold elsewhere by the attendant Xinqi and cannot now be seen; these are not recorded in full. What the wisdom-life of the Buddha and the Patriarchs rests upon is the Surangama Notes first and the Essentials of the Avatamsaka last. The school does not depart from the teaching, the Patriarch does not depart from the Buddha: in these it is most manifest and notable. Our Master often said of himself that whatever came from his brush or tongue was always gathered in spirit and entered into contemplation, realizing accord with the Buddha's mind; if it smacked ever so little of thought and deliberation, it was of no use. And this Essentials of the Avatamsaka, whose draft was completed, belongs to the year before his passing into cessation at seventy-seven, standing in place of Sakyamuni's last holding up of the flower between the twin trees. His power of samadhi and his spiritual light, vigorous and unceasing
the Qian Hexagram of the Book of Changes: "Heaven's movement is strong; the gentleman strengthens himself without cease."
, are fully present in the palm-leaf books of the Mahayana: how could thought and deliberation reach so far?
In that year began the karmic occasion of his return to Caoxi, leaving unfinished the public case of the Hanshan temple and the flesh-body succession to the Patriarch.
Here ends the Commentary on the Veritable Record of the Old Man of Hanshan's Own Chronicle.
Appendix: Thirty-Six Praises of the Ancient Buddha in the Flesh Who Restored Caoxi, the Patriarch-Successor Hanshan (with Preface and Titles)

I sigh in secret that the mani jewel is priceless, and that one seldom meets a merchant who can tell it. The poor son loses his treasure only because he has long been lost on the road home. That is why students of the Way are as many as the hairs of a cow, while those who awaken the mind are as rare as the horns of a qilin. I was born out of season, to meet the autumn of change and vicissitude; how fortunate am I in body to see the day when the ancient Buddha appears. This udumbara flower of Caoxi bloomed once three thousand years ago; the cause and fruit of the flesh-body meet again after five hundred lives. Dwelling where he should not dwell, he dwells in this body, and the ten thousand things are complete in me. Attaining where there is nothing to attain, he attains his place; and turning back upon himself and becoming sincere, there is no greater joy. Great Master Yongjia has said, "The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfected within the essence; the eight liberations and six penetrations are the seal of the mind-ground." Now the flesh-body bodhisattva, Great Master Hanshan, with just this mind-seal, seals all once and for all, and there is no other dharma. One gate steps beyond samadhi and dhyana, one gate enters straight into the wondrous adorned path. No need of clay or wood, of red or blue pigment: the Dharma-body fills the void. Why need of golden terraces and silver pavilions, when his image shines through the Dharma realm? Yet ignorant worldlings still complain that he went about in cangue and chains, driving his stake and pulling his oar. So, reading his chronicle, I set out its titles and made these thirty-six praises, in compliance with the request of Tan, the director of education, of Sao'an.
(A White-Robed Rebirth) ●

Not in the middle, nor within, nor yet without, he leaves the world more thirsting and more devout. The soiled robe, how could he bear to cast it down? I fear that beings will scarcely grasp it, one and all.
(The Knot of Doubt over Birth and Death) ●

Ere he had found the road to serve the King of Emptiness, he already knew to drill for light within the smoke. He burned up the three thousand great thousand worlds, and sought life within death, a rare device.
(Requiting Kindness and Winning Deliverance) ●

Old Lu, who handed on the robe, was then no monk; he smiled at old Cai who trudged the dusty road. To give this body and mind to dust-lands beyond all count, this, and this alone, is requiting the Buddha's grace.
(The Vow to Restore the Tradition) ●
He left home meaning to save every living thing; why then bring woe on all the temple's monks? He saved a crowd of idle fellows, and the jewelled hall of adornment stands within himself.
(Going to the Capital to Seek a Teacher) ●
Yongjia's word was uttered all amiss; to seek a teacher and ask the Way is the practice of Chan. Had he not braved the startling wave, no fish or dragon would have leapt aboard.
(Meeting the Master in Willow Lane) ●

The dragon-pearl was picked up, bright and at home; would he let it fall into another's pit a thousand fathoms deep? Broad as the land of Han may be, there is no other road; for a time he walks on with the children at his feet.
(Meeting a Friend at the Capital Gate) ●

Through you the mind-seal knows the face of old; like answers like with not a shred of guile. The frontier goose rose not because men startled it; the wind struck the reed-mist and filled the blue sky.
(Lying in the Snow at Mount Tai) ●

About to test the lotus in the red furnace's fire, fine gold refined a hundred times shines the brighter. With a ball of snow gripped in his hand he struck as was fitting, and first knew that cool clarity surpasses talk of Chan.
(Hiding Together in the Western Hills) ●

The Tathagatas of three ages declare with one voice, and only then one knows how many kalpas we have lain fast asleep. I hide nothing from you, and everything is just as it is; the osmanthus scent fills the air, and I regret that you say too much.
(Capital for Dwelling in the Mountains) ●

A poor man dwelling in the mountains with not a single string of cash calls out to the blue sky, bitter beyond bitter. The eighty thousand Dharma-gates enter from here, much like a merchant who has at last gained his capital.
(Reverencing the Patriarch at Shaolin) ●
The blue-eyed monk of the West came into the land of Han; why for nine years could he not open his mouth? Today I have caught this rank-smelling bearded fellow, and squeeze my fist against his cheek.
(Never Meeting Great Qian) ●

I have heard it said there is a Great Qian at Mount Song, and to this day the Chan of Shaolin has not been cut off. Had I known beforehand not to go to Mount Song, I would have feared to mislead beings as they lick at wild drool.
(Joyfully Meeting Faguang) ●
Faguang took up his staff and chased the hare; he whirled about and threw it back to strike the toad. The dead snake, not cut down, was let go its way, and the Chan school's device is boasted abroad.
(Listening to the Water at Dragon Gate) ●

He did not walk where the people of the day walk; instead he came to the bridge and listened to the sound of the stream. Suddenly he cut through the road of that sound: his ears heard nothing, and his eyes too were blind.
(Rising from Samadhi to Dust on the Cauldron) ●

How often the flowers bloomed and shadows climbed the wall, while on the crystal hall all tidings ceased. The axe-helve rotted, and he knew not the years; the gibbons cried all night, and never once did it stop.
(Protecting Mount Tai) ●
The breadth of Mount Tai, who could measure it, with a million piculs of grain from the emperor every year? How was this matter ever explained? At one glimpse of Lord Hu there was no more harm.
(Exchange with the Sages) ●

If you do not know the man, look at his friends: Manjusri and Maitreya air the family's shame. To dream and wake, to wake and dream, are all the same; if I had seen it, I would have hurried to beat the dog.
(The Birth of the Imperial Heir) ●

Pointing to heaven and earth when the Buddha was first born; among the five ranks of lord and minister he is the honoured one. The Ming prince is like a Buddha, and the mani pearl appears, fixing all the heavens and the earth.
(Dwelling Apart on Mount Lao) ●

A frontier monk by the sea has naught to tell; three meals a day, and when he is full he rests. Otherwise he would fail his lord the emperor, though east and west, south and north, were never set apart.
(Mother and Son Talking of the Profound) ●

He leaned on his staff and journeyed home once more; before he lifted a foot his mother met his eyes. Long years had not hidden the face his mother bore; with hoes in hand, mother and son laughed a while.
(The Requiting-Kindness Cause Cut Short) ●

The cause begun from the first could have raised up blessing; for ten years he cut his meals to thank the emperor's grace. Just as it neared fulfilment the Japanese came to the Korean land; that good things meet many demons has been heard since olden times.
(Harsh Interrogation at the Zhenfu Office) ●

How many times, at the brink of death, he won rebirth again; his compassion and filial piety need not fear the annals' brush. In the end the imperial heart awakened from this, and as at the first mother and son owed it to a true monk.
(Graciously Exiled to Leizhou) ●

The imperial grace was vast, the sentence lightly given; sent into exile at Leizhou, he walked with staff in hand. At the tip of one finger there is no second thing: all heaven and the whole earth are sheer light.
(As a Criminal, Audience at the Military Gate) ●

The governor's stern majesty had long been known; all the more, in cangue and chains, to face the military gate. Who would have thought that at the meeting he would be called a qilin and phoenix, and that from today the southern ridge would begin to honour monks?
(Dredging the Source at Caoxi) ●

Why was the Patriarch's seat so utterly desolate? The source had not been dredged, and all was toil in vain. Striking the crooked straight until it joined the blue of heaven, he forgot disgrace and glory, and saw the nature firm.
(Every Ruined Work Raised Up) ●

Conditioned effort never reaches the place of true emptiness; in the end it is the black hound that chases clods of earth. Snake-crawl and rat-dart have naught to do with it; the lightning rolls and the wind gallops, and still it is not swift.
(A Karmically Blinded Monk's Opposition) ●

In Jambudvipa, alas, for how many years has he been dragged along in the murk of morning and evening? How could he escape the staining of dust and grime? He hurries to gather up this old woman's Chan.
(Pardoned and Restored to His First Dress) ●

On the homeward road he could be an ox in the fire; one leaf had barely fallen and a whole world was in autumn. The moon is white, the waves are still, and there is nothing else to do: this heart still rests upon the fishing pole's tip.
(Gaining the Qilin on the Eastern Journey) ●

In the southeast Dharma cavern one rejoices in the many monks, yet none was seen to be a silent Vimalakīrti. Just then came Mr. Liang, seeking blessing and wisdom: among all those horns, you are the qilin.
(The Lotus Opens on Wuru Peak) ●

Nothing in the world excels the lotus flower; it pierces stone and threads sand, utterly without a speck of dust. Its fragrance fills all space, nor blooms nor fades; but fools, clinging to marks, are tangled like hemp.
(Entering Caoxi Once More) ●

Tidings, one should know, are the same as ever; of the old haunts the meaning is all the longer. The moon in the Caoxi water joins the three realms; seek out a fellow student, the better to take counsel together.
(No Moon at Mid-Autumn) ●

Spring has its hundred flowers, winter has its snow; summer has its cool breeze, autumn has its moon. Tonight, in mid-autumn, one watches only the stars: from of old the Unborn is all the more vast and clear.
(Sitting in Cessation in Worn Robes) ●

Stripped of the very trousers his mother bore, he is still an ordinary man; far removed from coming and going, he shows the blind how to inquire. Alone, aloof, his light before and behind: and still he fears the foolish ape may stir the jade-green pool.
(Building the Stupa at Mount Kuang) ●

When a man of attainment meets one, there is no negotiation; he raises the high banner and puts on his own foolishness. Uncomprehending of what lies within, one can but laugh aloud: welcoming and sending off, the better to hoodwink the eye.
(The Broken Niche Reveals the Buddha) ●

The comings and goings of folding and unfolding are subtle and profound; gods and men in crowds, who among them knows? A single command made Lord Song raise his precious sword; one thunderclap shook Mount Sumeru.
(The Flesh Body Sits in Mighty Steadfastness) ●

Insentient things preaching the Dharma make occasion for many words; the speechless withered stump is a master seen again. When host and guest meet, it is delusion still; light before and shining behind, the words run coarse and fine.
The Thirty-Sixth
Generation of Caoxi, [
Che Du * the Daoren ]
Yan, Great
Councilor, bowing with
joined palms,
reverently inscribed

blocks.text: 25. The Work Is Done; He Enters Stillness

inline.s: The Later Affairs of the Revival of Caoxi and of the Flesh-Body Patriarch Hanshan
Fushan, abbot of the Fayun Temple on Wuru Peak and former attendant of the Nārāyaṇa Cave of the Eastern Sea, records as follows:
In the third year of Tianqi, the year guihai, (1623), the Master was
seventy-eight and dwelling in the Chan Hall of Caoxi. The prefect
of Shaoyang, Lord Zhang, together with (all the officials and
gentlemen of the prefecture, entered the mountain and asked the Master
to preach. In the third month of spring the disciples of Wuyang
Dharma-Nature arrived. The Master, whose mind was then wholly set on the
gift of Dharma, first expounded the great precepts for them, then
the Awakening of Faith, the Consciousness-Only, and the Surangama.

In the fifth month of summer, Ma Jifang, a licentiate of Jizhou, and Wang Weizou, a provincial graduate, came to pay their respects. In the eighth month of autumn, when the assembly of the Patriarch was over, he sent an attendant to take leave of the provincial administrator Lord Wu. As he was about to set out, the Master charged him, saying: ‘In the Buddha’s and the Patriarchs’ spreading of the teaching, what matters is the season and the karmic occasion. When the occasion runs counter to the time, to what shall the teaching be entrusted? The business of one period is done; I am about to return.’ The assembly was wholly at a loss, and all took this for words of his wish to go back to Mount Kuang. He composed one poem, ‘Thoughts on the Mid-Autumn Moon.’

After the Double Ninth, for the attendant Shenguang he wrote out the poem on dwelling in the mountains, appending the note: ‘Though this old man is lazy with brush and inkstone, I fear that if a breath does not return, I shall again be a debtor to a future life. But if you look at them as poetry and calligraphy, then you greatly wrong my intent.’
On the first day of the tenth month of winter his disciple Tongjiong arrived from Mount Kuang and asked after the resident assembly of Wuru, and after the elders of the various monasteries
in the mountain; the Master’s heart was greatly gladdened. At that time his disciple Jingtai asked him to compose a self-praise, which set forth the whole purport of his life.

On the third day the Junior Minister Lord Xiao Xuanpu entered the mountain to visit him, and they talked deeply for three days and nights, greatly delighted. He asked for the essentials of the Dharma, and the Master accordingly composed two Dharma words and three poems and gave them to him. On the sixth day, when Lord Xiao was leaving the mountain, the Master charged him: ‘You are looked up to by the realm and the common people; take good care of yourself on the road ahead.’ Lord Xiao still planned another meeting. The Master said: ‘This mountain monk is old; the four elements are about to scatter. The karmic bond of another meeting with you must wait for the Dragon-Flower Assembly.’ So they parted, and he returned to the abbot’s quarters.
[The Dragon-Flower Assembly] Maitreya Bodhisattva now dwells in the Inner Court of the Tushita Heaven; in the future he will descend into the human world and become a Buddha, and
beneath the dragon-flower trees of the Dragon-Flower Grove in the Hualin Garden he will hold a Dharma assembly to save gods and men alike. This is called the Dragon-Flower Assembly.

On the eighth day he showed a slight illness. When the assembly inquired after him, he said only that the old man was weary, not ill. On the ninth day, when the medicine was brought, he would not take it, saying: ‘I am going; what use is medicine?’ The attendant Guangyi, hearing these words, asked in alarm: ‘Should the Master, alas, pass beyond , what charge have you to leave?’ The Master rebuked him: ‘You have attended this old

man for years; how can you hold such a view? You should all bear in mind that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence swift, and recite the Buddha’s name in earnest.’ Guangyi said again: ‘If the Master will not show us a single word, how shall we know how to conduct ourselves?’ The Master said: ‘What the golden mouth proclaimed has become old paper; of what use are my words?’ And so he showed not a single word.

The twelfth day was the Master’s birthday , and black-robed and white-robed disciples gathered like clouds. Lord Zhang Sanxing, prefect of Shaoyang, entered the mountain and brought a purple silk Chan
robe to congratulate the Master on his longevity, and they sat talking together the whole day. When evening came Lord Zhang withdrew. That very night the Master three times called for water to bathe.

The next morning he called for the Chan robe Lord Zhang had brought, put it on, and took his leave of Lord Zhang. Lord Zhang came again to the side of his couch, and the Master said: ‘This mountain monk is going. Many thanks for

the great protector’s abundant heart.’ Lord Zhang said: ‘The Master’s Dharma body is without ill; unworthy as I am I am the lord of this land, and all things rest with me.’ The Master smiled, joined his palms, and thanked him.

At noon Lord Zhang took his leave and departed. The Master at once called an attendant to fetch pure water to rinse his mouth, saying: ‘Today I cut off the tangled vine.’ Again he called for hot water to bathe and change his robes, and the assembly gathered about him reciting the Buddha’s name. He charged them: ‘You must not be alarmed. Follow the Buddha’s rule: you may not wear hemp or mourning garments, and you may not weep and wail; with one mind recite the Buddha’s name.’

At the third watch of the afternoon , the Master sat upright and passed away. That night a ray of light illumined the heavens, flocks of birds cried mournfully, and black-robed and white-robed lamented
aloud, their voices shaking the mountain valley. After his passing he sat upright for three days, his face fair, his lips red, his hands and feet soft, as though entered into Chan concentration.

Word was sent to Lord Zhang, who at once dispatched officials to offer condolences and seal the shrine. At that time Lord Xiao had been gone but five days and was still at Xiongzhou; hearing the news of the Master, he grieved the whole day. But when he further heard the circumstances of his passing, he rejoiced, saying: ‘The Master is a man of the holy ranks. Had he not seen through the juncture of birth and death, how could this have been?’ He at once composed an elegy and sent condolences, and further donated a hundred taels of silver, composing a text and charging the prefects of Nan and Shao to build a shadow hall for him.

When the Dharma kin of Wuru on Mount Kuang heard the news, the disciples Fushan and the rest, obeying the Master’s dying command, went at once to Caoxi and bore the Master’s reliquary back to Wuru, building a stupa at the place the Master himself had chosen. By then the shadow hall there was already finished, and the monks pressed hard to keep it. Fushan and the others again reported to the grand historian Wu, the assistant censor Wu, the provincial administrator Sheng, Wang Mengsu, Miao Mutai, and the other

officials of the society, and wrote to the authorities concerned to petition; and so the Supreme Commander Lord He of Wuwo and Lord Wang, the chief administrator of this province, a man of excellent virtue, sent a dispatch to the prefecture to escort the reliquary back to Mount Kuang, issuing a passport and travelling funds. On the twenty-first day of the first month of the yichou year it set out, and on the twenty-eighth day of the second month it reached the Fayun Temple on Wuru Peak of Mount Kuang.

○ The Master’s Dharma lineage consists of forty characters, with a verse that runs: ‘Great is the virtue, deep and wide the blessing; kind and benevolent, his measure is universal and equal. Cultivating and upholding, he transcends the Dharma-realm; awakening in accord, the wondrous mind blends. Still and tranquil, he awakens to constant joy; perfect and

bright, the essence of his nature penetrates. The light of wisdom shines on forever; the transformation of the Way long prospers and flourishes.’ (The character ‘De’ is Patriarch Hanshan’s Dharma taboo-name; ‘Da’ is the Dharma taboo-name of the Empress Dowager Cisheng of the Li family. He commanded that his disciples’ names begin with the generation of ‘Fu.’)

Zhang Yizhen, prefect of Shaoyang, styled Sanxing, also styled the Daoist of Suchness, wrote the preface to the chronicle, saying: “The chronicle of the Great Master Hanshan — his Dharma heir Xinqi came

and asked that a plan be made to give it to the block-carvers. For in former days, when I was prefect of Shaoshi, I welcomed the Master from Wuru to dwell at Caoxi; and when the Master showed h iscessation, I
went again to take leave of him — it seems there was a concurrence of former causes. I recall that in the past I sent the monk Ben’ang to welcome the Master. Earlier the Master had shuthimself in

retreat for eight months; on the day the welcoming company arrived, he opened the retreat and said to them: ‘I was going; you should have sounded the bell and drum early and waited.’ Theassembly of Wuru
gathered around him weeping and pressing him to stay. The Master said: ‘Caoxi is my own wish; the season and the karmic occasion — how dare I not accord with them? If I may beg thespirit of the Sixth

Patriarch to let me entrust my bones there, that would be fortune indeed.’ So he set off swiftly with his staff and bowl. Crossing the ridge, he sang: ‘One look at the five clouds and Ienter Nan’an; ten

thousand folds, a thousand turns, the sixty-six rapids. When I come to where the water ends and the mountains run out, plum blossoms beyond counting are seen at the ridge-top.’ That theMaster’s mind was

set on ending at Caoxi is a sign already plain enough. In the twelfth month of the renxu year he reached Caoxi; in the winter of the next year, at the face-to-face charge of the Masterof Rites Lord Xiao,

I made contributions in many quarters and divined a site on the sunny side of the mountain, where I built the burial stupa and roofed the shadow hall, relying on the strength of manyhands to finish the
work. Then the Master showed his cessation, and I forthwith arranged his burial. Of the Master’s wishes it seemed that none was unfulfilled. Not long after, I was transferred fromShao, and the Dharma

heirs of Wuru, borrowing the great power of those in authority, moved the remains to Mount Lu, leaving hair and nails behind at Caoxi; and the stupa and hall I had built were alsounharmed. Now all dharmas

are empty of marks and have neither going nor abiding; Caoxi and Wuru are alike a hall of blessing. To abide or to go — both return to dream and illusion; what mind could the Masterhave had in it? The
Master met the world with an empty heart and saved the world with a compassionate heart; above he illumined the sage’s virtue, below he pitied the people’s suffering; he took refuge in thePatriarch’s

court and kept the Chan lineage flowing; in hardship and in ease he was one and the same, from first to last unchanging; a guide for gods and men, a dragon-elephant of the Dharma gate. These thingsstand

out clearly, item by item, in the chronicle; how should I presume to add a single word of embellishing praise? Because his heir came to ask me, I have set down a rough outline of him, and that is all.”
○ Fuzheng notes: Zhang Sanxing, Lord Zhang, knew the Master, welcomed him to Caoxi a second time, personally escorted him at his cessation, and arranged his burial; his
wishes were all fulfilled. His power of the Way and his former causes were assuredly no small matter. And when, borrowing great power, the reliquary was moved, the stupa
and hall happily remained unharmed; on the day the stupa was moved to Wuru, reading those words about going and abiding as dream and illusion, how could his heart not
have been stirred with longing? When our Master returned once more to Caoxi and his flesh body appeared, it must have greatly comforted Lord Zhang’s heart’s wish; whether
Lord Zhang lived to see or hear of it, I do not know. If it had not been for those two welcomes and farewells, and for his crossing the Dayu Ridge, where the robe and
bowl could not be lifted, and coming back again to the very place divined that day for the burial shadow hall, facing Patriarch Lu, sending forth a great light to shine
through the kalpas — how could one see that our Master’s vow-power truly suffices to cut off all streams and to embrace heaven and earth? The one song sung as he crossed
the ridge can still be struck against metal and stone to this day; that he knew the subtle signs and was godlike in it must be seen at the juncture of birth and death.

Again I note: what Master Zhiwei Shan recorded — our Master’s cessation at Caoxi and the return of his reliquary to Wuru — were matters of the single year Tianqi renxu , and were not in time to be included in the chronicle. The preface written by Zhang Sanxing, Lord Zhang, sets forth the beginning and end of that earlier great matter of the going and coming between Caoxi and Wuru,

and may be called clear and complete. Our Master’s birthday was the twelfth day of the tenth month, and on the twelfth day of the tenth month of that very year he showed his illness and took leave of the prefect of Shao, Lord Zhang; one day later came the time of his passing. In going and coming he was wholly his own master: truly a rare thing since the beginningless kalpas.
After he reached Wuru he was reburied and given a floating offering, and down to the guiwei year of Chongzhen (1643), it was already twenty-two years since
the renxu year(1622). Then appeared once more the welcoming of the reliquary to Wuru and the return of the reliquary to Caoxi, the manifestation of the
flesh body, and the rivalry with Patriarch Lu — the whole beginning and end of the great matter. Yet of the supplementary chronicle and the various printed
records and biographies, not one or two parts in ten are clear. Because Fuzheng was released from his post at the Nanyong Academy, he lodged at Jiangning
between the Southern Mountain, the Rain-Flower Terrace, and the treetops; there he was able to follow the disciples who had personally attended and gone to
and fro with Patriarch Hanshan — Masters Rongcheng, Kuanju, Jianru, Mingji, and the rest of the Dharma kin — and to inquire of each the general outline;
gathering up the imperishable outlines of the Dharma gate’s pivotal matters, in preparation for another day, after the precedent of the posthumous title
Dajian granted to Patriarch Lu, to petition for a posthumous title. This is what I pray for. And so I recall how our Master, at the parting, patted Fuzheng
on the shoulder and said with a laugh: ‘The affairs after I am gone are entrusted to you.’ That day I was in the dark and did not know what he meant; now I
am able to pour out my heart and set down remembered events at the end of the chronicle — truly this came of the season and the karmic occasion. Thinking
back on that face-to-face charge, it is like waking from a dream: that he knew the subtle signs and was godlike in it— in my Master I believe it the more.

○ The abbot of Fayun, Miaorong, whose personal name was Guangcheng, and the abbot of Qixia, Jianru, whose personal name was Ciren, had both been among the Dharma-attendants who went and came twice between Caoxi and Wuru, on the days of the welcoming and the sending off of the reliquary. They told in full how our Master, on the eleventh day of the eleventh month of the winter of the renxu year, because the provincial administrator Wu Shengbo, the Shaozhou prefect Zhang Sanxing, and the Guangdong disciple, the licentiate Liu Qixiang, had time and again sent letters to Wuru earnestly inviting him, and

had even sent the hall-master of Baolin, Ben’ang, to come and receive him — our Master then resolved to leave Mount Kuang and enter Caoxi. On that very day he ascended the seat in the Wuru Dharma Hall and made it known to hall-master Ang, and likewise took leave of the assembly. He sat cross-legged for a long while, unaware that a great serpent had coiled itself beneath his body, its form pressed flat as a cushion. When he rose and saw it, he lit a flame to accompany the journey; it also foretold that, having entered Caoxi, our Master would remain but a single year and never return to Wuru again.

Also, on the day he arrived back at Caoxi, hall-master Ang invited him to ascend the hall and preach. Word by word he broke open the old case of the Sixth Patriarch’s flesh body and the incense-offerings, and the meaning of how what came before and what came after answer each

other; therein one sees the spirit of one who knows beforehand. The Dharma-words (Dream-Wanderings Collection, · Instructions to Hall-Master Ang of Baolin at Caoxi) run: ‘When the Sixth Patriarch had not yet come forth into the world , he was only a wood-seller of Xinzhou.

Because he had planted the spiritual root in former lives and long nourished his practice, the instant he heard the Diamond Sutra recited and the phrase “should dwell nowhere,” he cut off the birth-and-death of eons, awakened to his own mind, and so received the robe and bowl of

Huangmei. Is not the Baolin of today come down from the Sixth Patriarch’s shoulder-pole of firewood and the waist-stone of the rice-pounder? Hence it has such vast and boundless brightness that fills the whole world. Every word and phrase of the Chan school flows from that

firewood shoulder-pole and that husking waist-stone, and so today the incense and offerings are no different from when he was alive. The flesh body, firm and undecaying, is no different from one who speaks the Dharma now. Such blessings too come from that firewood shoulder-pole

and that husking waist-stone. This beam of prajñā-light that the Sixth Patriarch awakened to, every person has a share of, lacking not a hair’s breadth. If one can but awaken to one’s own mind, then one may churn the long river into ghee and turn the vast earth into gold;

plucking up a single blade of grass, make it a sixteen-foot golden body; and with that sixteen-foot golden body, serve as a single blade of grass. Naturally one then possesses great spiritual powers, transforming freely at will, doing whatever one pleases, nothing impossible.’

He further said: our Master, re-entering Caoxi, had it in mind to rebuild the great hall of Caoxi. The many monies he had raised from the three offices and the prefectures went entirely to purchasing iron-pyrus timber in western Guangdong and, as recorded in the chronicle under the wushen year, had already been hauled into Caoxi. The two gentlemen Wu and Zhang, together with hall-master Ang, shared in this vow, and so their pleas for his return were all the more devout. And our Master, knowing that his hour had come, said: ‘When conditions and the times run contrary, where shall the transformation find a place

to lodge?’ And so, in the winter of the guihai year, upon the thirteenth day of the tenth month, he passed away. There was, moreover, a plot that the vice-minister Xiao Xuanpu had asked the prefect Zhang to divine for a shadow hall, two li south of Nanhua Monastery in Shaozhou, named Tianzi Gang, the Hill of the Son of Heaven. An old prophecy said: ‘Head above Tianzi Hill, feet treading the Yellow Mud Pond; whoever is buried here, from generation to generation a Dharma-king will arise.’ The Guangdong congregation, having taken refuge, therefore raised a stupa on that spot and there interred his whole body.
The Wuru disciples Fushan, styled Zhiwei, together with Shenguang, styled Yihui, Guangyi, styled Xuzhong, and Ciren, styled Jianru, hastened to Guangdong to receive
the reliquary but could not obtain it. So they went about the Wu-Yue region and, by the Master’s dying command, laid the matter before the many patrons: Lord Wu Benru,
Lord He Zhiyue, Lord Wang Jie’an, and Lord Qian Shouzhi. These wrote to the Guangdong judicial commissioner Lord Lu Jingye, who sent a dispatch to Shaozhou; and
on the twenty-first day of the first month of the yichou year (1625) the shrine was opened and borne back to Mount Kuang. As the land there was dank and damp, Fushan
built a stupa-court and set the shrine floating upon it. The prefectural judge of Nankang, Qian Woxin, whose personal name was Qizhong, chose a place and buried it.
Eleven years later, in the yihai year (1635), fierce
tigers rose up in the mountains, and Fayun(Fayun Temple)
could no longer keep the assembly at peace. Fushan
blamed the unquiet site of the stupa, and again
brought the shrine forth to its floating platform, and
saw that the protective enclosure was half eaten by
ants, so that he dared not divine a place of burial.
Nine more years passed, and in the ninth month of the guiwei year (1643), the Lingnan disciple, the minister Chen Zizhuang,
sent a letter with ample provisions to welcome it. It happened that the Guangdong disciple Lord Liu Qixiang, serving
in the penal office of Ruizhou, was auditing the stores of Nankang, and he threw himself into the task of returning the
reliquary to Caoxi. When they reached Meiling, there was the newly appointed commander-in-chief of GuangdongLord Song
Zhaoming, named Ji, who ten years earlier, beneath the banner of the Guangdong governor-general, had formed a Dharma-affinity
with our Master. Crossing the ridge to take up office, he chanced upon the spiritual reliquary and, marveling beyond
measure at his fortune, ordered his soldiers to bear the reliquary in a carriageand escorted it in personinto Caoxi.
Months after taking his post he came again to Caoxi. The shrine-bearing disciples Guangcheng, styled Miaorong,
and Cili, styled Jianchi, seeing a crack in the shrine, secretly bored a small opening through it to peep
within, and there beheld the Master seated upright as if alive. They were debating whether to openthe
shrine, but no one dared decide. When Lord Song heard this, he at once drew his blade and split the crack open,
and they saw the twin cross-legged feetas if alive, the nails and hair both grown long, and their colour
a bright red. The robe and shoes were still new, and only when they met the wind did they crumble to pieces,
laying bare the five limbs. Suddenly a monk arrived and asked that, following the Indianrite, powdered
sandalwood from Hainan be smeared over the body until it was like lacquer. The smearing done, he departed.

Long before, in Caoxi, an unmarried girl had vowed to embroider a robe of a thousand Buddhas to offer in homage; fearing that her breath was unclean, she wrapped her mouth in yellow silk as she plied the needle and thread. When the robe was finished, our Master had already passed on into the shrine, and the robe was left in a chest of the Baolin storehouse. One day the abbot-monk, celebrating a penitential rite, wished to don this robe, but the monks clamoured and stopped him. Later, when our Master’s flesh

body returned to Caoxi and came forth from the shrine, the purple silk robe was suddenly scattered and torn by the wind, and the countryfolk snatched up the pieces as auspicious tokens. So they took the thousand-Buddha robe the girl had embroidered and clothed him in it; the robe had lain in the chest twenty years, yet its lustre was as fresh as new. Thereupon it was enshrined at the site of the old stupa-court, and the monastery was named Hanshan, half a li or so from the Baolin Hall of Nanhua Monastery.

The disciples attended him after the manner in which the Sixth Patriarch is attended at Baolin: at first light , they bring a basin of hot fragrant water, steam his face until it sweats, wipe it with a cloth, and set before him

food and drink with full reverent offerings, exactly as though he were alive. Once a year they bathe him, and the water of the washing is taken by the countryfolk to drink for the healing of sickness, and it is gone in a moment.

Every year the pilgrims of Caoxi, in the second and the eighth months, all the people of the province entering the mountains to pay their respects, would, after offering incense to the Sixth Patriarch, proclaim that they had come to offer

incense to the Seventh Patriarch; and so the title ‘the Seventh Patriarch of Caoxi’ arose. For the Guangdong pilgrims, of one accord, had in mind that bodhisattva in flesh, and in a single moment from the Southern Sea to the Northern Sea,

all within the realm heard this name and took it as a matter of course. Yet certain critics held that one must not overstep the five houses and schools nor yield to a passing word-of-mouth transmission, for fear of giving a handle to those

who would later revise the lamp-lineage. Fuzheng, not measuring his own worth, has hastily drafted three discussions — on the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ teaching, on the robe and bowl, and on the flesh body — to put to those of clear eye .

[The Seventh Patriarch of Caoxi] Master Yinguang, in his ‘Verses Inscribed on the Scroll of the Great Master Hanshan’s Six Hymns,’ says: “The Great Master Hanshan was a manifestation of great power. His work of spreading the Dharma was deep; those who envied him slandered and entrapped him. He was exiled to Guangzhou to guard against calamity and disorder. Happily there were great officials who looked on him with other eyes. He spread the Dharma at Caoxi, and the life of wisdom, broken, was continued. Teaching according

to circumstance, he caused mighty abuses to melt away. He protected the state and brought peace to the people; his merit rose high as the statutes. After his passing his flesh body neither decayed nor changed. Guangdong and Jiangxi contended for him; he returned to the bank of Caoxi. As Sixth Patriarch and Seventh Patriarch , he is proclaimed in the proverbs of the time. He added lustre to the Buddha’s sun and served as a moat for the Dharma-city. His writings were vast and broad; sun and moon are bright with them.”

○ Fuzheng notes: Above Śākyamuni they are called the seven Buddhas; from Śākyamuni’s transmission to Kāśyapa and below, down to Bodhidharma, they are called the twenty-eight patriarchs of the West. From Bodhidharma’s crossing

east and below, down to Caoxi, they are called the six patriarchs of the East; they are not called Buddhas, nor are they simply called masters. The Sixth Patriarch transmitted to Huairang and Xingsi — these are but two branches.

Huairang dwelt on Mount Nanyue, and so is called of the Nanyue line; he transmitted to Mazu. Nanyue is not heard to be called patriarch, yet Mazu alone is called patriarch. Is this not to say that he transmitted the Dharma to the many, and did not make a single transmission of the robe and bowl? Below Mazu there is Baizhang; below Baizhang there is Huangbo; both are called Great Masters, or else Chan Masters, and are nowhere heard to be called school-masters. At that time there was as yet no talk of dividing the schools.

Below Huangbo there is Linji, and only then is there talk of the Linji school; the name of ‘school’ begins from this. Before this there were two branches of names, but no two school-gates. Below Baizhang there is also Guishan; below Guishan there is Yangshan, and thus there is the Guiyang school. So from the single branch of Baizhang came two schools.

Xingsi dwelt at Qingyuan, and so is called of the Qingyuan line; he transmitted to Shitou. Below Shitou there is Dongshan; below Dongshan there is Caoshan; and taking advantage of the ease of the tongue, the name was turned about and called the Caodong school.
Below Shitou there is also Xuefeng; below Xuefeng there is Yunmen, called the Yunmen school. Later there is also the Fayan school. So from the single branch of Qingyuan came three schools.

Why is it that Huairang and Qingyuan are of one generation, Mazu and Shitou of another, Baizhang and Xuefeng of yet another, and the three generations below the Sixth Patriarch are not heard to bear the names of schools? Even Huangbo, of the fourth generation, is not heard to have set up a school-name in rivalry with men of the same generation as Guishan, Dongshan, and Yunmen. This is why Huangbo surpassed his peers and dared to take Mazu to task. Huangbo once said: ‘In the whole land of the Great Tang there are no Chan masters.’ A monk asked: ‘The venerable elders of every quarter all gather assemblies and open the teaching; why then do you say there are no Chan masters?’ Huangbo said: ‘I do not say there is no Chan; I only say there are no masters. Have you not seen that below the Great Master Ma there were eighty-four men sitting in the Dharma-hall, and that of those who obtained the Master Ma’s true Dharma-eye there were only two or three? The Elder Guizong was one of them. Now one who has left home must know that he has a share in the matter that has come down from above before he can be reckoned. Take, for instance, Niutou below the Fourth Patriarch: he spoke at length and in every direction, yet still did not know the pivotal device that points upward. Only with this eye can one distinguish the true from the false in the schools. And when it comes to the affairs of one’s own person, one cannot grasp it; one only knows to learn phrases and recite them, to stow them away in the skin-bag, and everywhere to say, “I understand Chan.” Can that redeem you from birth and death? To make light of the elder masters is to fall into hell as swift as an arrow flies.’ Great indeed are the words of Huangbo! The wisdom-eye and the Dharma-eye truly do not deceive me. Only the direct grandson of Mazu could carry on so. This is what is meant by blue coming from indigo yet being deeper than indigo, and curds coming from milk yet being richer than milk. When Linji set up the Dharma and divided the schools, Huangbo then had many sons. Guiyang, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan followed one after another in fame, splitting the gates and dividing the households; and so Mazu, Baizhang, Shitou, and Xuefeng then had many grandsons.

One flower, five leaves: we never hear of the flower and leaves being marked out as the root and trunk. Only because root and trunk are not two does the fruit ripen whole. If one flower can become a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million flowers, and five leaves can become fifty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million leaves, then the more flowers the more leaves. As the saying goes, ‘When the leaves are many the flower does not open; when the flowers are many the fruit does not set.’ These words are small, yet they may illustrate something great. If everyone seeks the flower and chases the leaves, where shall one ask after the root and trunk? Even if one can obtain fruit, it is the fruit of a flower grafted onto a strange stock; where then is the root? I am too foolish to understand wherein the reality of the schools lies.

‘The ten thousand dharmas return to the One’ — this is the teaching. ‘Where does the One return?’ — this is the school. The Dharma abides in the minds of all under heaven, and the mind of the Dharma cannot have five. The school abides in the mind of the good and wise teacher, and how can the mind of the school have five? When Bodhidharma came from the West, those who knew him called it only the Chan school. If the school has five, then the mind has five and Chan has five. I am too dull to understand wherein the reality of the five schools lies.

The five schools are gates; they are titles. The gate of a patriarch is in no way different from the gate of a Buddha; the title of a patriarch is in the end no different from the title of a Buddha. One who can be a patriarch must be able to become a Buddha, and one who cannot become a Buddha surely cannot be a patriarch. A patriarch comes from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. To give him another title may be permissible; to give him another gate, I fear, is not. Still more, to take five titles and set up five gates is like the children and grandchildren of a household seizing upon the ancestral estate and scattering the family goods in disorder; this I do not understand.

As to the division of titles, it is not only the Buddhas and patriarchs that are divided: even Śākyamuni has ten titles, and the Buddhas and bodhisattvas have countless and boundless titles, and these cannot be held up as equal. As to the union of gates, it is not only the Buddhas and patriarchs that unite: even the Tiantai Dharma-nature school, which takes as its school the Lotus and Nāgārjuna’s Madhyamaka; the Xianshou school, which takes as its school the Avataṃsaka and the contemplation of the Dharma-realm; the Nanshan Vinaya school; the Ci’en Dharmalakṣaṇa school, which sets forth the Consciousness-Only school; and the Vajraśekhara Yoga school of the three mysteries. Every teaching must have a school; without a school no teaching is established. They cannot be split into two. If they could be distinguished and split into two, they would assuredly belong to the heretics, the outer paths, and the Lesser Vehicle.

Know that the Pure Land is mind alone; this alone is the ten thousand dharmas returning to the One. The patriarch can come from the West; the Buddha can return to the West. From the west and from the east, from the south and from the north, none who think but submit — this is what is meant by Buddha and patriarch. The Buddha-Dharma is equal, with no high and no low. That titles differ, how can one insist that they are all the same? Yet for rebirth and for upholding the Dharma, one must first have the title; and the flesh-eye taking refuge rests wholly on the reverent name. Long ago I saw a Chan worthy whom the vulgar called ‘Lord’; Yunqi forbade it and it ceased. This is the meaning of Confucius’s rectification of names and the Spring and Autumn’s fixing of ranks.

In the present worldly order, unless one has founded a state and carried on a house, one may not be called a patriarch; yet among the hundred crafts and the myriad trades, all may be called masters. In the world-transcending order, they are called the twenty-eight patriarchs of the West and the six patriarchs of the East, and are not heard to be called masters. Mazu obtained the Dharma at Caoxi and Nanyue before the schools were divided; therefore it is fitting to call him patriarch. Hanshan, too, obtained the Dharma at Caoxi, and going to and fro between Nanyue and Qingyuan, in every place and every moment did nothing but speak the Dharma, practise the Dharma, and transmit the Dharma. Though he comes after the schools were divided, he still returns to the time before they were divided; therefore it is fitting, following the precedent of Mazu, to call him Patriarch Hanshan. Only those who personally attended him may call him our teacher; those who inherit the Dharma may call him the master of the house.

As for the titles of Great Master and Seventh Patriarch, these all follow the common custom. The Record of the Source Mirror quotes Bodhidharma’s words: ‘To illumine the Buddha-mind school, with no error whatsoever, and to have practice and understanding answer each other — this is called a patriarch.’ These words match the meaning of Patriarch Hanshan exactly. As for the Great Master Daguan’s ‘Praise Sent with the Portrait of Master Kang,’ in which he praises Master Hanshan, saying that ‘the flesh-Buddha of Caoxi has appeared,’ he means Patriarch Lu . If Patriarch Lu may be called flesh-Buddha, Patriarch Hanshan should be no

different; so let us call him the flesh-Patriarch of Caoxi. The Chan monks who push themselves forward in the world can truly bear no comparison. In general, those who divide the schools, the Dharma, and the Vinaya may be called school-masters, Dharma-masters, and Vinaya-masters; they may not be called school-patriarchs, Dharma-patriarchs, and Vinaya-patriarchs. Only when the three gates are hard to name may one be called patriarch. Thus Patriarch Lu, who obtained the school from Huangmei, the Dharma-seal from Yinzong, and the Vinaya from Zhiguang, is a model for Mazu, for Hanshan, and for those who come again in later ages.

○ Fuzheng further notes, in the outline of the life of Patriarch Lu: When the patriarch had received the robe and the Dharma from Huangmei, he came to the South Sea and met the Dharma-master Yinzong. Hearing the words about the wind and the banner, Yinzong invited the patriarch into his room and held the ritual of a disciple, and announced to the four assemblies: ‘This Layman Lu is a bodhisattva in the flesh.’ Gathering the famous worthies, he shaved his head; and further, before the Vinaya-master Zhiguang of the Dharma-Nature Monastery, he received the full precepts.

That ordination platform had been set up by the Tripitaka master Guṇabhadra in the time of the Liu Song. That master had recorded: ‘Hereafter a bodhisattva in the flesh shall receive the precepts on this platform.’ Observing this, we know that the patriarch who confers the robe and the bodhisattva in the flesh must be one and the same person, while the head-shaving Dharma-master, the precept-conferring Vinaya-master, and the Dharma-transmitting patriarch must not be one and the same person. The mind is one, the Way is one; their meanings differ, their rules differ.

Again, Patriarch Lu said to the four assemblies: ‘I have unworthily received the robe and the Dharma of Master Ren; now I preach the Dharma for you, but I do not transmit the robe.’ And one day he said to his disciples: ‘I wish to return to Xinzhou.’ The great assembly, mourning, begged the patriarch to remain: ‘When the Master goes from here, will he come back sooner or later?’ The patriarch said: ‘The leaf falls and returns to the root; when I come, I shall have no mouth.’

Again they asked: ‘The Master’s Dharma-eye — to whom is it transmitted?’ The patriarch said: ‘The one who has the Way obtains it; the one who is without mind penetrates it.’ Observing this, we know that the robe and bowl of the patriarchs had long been without trace since the Xiantian years of the early Tang. As for the robe and bowl now handed down at Caoxi, they did not come from Huangmei: they were bestowed in the first year of Shenlong of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang,

who sent the palace attendant Xue Jian to invite the patriarch. Patriarch Lu declined on the grounds of illness and did not go, and so discoursed with Xue Jian, saying: ‘The Way is realized by the mind; it does not lie in sitting in meditation and practising concentration.’ His words were very full (see (A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch). Jian received the instruction and was suddenly enlightened; he took his leave and returned to

court, memorialized the patriarch’s words, and an edict thanked the Master and bestowed upon him a patchwork kāṣāya, five hundred bolts of silk, and one bowl. Observing this, we know that the robe and bowl of Caoxi are merely royal offerings, not the tokens of the Fifth Patriarch. It is Mazu who transmitted the Dharma to the most disciples, and even among his own disciples there were many who disagreed. Therefore one may speak of his transmission of the Dharma, but not of

his transmission of the robe and bowl, of a token, or of a school. To take a material object as a token of transmission is something the outer paths often have. How could Mazu have had so many robes and bowls? The tale of the robe and bowl handed down through a thousand years is but dust for food and mud for soup; the life of wisdom of the Buddhas and patriarchs is in no way bound up with it. Only our Hanshan, a patriarch in the flesh, inherits the transmission of one

flower and five leaves, and so reaches a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million leaves. Set against those who raise a stick or give a shout, who point directly and transmit in a single line, one does not know which is the word that fits the head. ‘The one who has the Way obtains it; the one who is without mind penetrates it’ — the karmic occasion of Patriarch Lu gains all the more belief today. Truly, the former sage and the later sage accord in one standard!

○ Fuzheng: I further read Lang Gongying’s Sevenfold Revision of the Classified Draft, which says: ‘When the Sixth Patriarch passed away, the officials and disciples of Guangzhou, Shaozhou, and Xinzhou all strove to receive the true body, and the assembly could not decide. So they burned incense and prayed, saying: “Wherever the incense points, there shall the Master return.” Because the incense pointed to Caoxi, they moved the shrine together with the robe and bowl, built a stupa, and enshrined him. Later the flesh body came forth from the stupa-shrine, perfumed by incense like lacquer; when one stroked the beard and hair by hand, they were as though three or four days after a shaving. During

the rebellion of Huang Chao, when the brigands came to Caoxi and would have desecrated it, a wind and murk darkened the daylight, and they bowed in reverence, begged for mercy, and went away. At the end of the Song, Prime Minister Wen Tianxiang, in his poem “Gazing Toward Nanhua Monastery,” has the lines: “On and on I come to Nanhua, hurried as in a dream; the Buddha’s transformation, how much dust of knowing, and the sorrow is the same as mine.” The gentleman’s own note says that the Sixth Patriarch’s flesh body was wounded by rebel troops; but this is merely a means by which he lodged his own self-consolation. The title speaks of “gazing toward” Nanhua, so he had never himself seen it.’

The Gazetteer of Caoxi, which Patriarch Hanshan compiled, records: In the second year of Xiantian of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang, the Master entered nirvāṇa at Guoen Monastery in Xinzhou, and his whole body was placed in the Caoxi stupa. In the tenth year of Kaiyuan of Emperor Xuanzong, a filial son named Zhang Man, having received twenty strings of cash from the Silla monk Jin Dabei, was hired to take the patriarch’s head back to the sea-east for offering. The county magistrate Yang Kan and the prefect Liu Wutian, obtaining the writ, captured the thief and examined his case; and only because the patriarch’s disciple Lingtao pleaded with all his might was his life spared. Thereupon they moved the true body to the Faith-and-Vessel Tower so that it might be guarded, and the tower was later changed into the Patriarchs’ Hall. At the beginning of the Kaibao era of Emperor Taizu of Song, when the imperial army pacified the South Sea, the remnant troops of the Liu family made trouble, and the patriarch’s stupa and hall were reduced to ashes. The true body, protected by the stupa-keeping monk, suffered not the slightest loss. In the tenth year of Tiansheng of Emperor Renzong, a peaceful carriage was made ready and the patriarch’s true body, together with the robe and bowl, was received into the palace and offered to; thereafter a messenger was sent with an edict to return them to Caoxi.
In Patriarch Hanshan’s Gazetteer of Caoxi there is a ‘Hymn in Praise of the Sixth Patriarch’s Flesh Body,’ which says:
When the one yang returns, the warm breath draws near.
When the three yangs are full, all things are in spring.
When the one yin first comes, the flowing fire congeals within.
When the three yins first join, the grass and trees suddenly wither.
The powerful maker of change still causes withering and flourishing.
How much more the Unborn, in thought after thought perfuming.
Entering the void from what is, the four elements all dissolve.
Entering what is from the void, what is then does not decay.
When void and what is are both forgotten, one is the same as diamond.
The mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all the everlasting still light.
Therefore our Master is the king within the Dharma.

Fuzheng, having fully examined the records of the gazetteer, knows that the flesh body of Patriarch Lu was never in any way wounded. The stupa and the true body now both abide in the monastery, though not in the same place. Compared with Patriarch Hanshan, after his passing and the many years, the going in and out of the stupa-shrine, the former patriarch and the later patriarch are as if from a single track. The sutra says: ‘For one who is greatly enlightened, the Dharma-body and the reward-body are in no way two; he who does not treasure the reward-body is an outer-path heretic.’ Nāgārjuna says: ‘A bodhisattva newly on the ground, whose Way is not yet full, does indeed have the affair of burning the body.’ And the sutra says: ‘A bodhisattva who never retreats has not the eighty thousand families of worms in his body; therefore the flesh body does not decay, the hair and nails can grow, his dignity gathers beings, and through the kalpas the fragrant light endures.’ Even as the First Patriarch returned to the West, and the Second Patriarch Shenguang, and the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs of Huangmei, all had flesh bodies, so we know that the flesh body is to be treasured and cannot be compared with the burning of the body. To regard it as a flesh body is thus; to regard it as the Dharma-body is also thus. To regard it with the flesh-eye is thus; to regard it with the Dharma-eye is also thus.

You have spoken at length of how the teaching and the school return to the One, and of the principle that all things return to the Pure Land, even down to the matter of the Caoxi Sixth Patriarch’s robe, bowl, and flesh body, making the long night to dawn and the heavy mist to see the sun. It is indeed trustworthy and perfect, with no meaning left out, and the heart’s regard for

Patriarch Hanshan has no regret either. The sincere man completes himself and completes things; the gentleman acts first and speaks afterwards. But as for you yourself, at the juncture of birth and death, of going and coming, how do you place yourself? As for my own placing of myself, it is not only the teaching, the school, and the Pure Land that return to the One; even

theteachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism and the ten thousand dharmas, none of them fails to return to the One. Nor is it only in the chronicle of my teacher Hanshan, in the concluding discussion at the end, that the Way is first spoken of as One. From the two classics of Confucius and Mencius, through the eight thousand scrolls of the Compendium of the Sages, the

twothousand scrolls collected amid the new poems, down to the two classics of Nanhua and the Lisao held up for a second look, the Immortal Ancestor Jingsheng’s Book of Transformation, and the Dao-scriptures, whatever has been set down by the pen, nothing fails to be of the principle of one Way amid the three teachings. And yet words must have their root; the truthful message may

beverified again. I quote the scriptures and cite the traditions, I bring the ancients to prove the present, and I presume to say that I transmit and do not compose, that I do not fabricate what I have not learned. The heart’s regard for my teacher Hanshan is not a turning from Confucius to the Buddha, nor a turning from the Immortal Ancestor to the patriarch. Whatever my

teachertrod in his person, whatever he spoke from his mouth, whatever he wrote with his brush, all were of the principle of one Way amid the three teachings, without need of the kind of riving that the good and wise layman Fu Dashi, amid his very speaking and moving in robe and cap, set forth face to face for Emperor Wu of Liang. For example, among his writings beyond the Buddhist

canonare An Explanation of the Analects, A Direct Pointer to the Doctrine of the Mean, Resolving Doubts on the Great Learning, The Mind-Method of the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn, An Essay on the Influences of Laozi and Zhuangzi, An Explanation of the Daodejing, An Explanation of the Inner Chapters of Zhuangzi, On the Three Teachings, and The Finger-and-Palm of the

MysticDoor. While he dwelt at Caoxi, the scholars who wore the scholar’s cap came with their satchels to ask the Way; of such was Feng Changli’s company, who in all cases brought their examination compositions to be corrected and passed. My teacher, with the diamond eye, pointed them out one by one from the tip of his brush. Of old, Zhang Zishao went to Jingshan and theresolved

the meaning of ‘investigating things’ and ‘things being investigated.’ Later, because he contested in the sutra-lecture hall, he was banished far to Hengpu, and standing there leaning on his book, his twin cross-legged feet were hidden. He once said that the karmic cases the elder of Jingshan brought up were like a thousand gates and ten thousand doors, all thrown open atone

tread; it was no accident. My teacher’s compositions and preaching were not confined to the matter beneath the monk’s robe. Those who should be saved by the body of the great Da Luo immortal, to them he manifested the body of the great Da Luo immortal and preached the Dharma; those who should be saved by the body of the great general, to them he manifested the body of the

greatgeneral and preached the Dharma; those who should be saved by the body of the scholar, the graduate, the minister, the king, to them he manifested the body of the scholar, the graduate, the minister, the king, and preached the Dharma. Simply in this chronicle written at his death the preaching is without bound, such as the patriarchs of old rarely beheld with their eyes.
In my view, Confucius, wheeling round through the states and the ruts of his cart, means the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices — it is the Tathāgata’s
Chan. The self-cultivation and full realization of nature of Zisi and Mencius, knowing Heaven and establishing the mandate — it is thepatriarchs’ Chan.
My teacher, making himself a Buddha and a patriarch, did not depart from Confucius and Mencius. And I, a little one who learns Confucius andMencius, would I
dare abandon the Buddha and the patriarchs? Buddha and patriarch, Confucius and Mencius: though their practice of transformation be each in adifferent
quarter, how could their journey’s end be in a different place? Confucius and Mencius, when they take rebirth, must return to the Pure Land. And I,returning
to the Buddha, will in nothing abandon the Confucian. In the eastern land and in the western quarter, in every place and at every moment, I shall seeConfucius
and see the Buddha, and forever take refuge in the Immortal Ancestor. From this time on, for life after life, in fame, rank, riches, and honour Iwill
not contend to be first among men; in reading books and learning the Way I will not fall behind. The four rules of the Doctrine of the Mean, I strive forthem
yet cannot; the three warnings of the Analects, I hope to learn them. Just now the Hu comes and the Han comes; the body is in the midst of the greatdream,
and I would have all under heaven and above heaven truly hear these words. A verse says: ‘The Pure Land, mind alone — my heart longs for the west; theone
thread of Mount Ni, set upon coming east. East and west, coming and going, I rest upon Zisi and Mencius; whether I die young or live long, the body
iscultivated in the undivided womb.’ Again: ‘Thin soup and the three books are the true riches; the fish-trap and the rabbit-snare, nine turnings, win thespirit’s
flight. The household’s immortals and the world’s Buddhas hold no separate thought; in the end, the scholar’s cap is the very giving over of the robe.’
The Dharma-master Suhua (Master Ouyi, 1599-1655) made a ‘Verse and Preface
Expounding the Chronicle,’ saying: ‘In the summer of the jiaxu year (1634) I
lodged at the Huanzhu Hermitage in Wu and saw the chronicle of Old Man Han as
annotated by Zhu Baimin, and regretted that his comments still held much of
the Confucian scholar’s view and were not enough to know the state of a great
man. In the bingzi year (1636) I fell ill and entered Mount Jiuhua, where
all my hundred thoughts turned cold and my books were scattered, not one
remaining. In the spring of the xinmao year (1651) I wandered in a dream to
Changgan and saw again the chronicle of Old Man Han as narrated and commented
by Tan Saoyan (Fuzheng), and it was able, over the whole course of the great
affair, to verify the truth and examine it in detail, and to set forth fully
his spiritual power and the power of the Way. It had been gained during his
eastern travels through direct oral instruction, face to face, and was the
